m1159115017: The smallest, shallowest and coldest of the world's oceans, centered on the North Pole.
Surrounded by Eurasia and North America, bordered by the Bering Strait and the Greenland-Scotland Ridge.
Covered by sea ice most of the year, with satellite records showing a continuous decline in ice extent.
m1159115037: The southernmost waters of the World Ocean, encircling Antarctica south of 60°S latitude.
Its deepest point, surveyed in 2019 by the Five Deeps Expedition at over 7,400 m, has been proposed for the name Factorian Deep.
James Cook's voyages in the 1770s first proved that open water encircled the southern polar latitudes.
m1159115057: Separates the Americas from Africa and Europe, a divide that shaped the Age of Discovery and centuries of transatlantic trade.
The Norse were the first known people to cross it, but Columbus's 1492 voyage triggered the main wave of European exploration and colonisation.
Connects to the Arctic Ocean in the north, the Pacific in the southwest, and the Indian Ocean in the southeast.
m1159115079: The largest and deepest of Earth's oceans, stretching between Asia/Australia and the Americas.
Contains the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, the deepest known point on Earth at 10,928 m.
Includes major marginal seas such as the South China Sea, Sea of Japan and Coral Sea.
m1159115123: The third-largest of the world's oceanic divisions, bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east.
Geologically the youngest ocean, having formed as the Tethys Ocean fragmented around 20 million years ago.
It is the warmest of the oceans and strongly influences global climate through its interaction with the atmosphere.
m1159115171: A marginal sea between Europe and Asia, fed mainly by the Danube, Dnieper and Dniester rivers.
Connects to the Mediterranean via the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits.
Rimmed by the Pontic, Caucasus and Crimean Mountains, with Istanbul, Odesa and Sochi among its coastal cities.
m1159115197: A marginal sea of the western Pacific east of the Philippines, the largest sea in the world by surface area.
Enclosed by island arcs including the Ryukyus, Taiwan, the Philippines and the Marianas.
Home to the Philippine Trench and the Mariana Trench, containing the deepest point on Earth.
m1159117285: The world's largest coral reef system, made up of over 2,900 reefs and 900 islands off Queensland, Australia.
Built by billions of tiny coral polyps, it is the largest structure on Earth made by living organisms and visible from space.
Has lost more than half its coral cover since 1985 due to bleaching, pollution and cyclone damage.
Long used by Aboriginal Australian and Torres Strait Islander peoples and now a major tourism draw.
m1159115233: A marginal sea of the South Pacific separating Australia and New Zealand.
Named after Dutch explorer Abel Tasman, the first known European to cross it, in 1642.
Later extensively navigated by James Cook during his 1770s voyages of exploration.
m1159115253: The northeastern part of the Indian Ocean, lying between the Indian subcontinent and the Indochinese Peninsula.
Receives major rivers including the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Irrawaddy.
Its coast includes the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest.
m1159115273: A marginal sea of the western Pacific bounded by China, the Indochinese Peninsula and the Philippines.
One of the world's busiest shipping routes, carrying over $3 trillion in trade in 2016.
Its scattered islands and reefs are subject to competing sovereignty claims by several countries.
m1159115343: A region of the northern Indian Ocean bounded by the Arabian Peninsula, Pakistan, India and Somalia.
The Straits of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb at its ends have linked Old World trade networks since the 3rd millennium BC.
Trade here was historically governed by seasonal monsoon winds.
m1159115359: An Arctic marginal sea north of Alaska and Canada's Northwest Territories, named after hydrographer Sir Francis Beaufort.
Receives the Mackenzie River and holds significant undersea oil and gas reserves discovered between the 1950s and 1980s.
Frozen most of the year, though the ice-free season has grown substantially due to Arctic climate change.
m1159115379: A sea of the North Atlantic bounded by the Greater and Lesser Antilles, South America, and Central America.
Its deepest point, the Cayman Trough, reaches nearly 7,700 m below sea level.
Home to the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the world's second-largest barrier reef system.
m1159115399: A marginal sea of the Atlantic bounded by the US Gulf Coast, Mexico and Cuba, connected to the Atlantic via the Straits of Florida and to the Caribbean via the Yucatán Channel.
One of the world's largest offshore petroleum production regions, supplying 14% of US crude oil output.
Its moisture drives severe weather across the US, including storms in Tornado Alley.
m1159115419: An arm of the North Atlantic between the Labrador Peninsula and Greenland, connecting to Baffin Bay via the Davis Strait.
Formed as the North American and Greenland plates separated starting about 60 million years ago.
A major source of North Atlantic Deep Water, a cold water mass that circulates at great ocean depths.
m1159115441: A large inland sea of saltwater in northeastern Canada, politically part of Nunavut though bordered by Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba.
Connects to the Atlantic via the Hudson Strait and to the Arctic Ocean via the Foxe Channel.
Its drainage basin extends south into several U.S. states, including Minnesota and Montana.
Its southern arm is known as James Bay.
m1159115461: The world's largest inland body of water, an endorheic basin situated between the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Iranian Plateau.
Bordered by Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan, and fed mainly by the Volga, Europe's longest river.
Its name comes from the ancient Caspi people who once lived along its shores.
m1159115483: An Arctic marginal sea between Baffin Island and Greenland, connected to the Atlantic via the Davis Strait.
Ice-covered most of the year, except for a summer polynya called the North Water that supports most of its marine life.
m1159115503: An arm of the Pacific along Alaska's southern coast, lined with glaciers including the Malaspina and Bering glaciers.
Home to Lituya Bay, site of the largest tsunami ever recorded.
Kept ice-free year-round by the warm North Pacific Current.
m1159115521: An inlet of the Indian Ocean between the Arabian Peninsula and Africa, connected via the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait.
Lies above the Red Sea Rift, part of the Great Rift Valley, and leads north to the Suez Canal.
Mostly shallow, with extensive shelves supporting over 1,000 invertebrate species and 200 types of coral.
m1159115541: A marginal sea of the northwestern Pacific, bounded by Kamchatka, the Kuril Islands, Hokkaido and Sakhalin.
Named after the port of Okhotsk, itself named for the Okhota River.
m1159115579: A part of the Southern Ocean off Antarctica, bounded by Coats Land and the Antarctic Peninsula.
Much of its southern part is covered by the massive Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf.
Famed for having some of the clearest water of any sea, and for trapping Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance in its ice.
m1159115597: An extension of the Indian Ocean between the Arabian Peninsula and Iran, connected to the Gulf of Oman via the Strait of Hormuz.
Formed as the Persian Gulf Basin flooded when sea levels rose after the last glacial period.
Known for extensive fishing grounds and pearl oyster beds, though industrialization and oil spills have damaged its ecology.
m1159115635: Bordered by the Sulu Archipelago, Mindanao, the Sangihe Islands and Sulawesi.
Formed from an ancient ocean basin roughly 42 million years ago.
Opens into the Java Sea through the Makassar Strait.
m1159115655: Separated from the South China Sea by Palawan and from the Celebes Sea by the Sulu Archipelago.
Home to the Tubbataha Reef, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
m1159115675: Lies northwest of Norway between the North Sea and Greenland Sea, separated from the Atlantic by a ridge between Iceland and the Faroe Islands.
Mostly deep ocean floor rather than continental shelf, averaging about two kilometres deep.
Kept ice-free year-round by the warm North Atlantic Current, unlike the neighbouring Arctic seas.
m1159115695: A body of water between Greenland, Svalbard and the Norwegian Sea, sometimes classed within the Arctic Ocean.
A major breeding ground for harp and hooded seals, hunted here for over 200 years.
m1159115717: One of four seas surrounding Indonesia's Maluku Islands, connected to the Pacific Ocean and encircled by hundreds of islands including Timor.
Stretches about 1,000 km east to west and 500 km north to south.
m1159115729: A strait in the western Pacific between Luzon in the Philippines and Taiwan, linking the Philippine Sea to the South China Sea.
An important migratory corridor for seabirds and marine mammals, including humpback whales, fed by nutrient-rich Kuroshio Current water.
Distinct from the shallower Taiwan Strait between Taiwan and the Chinese mainland.
m1159115749: A gulf of the northeast Atlantic along the coasts of France and Spain, known for rough seas and reaching depths over 4,700 m.
m1159115771: An arm of the Indian Ocean between Madagascar and Mozambique, about 1,700 km long.
The warm Mozambique Current flows southward through it into the Agulhas Current off southern Africa.
m1159115791: Northeasternmost part of the tropical Atlantic Ocean, between Gabon and Liberia.
Contains Null Island, the notional point where the Equator meets the Prime Meridian.
Receives the Niger and Volta rivers, with a coastline including the Bight of Benin and Bight of Bonny.
m1159115811: A sea at the northern edge of the Southern Ocean, bounded by the Drake Passage and the Scotia Arc island system.
Named after the expedition ship Scotia; many icebergs melt in its waters.
m1159115831: An arm of the Atlantic enclosed by Scandinavia and the North/Central European Plain, and the world's largest brackish water basin.
Drains through the Danish Straits into the Kattegat, with limited exchange with the open Atlantic.
Connected artificially to the White Sea and, via the Kiel Canal, to the North Sea.
m1159115861: A shallow marginal sea of the Arctic Ocean, divided between Norwegian and Russian waters.
Bordered by the Kola Peninsula, Svalbard, Franz Josef Land and Novaya Zemlya.
Warming faster than much of the Arctic, a process sometimes called 'Atlantification'.
m1159115879: Lies between Great Britain, Scandinavia and continental Europe, connecting to the Atlantic via the English Channel and the Norwegian Sea.
A major fishery and shipping route, and a significant source of offshore wind and oil and gas.
Was the centre of the Vikings' rise and later a focus of Hanseatic, Dutch and British competition for trade and sea power.
m1159115891: A major inlet between South Wales and South West England, extending from the Severn Estuary to the Atlantic.
Formerly known as the Severn Sea, a name still used in Welsh and Cornish.
m1159115921: A sheltered part of the North Atlantic off northwest Scotland, between the mainland/Inner Hebrides and the Outer Hebrides.
Designated a Marine Protected Area in 2020 to protect basking sharks and minke whales.
m1159115935: Separates the islands of Ireland, the Isle of Man and Great Britain.
Connects to the Celtic Sea via St George's Channel and to Scotland's inner seas via the North Channel.
Carries major passenger and freight traffic between Great Britain and Ireland.
m1159115959: A shallow sea on the Sunda Shelf between Borneo, Java, Sumatra and Sulawesi in Indonesia.
Linked to the South China Sea via the Karimata Strait, and sometimes classed as part of the Indian Ocean.
m1159115987: A marginal sea of the northeastern Indian Ocean, bounded by Myanmar and Thailand and separated from the Bay of Bengal by the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Historically known as the Burma Sea; its coral reefs and islands are popular tourist destinations.
Its fishing and tourism infrastructure was severely damaged by the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami.
m1159115999: A marginal sea of the western Pacific between mainland China and the Korean Peninsula, also known as the North Sea.
Forms the northwestern extension of the East China Sea.
m1159116027: A marginal sea of the western Pacific off eastern China, bounded by Japan's Kyushu, the Ryukyu Islands and Taiwan.
Mostly shallow, averaging 350 m deep, with the Okinawa Trough reaching 2,716 m.
Connects to the Sea of Japan, South China Sea and Philippine Sea through several straits.
m1159116037: A marginal sea of the Arctic Ocean between Wrangel Island, Russia and Point Barrow, Alaska.
Connected to the Pacific Ocean via the Bering Strait at its southern limit.
m1159116059: A bay in the southern Gulf of Mexico, forming the north side of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, bordered by three Mexican states.
m1159116081: Lies southeast of the Malay Archipelago, overlying the continental shelf between Australia and Western New Guinea.
Part of the western Pacific Ocean separating Indonesia from Australia.
m1159116101: A shallow sea in the Indian Ocean between Timor and Australia, with the deep Sunda Trench marking its boundary with Asia.
Prone to earthquakes, tsunamis and cyclones due to its location on the Ring of Fire.
Contains significant hydrocarbon reserves that led to international disputes over the Timor Sea Treaty.
m1159116123: A shallow inlet of the South China Sea bounded by Mainland Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula.
Surrounded by Thailand, Cambodia and the Mekong Delta region of Vietnam.
m1159116143: A warm sea bordering India, the Maldives and Sri Lanka, rich in marine biodiversity.
Named after the Laccadive (Lakshadweep) Islands in its northwest.
m1159116169: A marginal sea along the west side of the Antarctic Peninsula, named after Russian navigator Fabian von Bellingshausen, who explored it in 1821.
Reaches a maximum depth of about 4.5 km and connects to the Amundsen Sea to the west.
m1159116181: An arm of the Southern Ocean off Marie Byrd Land in western Antarctica, named after explorer Roald Amundsen.
Mostly ice-covered, fed by the Thwaites Ice Tongue draining part of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet.
m1159116205: Connects the Labrador Sea to Baffin Bay between Greenland and Baffin Island.
Named after English explorer John Davis, who searched for the Northwest Passage; later used for whale hunting.
m1159116231: A marginal sea of the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia, between the Barents Sea and the Laptev Sea.
Ice-bound for all but about two months a year, yet holds significant undeveloped oil and gas reserves.
m1159116253: A marginal sea of the Arctic Ocean between Siberia's Taymyr Peninsula and the New Siberian Islands.
Frozen most of the year, with low salinity and shallow depths mostly under 50 metres.
Named after Russian explorers Dmitry and Khariton Laptev.
m1159116269: A stretch of water between Cape Horn, Chile and Antarctica's South Shetland Islands, linking the Atlantic and Pacific.
One of the most treacherous voyages for ships, with waves regularly topping 40 feet due to the unimpeded Antarctic Circumpolar Current.
As the narrowest choke point around Antarctica, it strongly shapes global ocean circulation and climate.
m1159116315: A large open gulf off the southern coast of mainland Australia, generally considered part of the Indian Ocean.
Formed about 50 million years ago when Gondwana broke apart, separating Australia from Antarctica.
Known for whale-watching along its cliff-lined coastline.
m1159116333: A deepwater gulf of the Indian Ocean linking the Red Sea, via the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, to the Arabian Sea.
Widening by about 15 mm a year due to tectonic activity along the Aden Ridge.
Important to ancient Greek trade and part of the Suez Canal shipping route.
m1159116359: A gulf of the Indian Ocean connecting the Arabian Sea to the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf.
Borders Iran and Pakistan to the north, Oman to the south, and the UAE to the west.
m1159116377: Part of the Mediterranean off Italy's western coast, named after the ancient Tyrrhenian people, identified with the Etruscans.
m1159116395: A southern inlet of the Barents Sea on Russia's northwest coast, entirely within Russian internal waters.
Historically Russia's main center of international maritime trade before becoming a key Soviet naval base.
One of four seas named after a common color, alongside the Black, Red and Yellow seas.
m1159116409: Shallowest sea in the world, with depths ranging from just 0.9 to 14 metres.
Connected to the Black Sea by the narrow Strait of Kerch.
Fed mainly by the Don and Kuban rivers, giving it low salinity and high fish productivity.
m1159116431: A bay at the southern end of Hudson Bay, bordered by Quebec and Ontario, with its waters and islands in Nunavut.
Extensively modified by dams for major hydroelectric projects, while remaining the last part of Hudson Bay to freeze and the first to thaw.
m1159116451: A sea off northern Australia, bounded by Cape York Peninsula and Arnhem Land.
Was dry land connecting Australia to New Guinea during the last ice age, when sea levels were far lower.
Hosts a submerged coral reef province discovered only recently.
m1159116479: A marginal sea of the Pacific separating Mexico's Baja California peninsula from the mainland, also called the Sea of Cortés.
One of the most ecologically diverse seas on Earth, home to over 5,000 species of micro-invertebrates, with parts listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
m1159116501: A strait in Nunavut linking the Atlantic and Labrador Sea to Hudson Bay, between Baffin Island and Quebec's Nunavik.
Named after English explorer Henry Hudson, who sailed it in 1610 aboard the ship Discovery.
m1159116517: The easternmost arm of the Baltic Sea, lying between Finland and Estonia, with Saint Petersburg at its eastern end.
The river Neva drains into it at Saint Petersburg, making it a strategically important seaway for Russia.
Helsinki and Tallinn, on opposite shores, have been proposed to be linked by an undersea tunnel beneath the gulf.
m1159116535: An arm of the Atlantic Ocean separating southern England from northern France, the world's busiest shipping area.
Narrows to just 34 km wide at the Strait of Dover, its northeastern end linking to the North Sea.
Helped the United Kingdom resist invasion, including during the Napoleonic Wars and World War II.
m1159116553: A large inlet of the Caribbean Sea along Mexico, Belize, Guatemala and Honduras.
Lined by the Belize Barrier Reef, part of the second-largest coral reef system in the world.
Was a haunt of the pirate Blackbeard during the winter of 1717-18.
m1159116571: A wide Mediterranean embayment along the coasts of Catalonia, Languedoc-Roussillon and Provence.
Known for the cold, blustery Mistral and Tramontane winds.
m1159116589: An arm of the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Finland, divided into the Bothnian Sea and Bothnian Bay.
The Åland Islands lie at its mouth.
m1159116607: The northernmost arm of the Mediterranean Sea, separating the Italian Peninsula from the Balkans.
Contains more than 1,300 islands, mostly along its eastern coast.
Its waters are less saline than the rest of the Mediterranean because it collects about a third of the sea's fresh water inflow.
m1159116625: A strait between the Florida Keys and Cuba, connecting the Gulf of Mexico to the Atlantic Ocean.
Carries the Florida Current, the beginning of the Gulf Stream.
m1159116661: An Arctic sea route through Canada's Arctic Archipelago linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
First fully navigated by ship in 1903-1906 by Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen, after centuries of failed European attempts.
Canada claims it as internal waters while the US and others argue it is an international strait.
m1159116697: An elongated bay of the Mediterranean Sea between southern Italy, Albania and western Greece.
Home to Calypso Deep, the deepest point in the Mediterranean at 5,109 m.
One of the most seismically active maritime areas in the world.
m1159116715: Connects the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean via the St. Lawrence River.
Fringed by Quebec, the Maritime provinces and Newfoundland, plus France's Saint-Pierre and Miquelon.
m1159116731: Lies in the western Pacific between the Indonesian islands of Sulawesi, Halmahera and the Sula Islands.
Overlies the Molucca Sea Plate, a microplate being subducted in two opposite directions, making the sea prone to earthquakes.
m1159116735: A sea in the southwestern Pacific northeast of New Guinea and south of the Bismarck Archipelago, within Papua New Guinea's waters.
m1159116767: A sea within the Pacific Ocean between Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands.
The site of major naval battles during World War II.
m1159116787: A gulf at the northwestern South China Sea, off northern Vietnam and South China.
Known in Chinese sources as Beibu Wan, or 'Northern Gulf'.
m1159116797: Highest tidal range in the world, averaging about 16 m due to tidal resonance in its funnel-shaped basin.
About 100 billion tonnes of water flow in and out every half-day tidal cycle, twice the combined flow of the world's rivers.
Lies between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, an arm of the Gulf of Maine.
m1159116815: An estuary formed by the Uruguay and Paraná rivers meeting between Argentina and Uruguay before reaching the Atlantic.
If classified as a river, it is the widest in the world, reaching 220 km across at its mouth.
Its shores hold the port cities of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, cradle of tango culture.
m1159116835: A narrow strait between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra linking the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
The busiest shipping strait in the world, carrying about a quarter of global traded goods including oil and coal.
Historically fought over by powers such as the Srivijaya empire, the Malacca Sultanate and the British Straits Settlements.
m1159116861: A strait between the Strait of Malacca and the South China Sea, bordered by Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
One of the busiest waterways in the world, with about 2,000 merchant ships passing through daily.
m1159116881: A strait between Borneo and Sulawesi in Indonesia, linking the Celebes Sea to the Java Sea.
An important regional shipping route, with ports including Makassar and Balikpapan.
m1159116897: A small sea between the Indonesian islands of Buru and Seram, once known as the spice-rich South Moluccas.
A historically busy shipping route for nutmeg, cloves and peppercorns, and a tectonically active area.
m1159116927: Separates Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, three of Japan's four main islands, linking the Pacific Ocean to the Sea of Japan.
Was the main transport link between the Kansai and Kyushu regions before the San'yo Main Line was built.
Connected by the Honshu-Shikoku Bridge Project since the 1980s, including the Great Seto Bridge.
m1159116947: A strait separating Taiwan from mainland China, connecting the South China Sea to the East China Sea.
Narrows to about 126 km wide at its narrowest point.
m1159116967: A 180-mile inlet stretching from the Gulf of Alaska to Anchorage, branching into the Knik and Turnagain arms.
Alaska's most populated watershed, fed by glacial rivers and home to the active volcano Mount Redoubt.
m1159116991: The easternmost arm of the Bering Sea in Southwest Alaska, fed by rivers including the Nushagak and Kvichak.
Home to some of the highest tides in the world, exceeding 10 m in its upper reaches.
One of the most dangerous regions for large vessels due to shoals and strong winds.
m1159117021: Bounded by Cape Cod in Massachusetts and Cape Sable Island in Nova Scotia.
Includes Massachusetts Bay, Penobscot Bay and the Bay of Fundy as arms of the gulf.
Named after the English colonial Province of Maine.
m1159117043: The largest estuary in the United States, separated from the Atlantic by the Delmarva Peninsula.
More than 150 rivers and streams feed its drainage basin, spanning six states and Washington, D.C.
Stretches about 200 miles from the Susquehanna River to the Atlantic Ocean.
m1159117067: A narrow strait connecting the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea, separating Europe from Africa.
Narrows to just 14 km between Spain and Morocco, crossed by ferry in as little as 35 minutes.
Lies in the territorial waters of Morocco, Spain and the British territory of Gibraltar.
m1159117105: A small Mediterranean sea between Spain's mainland and the Balearic Islands, fed by the Ebro River.
m1159117123: An arm of the Mediterranean between Greece and Turkey, connected north to the Sea of Marmara and Black Sea via the Dardanelles and Bosphorus.
Cradle of Ancient Greek civilisation, whose many islands - including Crete, Rhodes and the Cyclades - linked Europe and Asia.
Later passed through Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman control before modern Greece and Turkey emerged on its shores.
m1159117135: A large, shallow bay of the Laccadive Sea between southeastern India and western Sri Lanka.
Separated from Palk Bay to the north by the chain of islets known as Adam's Bridge.
Home to the dugong, or sea cow.
m1159117171: A gulf on China's east coast, the innermost extension of the Yellow Sea, enclosed by four Chinese provinces/municipalities.
Declared part of China's inland waters in 1958, it lies close to Beijing and Tianjin and is heavily trafficked by shipping.
m1159117185: Lies between the Kutch and Saurashtra peninsulas in India's Gujarat state, opening toward the Arabian Sea.
Its southern coast, rich in marine life, includes protected parks and sanctuaries amid islands, mud flats and coral reefs.
Major shipping harbours including Kandla line its northern shore.
m1159117203: A gulf of the Pacific off southern Panama, where the Panama Canal links to the Pacific side.
Panama City sits on its shore, with the 200-plus-island Pearl Islands archipelago nearby.
m1159117223: Lies in Canada's Northwest Territories, explored by Roald Amundsen between 1903 and 1906.
Marks the western end of the Northwest Passage between the Atlantic and Pacific.
m1159117301: A strait between Mexico and Cuba connecting the Yucatán Basin of the Caribbean Sea with the Gulf of Mexico.
Reaches nearly 2,800 m deep near the Cuban coast.
m1159117319: A marginal sea of the North Pacific, forming the divide between Eurasia and the Americas along with the Bering Strait.
Named after Vitus Bering, the Danish-born Russian navigator who first explored it systematically in 1728.
Bordered by Alaska, the Russian Far East, the Kamchatka Peninsula and the Aleutian Islands.
m1159117337: A marginal sea of the Arctic Ocean between the New Siberian Islands and Wrangel Island.
One of the least studied Arctic seas, with shallow depths, low salinity and heavy ice cover most of the year.
Historically inhabited by Yukaghir, Chukchi, Even and Evenk peoples.
m1159117355: A body of water in the Arctic Ocean between Canada's Ellesmere Island and Greenland.
Covered year-round by the thickest sea ice in the Arctic Ocean, up to 15 m thick.
Named after Robert Todd Lincoln during an 1881-1884 US Arctic expedition.
m1159117373: A strait separating Tasmania from mainland Australia, formed about 8,000 years ago by rising sea levels.
Named after English explorer George Bass, who helped prove Tasmania was an island.
m1159117579: The southernmost passable body of water on Earth, in Antarctica, discovered by Captain James Clark Ross in 1841.
Serves as the resupply route for McMurdo Station via ice runways and icebreaker-opened shipping channels.
m1159117723: A strait connecting the North Sea and the Kattegat, running between Denmark, Norway and Sweden.
One of the busiest shipping routes in the world and historically the only access to the Baltic Sea before the Eider Canal was built in 1784.
Held strategic importance for Germany in both World Wars.
m1159117781: Norway's longest and deepest fjord, nicknamed the 'King of the Fjords', stretching 205 km inland in Western Norway.
m1159117797: Norway's third-longest fjord, stretching 130 km through Trøndelag county past the city of Trondheim.
Has the largest biological production of any Norwegian fjord, with deep-water corals discovered near Trondheim.
Was an important waterway during the Viking Age and remains so today.
m1159117819: A sea between Denmark and Sweden where the Baltic Sea drains through the Danish Straits.
Shallow and dangerous to navigate due to sandy reefs and shifting currents; Gothenburg and Aarhus are its largest ports.
m1159117827: A bay on India's Arabian Sea coast in Gujarat, also known as the Gulf of Cambay, fed by the Narmada, Tapti, Mahi and Sabarmati rivers.
Separates the Kathiawar Peninsula from southeastern Gujarat.
m1159117845: A strait between Tamil Nadu, India and Mannar Island, Sri Lanka, linking the Bay of Bengal to the Laccadive Sea.
Bordered by the chain of islets and shoals known as Ram Setu, or Adam's Bridge.
m1159117919: Connects the Sea of Japan with the Pacific Ocean between Honshu and Hokkaido.
The Seikan Tunnel passes beneath it at its narrowest point, about 19.5 km.
Japan limits its territorial waters here to three nautical miles to allow US nuclear-armed vessels through.
m1159117937: Divides Russia's Sakhalin Island from the Asian mainland, connecting the Sea of Okhotsk to the Sea of Japan.
Extremely shallow at its narrowest point, only about 4 m deep.
m1159117955: A UNESCO World Heritage Site in Western Australia known for its stromatolites, some of the oldest life forms on Earth.
Home to one of the largest and most diverse seagrass beds in the world and a large population of dugongs.
m1159117973: A gulf on Tunisia's east coast in the Mediterranean, also known as the Lesser Syrtis, spanning from Sfax to Djerba.
Known for unusually large tides for the Mediterranean and for sponge and tuna fisheries at its ports.
m1159118151: A large Pacific Ocean inlet between Ecuador and Peru, named after the city of Guayaquil.
Underlain by active geological faults capable of generating dangerous earthquakes.
m1159118231: A strait separating Russia's Sakhalin Island from Japan's Hokkaido, linking the Sea of Japan with the Sea of Okhotsk.
Named after French naval officer Jean-François de Galaup, comte de Lapérouse, who explored it in 1787.
Known in Japan as the Sōya Strait.
m1159118281: Separates New Zealand's North and South Islands, connecting the Tasman Sea to the South Pacific.
Named after James Cook, the first European to sail through it, in 1770.
Known for strong, unpredictable tidal flows and several historic shipwrecks.
m1159118303: A strait between Australia's Cape York Peninsula and Papua New Guinea, also known as Zenadh Kes.
Named after Spanish navigator Luís Vaz de Torres, who sailed through it in 1606.
m1159118329: Located on the southern coast of New Guinea, part of Papua New Guinea's coastline.
Receives the outflow of the Fly River, one of New Guinea's largest rivers.
m1159118365: A bay of the Baltic Sea between Latvia and Estonia, partly sheltered by Estonia's Saaremaa island.
Connects to the open Baltic mainly through the narrow Irbe Strait.
m1159118385: An intertidal zone in the southeastern North Sea, stretching along the Frisian Islands from the Netherlands to Denmark.
A vital breeding and migration habitat for birds; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009.
Historically prone to catastrophic floods, including the Saint Marcellus' floods of 1219 and 1362.
m1159118407: A Mediterranean gulf on Libya's northern coast, historically known as the Great Sirte or Greater Syrtis.
Named after the oil port of Sidra and the city of Sirte.
m1159118425: The southern part of the Aegean Sea, lying north of Crete and bounded by the Cyclades and Dodecanese islands.
Reaches depths of nearly 3,300 m off the northeastern coast of Crete.
Major ferry routes to Piraeus, Heraklion and the Dodecanese cross this sea.
m1159118439: An arm of the Mediterranean Sea off the northwest coast of Italy.
Thought to be named after the ancient Ligures people who once inhabited the region.
m1159118457: The westernmost part of the Mediterranean Sea, lying between Spain and Morocco/Algeria.
The Strait of Gibraltar, connecting the Mediterranean to the Atlantic, lies at its western end.
m1159118475: A bight within the Gulf of Guinea on West Africa's coast, bordering Nigeria, Benin and Ghana.
Its shores were historically a major embarkation point in the Atlantic slave trade, giving the nearby coast its old name, the Slave Coast.
m1159118493: A bight on the west-central African coast, at the easternmost part of the Gulf of Guinea.
Marks the point where Africa's coastline turns from a north-south to an east-west orientation.
m1159118537: A sound off the Gulf of Alaska on the Kenai Peninsula, home to the port of Valdez, terminus of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.
Contains numerous small islands and settlements including Cordova and Whittier.
m1159118553: A navigable sea route in southern Chile separating mainland South America from Tierra del Fuego.
Named after Ferdinand Magellan, whose 1520 expedition was the first European passage through it.
Shorter and more sheltered than the storm-prone Drake Passage around Cape Horn.
m1159118715: A sea along East Antarctica's coast between the West Ice Shelf and Shackleton Ice Shelf.
Discovered by the Australian Antarctic Expedition (1911-1914) and named for Captain John King Davis.
m1159118783: A funnel-shaped inlet of the East China Sea bordered by Zhejiang province and Shanghai.
Home to the Port of Ningbo-Zhoushan, the world's busiest port by cargo tonnage.
The Qiantang River flows into it at Hangzhou, giving the bay its alternate name.
m1159118835: Connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara, straddled by the city of Istanbul.
World's narrowest strait used for international navigation.
Forms one of the continental boundaries between Asia and Europe, separating Asia Minor from Thrace.
m1159118853: A strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean.
A major global chokepoint for shipping between Europe and Asia via the Suez Canal.
m1159119037: Connects the Great Lakes to the North Atlantic Ocean, flowing from Lake Ontario to the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Has the second-highest discharge of any river in North America, after the Mississippi.
Played a key role in Canadian history and the growth of Montreal and Quebec City.
m1159119095: A shallow, highly saline lagoon off the Caspian Sea in northwestern Turkmenistan.
Separated from the Caspian by a narrow rocky ridge through which seawater flows in, evaporating in its salt pans.
m1159119103: A gulf at the northern end of the Red Sea, west of the Sinai Peninsula, marking part of the boundary between Africa and Asia.
Leads to the Egyptian city of Suez and the entrance of the Suez Canal, making it a key maritime corridor.
m1159119119: A bay of the Arctic Ocean at the mouth of Russia's Ob River, considered the world's longest estuary.
Separates the Yamal Peninsula from the Gydan Peninsula in Russia's far north.
m1159119155: A narrow strait in northwestern Turkey linking the Sea of Marmara to the Aegean, forming part of the Asia-Europe boundary alongside the Bosphorus.
Site of the deadly Gallipoli campaign in World War I.
The first fixed crossing, the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge, opened in 2022.
m1159119181: A small inland sea entirely within Turkey, linking the Black Sea and Aegean Sea via the Bosporus and Dardanelles.
Separates Turkey's European and Asian sides.
Considered the smallest sea in the world, measuring roughly 280 by 80 km.
m1159119199: A gulf at the northern tip of the Red Sea, southeast of the Sinai Peninsula.
Its coastline is shared by Egypt, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.
m1159119215: A lake in northwestern Venezuela that, hydrologically, functions more like an estuary connected to the Gulf of Venezuela.
If counted as a lake, it would be South America's largest, and is among the oldest lakes on Earth at roughly 36 million years.
Rich in oil and gas; the surrounding area experiences the Catatumbo lightning, among the most frequent lightning activity on Earth.
m1159119235: Carries cold Arctic water south into the North Atlantic over the Denmark Strait cataract, the world's largest underwater waterfall.
m1159119247: A bay on the Gulf of Maine along the central Massachusetts coastline.
Boston, the largest city in Massachusetts, sits on its western shore.
m1159119271: The estuary outlet of the Delaware River between the states of Delaware and New Jersey.
A designated Ramsar Wetland of International Importance and a major breeding ground for horseshoe crabs.
Crossed by the Cape May-Lewes Ferry.
m1159119293: A tidal estuary of the Atlantic lying between Connecticut and Long Island, New York.
Forms part of the Intracoastal Waterway, stretching from the East River to Block Island Sound.
m1159119471: An estuary in southeastern Louisiana, despite its name, connecting to the Gulf of Mexico through the Rigolets strait.
Named in 1699 by French explorer Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville after a minister of Louis XIV.
Forms the core of the Pontchartrain Basin, one of the largest wetland systems on the Gulf Coast.
m1159120073: Lies north of Bali and south of Kangean Island, forming the southwestern part of the Flores Sea.
The Madura Strait opens into it from the west.
m1159120109: A regional sea in eastern Indonesia between Halmahera and the Pacific, part of the Australasian Mediterranean Sea.
Three deep bays - Weda, Buli and Kao - cut into Halmahera island's coast, giving it four large peninsulas.
m1159120167: Bounded to the north by Sulawesi and to the south by the islands of Flores and Sumbawa in Indonesia.
Lies within the Coral Triangle, a global centre of marine biodiversity among Indonesia's seas.
m1159120183: A small sea in the Philippines separating Luzon from the Visayas.
Its southern part is nicknamed 'the Galápagos of Asia' for its isolation and biodiversity.
m1159120253: A sea between the Visayas and Mindanao in the Philippines, also called the Mindanao Sea.
Connects to the Philippine Sea, Camotes Sea and Sulu Sea through several straits.
m1159120401: Surrounded by the Philippine islands of Masbate, Panay, Leyte, Cebu and Negros.
A major fishing ground for sardines, mackerel and herring, with an annual closed season to protect stocks.
Connects to the Sibuyan Sea, Samar Sea, Guimaras Strait and Camotes Sea.
m1159120417: A small sea within Indonesia, named for Savu Island, bounded by Timor, Flores, Sumba and Rote.
Reaches depths of about 3,500 m despite its modest size.
m1159120609: A strait separating Zealand (Denmark) from Scania (Sweden), one of four waterways linking the Baltic to the Atlantic.
Crossed by the Øresund Bridge since 2000, connecting Copenhagen and Malmö in a shared metropolitan region of nearly 4 million.
Formed about 8,500 years ago when rising seas opened the modern salt-water Baltic Sea.
m1159120667: A region of the Atlantic Ocean bounded by four currents forming the North Atlantic Gyre, and the only named sea without land boundaries.
Known for its distinctive brown Sargassum seaweed and unusually calm, clear blue water.
Bermuda lies near its western fringe.
m1159120685: A tidal estuary in California that gives its name to the San Francisco Bay Area, dominated by San Francisco, San Jose and Oakland.
Drains about 40% of California's water via the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers before meeting the Pacific through the Golden Gate strait.
A Ramsar Wetland of International Importance since 2013, with the Port of Oakland among the busiest on the US west coast.
m1159120759: A marginal sea of the Pacific between British Columbia and Washington state, including the Strait of Georgia and Puget Sound.
Partially sheltered from the open Pacific by Vancouver Island and the Olympic Peninsula.
Anchored by Vancouver to the north and Seattle to the south, home to 8.76 million people.
m1159120779: A large bay of the Bering Sea in far northeastern Siberia.
One of the easternmost bays in Russia, opening onto the Bering Sea close to Alaska.
m1159115321: An intercontinental sea almost entirely enclosed by land between Europe, Asia and Africa, linked to the Atlantic only through the narrow Strait of Gibraltar.
Also connects to the Black Sea via the Bosporus and to the Red Sea via the Suez Canal.
Includes marginal seas such as the Aegean, Adriatic, Tyrrhenian and Marmara.
Around 5.9 million years ago it was cut off from the Atlantic and largely dried up during the Messinian salinity crisis, before being refilled by the Zanclean flood.
m1159115615: A deep bay of the Southern Ocean and the southernmost sea on Earth, named after explorer James Clark Ross.
Covered by the Ross Ice Shelf in its southernmost part, about 200 miles from the South Pole.
Supports a rich marine ecosystem fed by nutrient-laden circumpolar deep water.
m1159115219: A marginal sea of the South Pacific off northeastern Australia, named for its numerous islands and reefs.
Contains the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest reef system and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981.
Site of the Battle of the Coral Sea, a major World War II naval confrontation between Japan and the Allies.
m1159115305: A marginal sea between the Japanese archipelago, Sakhalin, the Korean Peninsula and the Russian Far East.
Nearly fully enclosed, giving it almost no tides, similar to the Mediterranean Sea.
Elevated dissolved oxygen levels make it highly productive for fishing.
m1159116907: A sea passage between the Korean Peninsula and Japan, connecting the East China Sea, Yellow Sea and Sea of Japan.
Split by Tsushima Island into western and eastern channels; a proposed undersea tunnel would link Japan and Korea.
r1159102343: The easternmost of Spain's Canary Islands, about 125 km off the African coast.
Known for the volcanic Timanfaya National Park and designated a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 1993.
Named after Genoese navigator Lancelotto Malocello, who first charted it.
r1159102345: A Tanzanian island in the Zanzibar Archipelago, part of the Swahili Coast in the Indian Ocean.
r1159102347: The largest island of Seychelles, home to the capital Victoria and about 86% of the country's population.
Named after Bertrand-François Mahé de La Bourdonnais, an 18th-century French colonial governor.
r1159102351: Lies in the Mozambique Channel between Madagascar and the African mainland.
A French overseas department and part of the eurozone, among the most densely populated territories in the region.
Comprises a main island, Grande-Terre, and a smaller island, Petite-Terre.
r1159102353: An autonomous volcanic island in the Comoros archipelago in the southwestern Indian Ocean.
Historically also known in English as Johanna; its chief town is Mutsamudu.
r1159102355: An island off the coast of Tanzania, the main island of the Mafia Archipelago, administratively separate from Zanzibar.
Its economy relies on fishing and subsistence farming, with growing tourism from scuba divers and birdwatchers.
r1159102757: One of Indonesia's Lesser Sunda Islands, named by Portuguese explorers for its flowers.
Lies near Komodo and Rinca islands, home to the Komodo dragon.
r1159102361: An island in the Azores whose volcano, Ponta do Pico, is the highest mountain in Portugal.
Known as the 'Black Island' for its volcanic soil, which nourishes UNESCO-listed vineyards.
The youngest and second-largest island in the Azores, formed around 300,000 years ago.
r1159102363: A volcanic island in Portugal's Azores archipelago, home to Angra do Heroísmo, the archipelago's oldest city and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Hosts a major Portuguese Air Force base with a US Air Force detachment.
r1159102367: An island in Cape Verde's Sotavento group, reaching the archipelago's highest point at its active volcano, Pico do Fogo.
r1159102371: The northwesternmost and second-largest island of Cape Verde, part of the Barlavento Islands group.
r1159102373: One of Cape Verde's sandy eastern islands, known for white sand beaches and over 350 days of sunshine a year.
Hosts the second-largest rookery for Caretta (loggerhead) turtles in Cape Verde, the world's largest nesting aggregation for the species.
r1159102375: The third largest island of Cape Verde, a desert-like island known for its beaches and sea turtles.
The easternmost Cape Verde island, closest to the African mainland.
r1159102379: Second-largest of Spain's Canary Islands, located about 97 km off North Africa.
Geologically the oldest island in the Canary archipelago; declared a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2009.
r1159102381: A volcanic island in the Indian Ocean, part of the Mascarene Islands near Mauritius and Madagascar.
Was uninhabited until French colonization in the 17th century, which brought a plantation economy built on enslaved African labor.
As a French overseas department, it is part of the European Union and the eurozone.
r1159102383: The southernmost and westernmost of Spain's Canary Islands, nicknamed "Meridian Island".
The second-smallest of the eight inhabited Canary Islands, with its capital at Valverde.
r1159102385: The northwesternmost of Spain's Canary Islands, home to the Caldera de Taburiente National Park.
Gave the word 'caldera' to geology, after 19th-century geologist Leopold von Buch studied its volcanic crater.
Its Roque de los Muchachos is the second-highest peak in the Canaries after Tenerife's Teide.
r1159102393: A remote, uninhabited Canadian Arctic island, the westernmost of the Queen Elizabeth Islands.
Historically icebound year-round, making it one of the least accessible parts of Canada.
First sighted by Europeans in 1853 during the Edward Belcher expedition.
r1159102403: An Arctic Archipelago island in Nunavut, Canada's 15th-largest island, with its sole community at Gjoa Haven.
Visited and wintered over by several polar explorers searching for the Northwest Passage.
r1159102407: An uninhabited island in Canada's Arctic Archipelago, part of Nunavut, separated from neighboring islands by several straits and channels.
Canada's twelfth-largest island, home to the seasonal Arctic Watch Lodge.
r1159102433: Atoll capital of Kiribati in the central Pacific's Micronesia region.
Site of the Battle of Tarawa during World War II.
South Tarawa holds about half the country's entire population.
r1159102435: A solitary raised coral island of Kiribati, formerly known as Ocean Island, the westernmost point of the country.
One of the Pacific's important phosphate-rich elevated islands, along with Nauru and Makatea.
r1730070385: A group of 52 coral islets forming the smallest of Tokelau's three atolls, in the south Pacific.
The northernmost territory under New Zealand sovereignty.
r1159102529: The southernmost island of the Kuril Islands, under Russian administration since the end of World War II.
Claimed by Japan as part of its "Northern Territories".
r1159102533: An island off the Kamchatka Peninsula in the Bering Sea.
r1159102543: The largest island of Cape Verde, home to half the nation's population and its capital, Praia.
Its town of Ribeira Grande, founded in 1462, was the first European settlement in the islands and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
r1159102545: The largest and most populous island of Portugal's Azores archipelago, nicknamed 'The Green Island'.
Home to Ponta Delgada, the Azores' largest city.
r1159102547: The largest island of Comoros, made up of two shield volcanoes including Mount Karthala, the country's highest point.
Home to the national capital, Moroni, and most of its population is of the Comorian ethnic group.
r1159102555: Located in the Bering Sea, closer to Russia and Asia than to mainland Alaska.
Thought to be one of the last exposed remnants of the Pleistocene land bridge between Asia and North America.
Jointly owned by the Siberian Yupik villages of Gambell and Savoonga.
r1159102561: A sparsely populated island in Quebec, Canada, within the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Separated from mainland Quebec by the Jacques Cartier and Honguedo straits.
r1159102603: A 56-km quartzite scarp in South Africa running through Johannesburg, named "white water ridge" in Afrikaans for its waterfalls.
Its gold deposits gave the South African currency, the rand, its name in 1961.
Forms a continental divide, with runoff draining to both the Indian and Atlantic Oceans.
r1159102607: A mountain range in Utah forming the western edge of the Rocky Mountains and eastern edge of the Great Basin.
Its name comes from the Ute language, meaning roughly 'mountain pass' or 'low pass over high range'.
r1730070733: Straddles the border between Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with permanently snow-capped and glaciated peaks.
One of the sources of the Nile, historically linked by European explorers to Ptolemy's legendary 'Mountains of the Moon'.
r1159102615: A Moroccan mountain range, the northernmost and second highest of the country's three Atlas chains.
Separated from the High Atlas by the Moulouya and Um Er-Rbiâ rivers.
Native habitat of the Barbary macaque.
r1730070755: The largest peninsula in Costa Rica, on the Pacific coast, known for its beaches and tourism.
Home to Nicoya, one of the oldest settlements in Costa Rica.
r1159102625: A vast salt pan in Botswana's savanna, one of the largest salt flats in the world, remnant of the long-vanished Lake Makgadikgadi.
Human mitochondrial DNA studies suggest modern Homo sapiens may have begun evolving in this region around 200,000 years ago, when it was a fertile lake-studded landscape.
r1730070763: A large endorheic salt pan in northern Namibia, the centerpiece of Etosha National Park, the country's second-largest wildlife park.
Mostly dry, but floods with a thin, heavily salted layer of water after heavy rains.
r1159102635: A dry lakebed remnant of Pleistocene Lake Lahontan in Nevada's Great Basin, part of a national conservation area.
Hosts the annual Burning Man festival and has been used for land speed record attempts.
Settled by the Paiute people around 1300 CE and later crossed by 19th-century emigrant trails to California.
r1159102643: A sandstone plateau in northeastern Chad, shaped by wind and temperature erosion within the Sahara.
Home to rock art depicting cattle dating back nearly 7,000 years.
Inhabited seasonally today by semi-nomadic herding communities.
r1159102645: A plateau near the center of Nigeria, giving its name to Plateau State and its capital, Jos.
Developed as a tin-mining hub by the British in the early 20th century, drawing migrant workers from across Nigeria.
r1159102657: An island in Vanuatu's Shefa Province, home to the capital city, Port Vila.
Originally named Sandwich Island by early European explorers.
r1159102667: Largest island and capital of the Northern Mariana Islands, a US territory in the western Pacific.
Passed through Spanish, German and Japanese rule before the US took control after the Battle of Saipan in World War II.
r1159102671: One of the main Hawaiian Islands, long shaped by cattle ranching, pineapple and sugarcane farming.
Home to the Kalaupapa Peninsula, where a leprosy quarantine settlement operated from 1866 to 1969, now a national historical park.
r1159102675: A volcanic island in French Polynesia, 17 km northwest of Tahiti, part of the Society Islands.
Formerly known as ʼAimeho; early Western visitors also called it York Island.
r1159102679: The sixth-largest of the Hawaiian Islands, nicknamed 'the Pineapple Island' for its past as an island-wide plantation.
About 98% of the island is owned by Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison.
Separated from Molokaʻi by the Kalohi Channel and from Maui by the Auʻau Channel.
r1159102681: The westernmost of Hawaii's main islands, southwest of Kauai across the Kaulakahi Channel.
Privately purchased from the Kingdom of Hawaii in 1864 by Scottish plantation owner Elizabeth Sinclair.
The only place where Hawaiian remains the primary spoken language, undisplaced by English.
r1159102685: Samoa's second-largest and most populous island, formed by a basaltic shield volcano, home to the capital Apia.
Has no historically recorded eruptions, though evidence shows lava flows within the past few thousand years.
r1159102687: The largest and most populous island of American Samoa, part of the Samoan Islands chain.
Home to Pago Pago, the territory's capital, situated on a large natural harbour.
Popular with tourists for its beaches, coral reefs and World War II relics.
r1159102691: Tonga's main island and home to its capital, Nukuʻalofa.
The most populous island in the country, with about 70% of Tonga's total population.
Has developed as the nation's business and trade centre.
r1730070893: A self-governing coral island in Polynesia, in free association with New Zealand and nicknamed "The Rock".
Terrain rises from a coastal terrace to a limestone plateau about 60 m above sea level.
Most Niueans live in New Zealand, far outnumbering those on the island itself.
r1159102695: A large coastal island in Brazil's Pará state, the second-largest island in South America.
Was home from around 400 BC to 1600 AD to the advanced Marajoara culture, which may have numbered over 100,000 people.
Today known for its large water buffalo population and the pororoca tidal bore in its surrounding rivers.
r1159102717: An Arctic island of Russia's Chukotka region, lying astride the 180th meridian between the Chukchi and East Siberian Seas.
Home to the last known surviving population of woolly mammoths, which persisted there until about 4,000 years ago.
A strictly protected nature reserve since 1976 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004.
r1159102725: Part of the New Siberian Islands' Anzhu subgroup, between the Laptev and East Siberian Seas.
One of the 50 largest islands in the world, connected to Faddeyevsky Island by the low-lying Bunge Land.
r1159102733: Australia's third-largest island, in South Australia southwest of Adelaide.
Known for sea lion colonies at Seal Bay and little penguin populations.
Settled permanently from 1836 during British colonization of South Australia, with agriculture and tourism as key industries.
r1159102735: A World Heritage-listed sand island off Queensland, Australia, formerly known as Fraser Island.
Traditional land of the Butchulla people, officially renamed K'gari (meaning "Paradise") in 2023.
Visited by up to 500,000 people a year despite a tiny permanent population.
r1159102743: A leaf-shaped island separated from New Guinea by the narrow Muli Strait, part of Indonesia's South Papua province.
Known as Frederik Hendrik Island until 1963; Indonesia's 11th-largest island.
Home to about 11,000 people speaking Kolopom languages, with very low population density.
r1159102745: The third largest island in Indonesia's Maluku Islands, between the Banda and Seram Seas.
Home to the indigenous Buru people alongside several smaller ethnic groups.
Most of the island is covered by tropical forest rich in endemic bird and mammal species.
r1159102759: An Indonesian island in the Lesser Sunda Archipelago, roughly the size of Jamaica or Hawaii island.
Separated from Flores by the Sumba Strait and from Timor by the Savu Sea.
r1159102761: One of Indonesia's Lesser Sunda Islands, between Lombok and Flores.
Traditionally known as a source of sappanwood, honey and sandalwood.
Marks a cultural boundary between islands influenced by Indian religions to the west and those less influenced to the east.
r1159102763: An Indonesian island in the Lesser Sundas, separated from Bali by the Lombok Strait.
Shares cultural ties with neighboring Bali despite being administratively distinct, within West Nusa Tenggara province.
r1159102765: The westernmost of the Lesser Sunda Islands, east of Java and west of Lombok.
Indonesia's only Hindu-majority province, with over 86% of residents practising Balinese Hinduism.
Its arts, dance, sculpture and music have made it Indonesia's leading tourist destination, with tourism making up 80% of its economy.
r1159102767: An Indonesian island off the northeastern coast of Java, part of East Java province.
Separated from Java by the narrow Madura Strait.
r1159102769: An island off Sumatra's east coast in the Java Sea, known historically for pepper and tin mining.
Controlled by Britain from 1812 until ceded to the Netherlands under the 1824 Anglo-Dutch Treaty.
Home to the UNESCO-recognised Belitung Geopark, with 17 designated tourist attractions.
r1159102771: Indonesia's 9th largest island, east of Sumatra, home to the provincial capital Pangkal Pinang.
Its tin mining industry has caused considerable environmental damage on and offshore.
r1159102783: An island off the western coast of Sumatra, Indonesia, giving its name to the surrounding Nias archipelago.
The archipelago also includes the Batu Islands to the southeast and the Hinako Islands to the west.
r1159102787: Estonia's largest and most populous island, the main island of the West Estonian archipelago in the Baltic Sea.
Known historically in much of the world as Ösel from the 13th century until the early 20th century.
Its administrative centre is the town of Kuressaare.
r1159102793: Sweden's largest island, home to the main town of Visby and smaller islands including Fårö and Gotska Sandön.
Historically spoke the distinct Gutnish language before Swedish became dominant.
Fully integrated into Sweden with no special autonomy, unlike some other European offshore island groups.
r1159102795: Denmark's largest and most populous island, home to the capital Copenhagen.
Linked by bridges to Funen, Amager and, via the Øresund Bridge, to Scania in Sweden.
Comprises about 40% of Denmark's total population.
r1159102797: An archipelago in Norway's Nordland county known for dramatic mountains, open sea and sheltered bays.
Has unusually mild winters for its northerly latitude and attracts about a million tourists a year, many for the northern lights.
r1730071111: A peninsula in southern Greece, the southernmost region of the Balkans, linked to the mainland by the Isthmus of Corinth.
Known from the late Middle Ages until the 19th century as the Morea.
The isthmus separates the Gulf of Corinth from the Saronic Gulf.
r1159102803: The largest of Greece's Dodecanese islands, northeast of Crete, once home to the Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
Ruled by the Knights of Saint John from 1310 to 1522, giving it the nickname 'Island of the Knights'.
Its medieval Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
r1159102805: Largest island of Greece and fifth-largest in the Mediterranean, bordering the Aegean and Libyan Seas.
Cradle of Europe's first advanced civilization, the Minoans, from around 2700 to 1420 BCE.
Later ruled successively by the Mycenaeans, Rome, the Byzantine Empire and briefly by Andalusian Arabs.
r1159102815: The largest and most populous island of the Maltese Archipelago, south of Italy and north of Libya.
Valletta is its capital, with the landscape characterised by low hills and terraced fields.
r1159102817: One of Spain's Balearic Islands, its name meaning 'smaller island' in contrast to nearby Mallorca.
Its capital, Mahón, and the town of Ciutadella de Menorca are its main ports.
Its highest point, El Toro, rises only 358 m above sea level.
r1159102819: Largest of Spain's Balearic Islands, with Palma as its capital.
A major holiday destination, especially for tourists from the Netherlands, Germany, Ireland and the UK.
Two smaller islands, Cabrera and Dragonera, lie just off its coast.
r1159102821: A Spanish island in the Mediterranean off the Iberian coast, one of the Balearic Islands and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Famous worldwide for its nightlife and electronic dance music club scene.
r1159102823: Also called Bear Island, the southernmost island of Norway's Svalbard archipelago, discovered by Dutch explorers in 1596.
Uninhabited except for a meteorological station; became a Norwegian nature reserve in 2002.
r1159102825: A Greek island in the northeastern Aegean Sea, the third largest in Greece and eighth largest in the Mediterranean.
Separated from Asia Minor by the narrow Mytilini Strait.
Its capital, Mytilene, was founded in the 11th century BC.
r1159102831: The largest and only permanently populated island of Norway's Svalbard archipelago in the Arctic Ocean.
About 58% covered in ice, with Longyearbyen as its administrative center.
First used as a 17th-18th century whaling base, later developed for coal mining under the 1920 Svalbard Treaty.
r1159102833: The second-largest island in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, mostly covered by ice caps.
Uninhabited and entirely within the Nordaust-Svalbard Nature Reserve, home to reindeer and walruses.
r1159102835: An island in the Arctic Sea between the Pechora Sea and the Kara Sea, off northern Russia.
Separated from the Russian mainland by the Yugorsky Strait and from Novaya Zemlya by the Kara Strait.
r1159102839: A Norwegian volcanic island in the Arctic Ocean with no permanent population, partly covered by glaciers around the Beerenberg volcano.
Home to Beerenberg, the world's northernmost active subaerial volcano.
Formed by the Jan Mayen hotspot and classified by geologists as a microcontinent.
r1159102841: The largest and most populous island of São Tomé and Príncipe, lying in the Gulf of Guinea just north of the Equator.
Home to about 96% of the country's population.
r1159102843: The smaller, northern major island of São Tomé and Príncipe, off the west coast of Africa in the Gulf of Guinea.
A heavily eroded volcano speculated to be over three million years old.
r1159102847: A group of islands off mainland Tanzania, also known as the Spice Islands.
Main islands include Unguja (Zanzibar Island), Pemba and Mafia.
Most of the archipelago forms Zanzibar, a semi-autonomous region of Tanzania.
r1159102849: A remote Yemeni island in the Indian Ocean, geologically part of Africa though administered by Yemen.
Famous for extreme endemism, with about a third of its plant species found nowhere else, earning it the nickname 'the most alien-looking place on Earth'.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.
r1159102851: Equatorial Guinea's main island, home to the former capital Malabo, located off the coast of Cameroon.
Africa's fourth-largest island, part of the volcanic Cameroon line, with Pico Basile as its highest peak.
r1159102853: The largest and most populous island of Spain's Canary Islands, off the northwest coast of Africa.
Dominated by Teide, a volcanic peak that is the highest mountain in Spain and in the Atlantic islands.
Was home to the Indigenous Guanche people before its conquest by the Crown of Castile in 1496.
r1159102855: The third-largest and second-most-populous of Spain's Canary Islands, off northwest Africa.
Its capital, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, is the largest city in the Canary Islands and the ninth-largest in Spain.
Rises to 1,956 m at Morro de la Agujereada, making it the third-highest island in the archipelago.
r1159102857: The largest island of Portugal's Madeira Archipelago, the summit of a massive submerged shield volcano in the Atlantic.
Formed by volcanic activity beginning over five million years ago, with its most recent eruptions just 6,500 years ago.
Its central mountain ridge peaks at Pico Ruivo, 1,862 m, with steep ravines shaping where its villages sit.
r1159102859: A densely populated island in southeastern New York, extending into the Atlantic and comprising Brooklyn, Queens, Nassau and Suffolk counties.
Shaped largely by glacial processes during the Pleistocene, including terminal moraines and outwash plains.
Brooklyn and Queens, its western boroughs, are part of New York City, while Nassau and Suffolk form its more suburban east.
r1159102867: An uninhabited member of Canada's Queen Elizabeth Islands in the Arctic Archipelago, Canada's eighth-largest island.
Home to some of the largest mountains in the western Canadian Arctic, reaching about 750 m.
Split between the Northwest Territories and Nunavut along the 110th meridian west.
r1159102869: A large island at the entrance to Hudson Bay, part of Canada's Arctic Archipelago, Canada's seventh-largest island.
Its only settlement, Coral Harbour, is known as Salliq in Inuktitut.
The only area in Nunavut that does not observe daylight saving time.
r1159102871: An uninhabited Arctic island in Nunavut, part of the Arctic Archipelago between Victoria Island and Somerset Island.
Lies south of the Queen Elizabeth Islands, with no permanent settlements.
r1159102873: An uninhabited Canadian Arctic island, part of the Sverdrup and Queen Elizabeth Islands.
Known for unusual fossilised forests dating from the Eocene period.
r1159102875: The largest uninhabited island in the world, in Baffin Bay within Canada's Arctic Archipelago.
Its highest point is the Devon Ice Cap, part of the Arctic Cordillera.
Its surface, including the Haughton impact crater, closely resembles Mars and has drawn scientific interest for that reason.
r1159102877: The largest island in Alaska's Kodiak Archipelago and the second-largest island in the United States.
Home to the native Kodiak bear and a major US Coast Guard base, with fishing as its leading industry.
r1159102979: The northern part of Namibia's Atlantic coast, called 'The Land God Made in Anger' by the indigenous San people.
Known for dense ocean fogs from the cold Benguela current and constant heavy surf.
Features high sand dunes north of Terrace Bay and gravel plains to the south.
r1159102981: A mountain range in Belize and eastern Guatemala, in Central America.
Largely covered by tropical rainforest and home to protected wildlife areas including the Cockscomb Basin.
r1159102987: The largest mountain plateau of its kind in Europe, in central southern Norway.
Home to the Hardangerjøkulen glacier and largely protected within Hardangervidda National Park.
r1159103005: A mountainous region in northern Morocco, bounded by the Mediterranean, the Atlantic, and the Ouergha and Moulouya rivers.
Homeland of the Riffian Berber peoples and the heart of the short-lived Republic of the Rif, which fought Spanish colonial forces in the 1920s Rif War.
Split linguistically between an Arabized western Jebala and a predominantly Berber-speaking eastern Rif.
r1730071533: A mountain chain over 1,500 km long in northern Algeria, forming a natural barrier between the Mediterranean and the Sahara.
Algiers and Oran lie at its base, while Constantine sits directly within the range.
Its highest summit is Lalla Khedidja in the Djurdjura Range.
r1159103013: The highest mountain range on mainland Australia, part of the Great Dividing Range in the southeast.
The only Australian mainland region with annual deep snowfall, comprising the Snowy Mountains and the Victorian Alps.
r1159103017: A mountainous region on Sydney's western outskirts in New South Wales, Australia, part of the Great Dividing Range.
Opened to British settlement by the 1813 Blaxland, Wentworth and Lawson expedition.
Severely affected by major bushfires since the early 2010s, yet still drew 8.4 million visitors in 2018.
r1159103035: A mountain range running nearly 1,700 km along western Sumatra, mostly volcanic and densely forested.
Home to the supervolcano Toba, whose caldera-forming eruption about 74,000 years ago was among the largest ever recorded.
Protected within a UNESCO World Heritage Site recognizing Sumatra's exceptional rainforest biodiversity.
r1159103037: A mountain range in northeastern Mongolia, within the Töv and Khentii provinces.
Considered part of the traditional Mongol homeland, in the region associated with the rise of Genghis Khan.
r1159103059: A north-south mountain range extending the Hindu Kush system through western Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan.
Forms the eastern edge of the Iranian Plateau, bordering the Indus River Valley plains.
Its highest subrange peak, Koh-i-Zarghun, lies near Quetta in the Central Brahui Range.
r1159103069: A mountain range on the Turkmenistan-Iran border, running about 650 km southeast of the Caspian Sea.
Part of the larger Alpide belt, bordering the Alborz mountains to the southwest.
Its highest peak in Turkmenistan, Mount Rizeh, lies near the capital Ashgabat.
r1730071661: One of the highest mountain ranges on the Arabian Peninsula, shared between Oman and the UAE.
Separates Oman's low coastal plain from the high desert plateau inland.
r1159103077: Separates Turkey's Mediterranean coast from the central Anatolian Plateau.
Part of the Alpide mountain belt, extending from Lake Eğirdir to the upper Euphrates and Tigris rivers.
r1730071679: Also known as the Transylvanian Alps, a group of ranges in southern Romania bounded by the Balkan Mountains in Serbia to the south.
r1159103087: A mountain range in northern Greece and southern Albania, known colloquially as the 'spine of Greece'.
Geologically an extension of the Dinaric Alps that dominate the western Balkans.
r1159103091: A highland area in northern Germany spanning Lower Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
Its highest peak, the Brocken, reaches 1,141 m above sea level.
r1159103093: A range of medium mountains in eastern France near the German border, forming the western edge of the Upper Rhine Plain.
Its highest peak, the Grand Ballon, reaches 1,424 m.
r1159103095: A mountain subprovince of the Bohemian Massif shared by the Czech Republic, Poland and Germany.
Its highest peak, Sněžka, is also the highest point in Bohemia and Silesia.
r1159103099: A range along the Czech-German border separating Bohemia from Saxony.
Heavily shaped by centuries of mining, which also helped drive the early transformation of metallurgy into a large-scale industry preceding the Industrial Revolution.
Its highest peaks are the Klínovec in the Czech Republic and the Fichtelberg in Germany.
r1159103101: A forested, hilly natural region spanning Belgium, Luxembourg, and parts of France and Germany.
Geologically a western extension of the Eifel, both uplifted during the Devonian period roughly 383 million years ago.
Covers most of southeastern Wallonia and forms the northern third of Luxembourg, where it is called the Oesling.
r1159103103: A sub-alpine range just north of the Western Alps, forming much of the French-Swiss border.
Continues as the unfolded 'Table Jura' through northern Switzerland and Germany.
r1159103107: A series of mountain ranges in Wales, named from the country's Latin name Cambria.
Now usually refers to the Elenydd uplands of Mid Wales, a sparsely populated area sometimes called the 'Desert of Wales'.
Includes the sources of the River Severn and River Wye; Plynlimon is its highest point at 752 m.
r1159103109: Iceland's largest ice cap by volume, covering about 8% of the country in its southeast.
The second-largest ice cap by area in Europe after Novaya Zemlya's Severny Island ice cap.
r1159103121: A high, almost entirely volcanic mountain range in eastern Alaska, within Wrangell-St. Elias National Park.
Includes Mount Blackburn and Mount Sanford, the second- and third-highest volcanoes in the US.
Named for Mount Wrangell, one of the largest andesite shield volcanoes in the world and the range's only active volcano.
r1730071761: A circular dome of mountains in northeastern New York State, home to Mount Marcy, the state's highest point.
Contains over 200 named lakes, including Lake Placid, amid thousands of square miles of boreal forest.
Though built from rock over a billion years old, the mountains themselves are geologically young, uplifted during recent glaciation.
r1159103123: A physiographic province of the Appalachians running from Pennsylvania through Georgia.
Known for their blue haze, caused by isoprene released by the mountains' forests.
Home to Shenandoah and Great Smoky Mountains national parks, linked by the Blue Ridge Parkway.
r1159103131: An outlying subrange of the Rocky Mountain system rising from the Great Plains in South Dakota and Wyoming.
Sacred to the Lakota, who call it Pahá Sápa, after taking the territory from the Cheyenne in 1776.
Formed by the upwarping of ancient rock, later shaped by stream erosion into its present rugged topography.
r1159103171: A peninsula in Azerbaijan extending into the Caspian Sea, home to the capital Baku.
Often likened to the beak of the eagle shape of Azerbaijan's territory.
Ends in the dune spit of Shah Dili, the easternmost point of mainland Azerbaijan, now a national park.
r1159103173: A mountainous peninsula extending from the Arabian Peninsula between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
Divided between the United Arab Emirates and Oman, overlooking the Strait of Hormuz.
r1159103177: A peninsula projecting into the Sea of Japan from Ishikawa Prefecture on Japan's main island of Honshu.
Its main industries are agriculture, fisheries and tourism.
r1159103197: A large peninsula in Southcentral Alaska, named after the Kahtnuht'ana Dena'ina people who historically inhabited the area.
Its name derives from 'Kenaitze,' meaning the local Athabascan tribe.
r1159103199: A remnant of the Bering land bridge that once connected Siberia with Alaska during the Ice Age.
Named after William H. Seward, who negotiated the US purchase of Alaska.
Archaeological sites here have revealed insights into prehistoric human migration from Asia.
r1159103211: A highland region in central Guinea, roughly corresponding to the historic Middle Guinea area of West Africa.
r1159103215: A remote sandstone plateau in southwest Egypt and southeast Libya, whose name means "the Great Barrier".
Known for dramatic cliff paintings and rock carvings depicting an earlier, more fertile era.
r1159103231: A plateau in eastern India covering much of Jharkhand and parts of neighbouring states.
Bounded by the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the north and the Mahanadi River basin to the south.
r1159103243: A highland region of mountains and plateaus covering about 15% of mainland France.
Shaped by volcanism that subsided within the last 10,000 years, separated from the Alps by the Rhône river valley.
Remained a barrier to transport within France until the A75 motorway opened access to the region.
r1159103251: A semidesert region of South Africa known for arid air, cloudless skies and extreme heat and cold.
Exposes fossil-rich rocks of the Karoo Supergroup, recording ecological change from the Middle Permian to Early Jurassic.
Historically formed a forbidding barrier between Cape Town and the interior Highveld.
r1159103253: The largest salt flat in the world, in southwestern Bolivia near the crest of the Andes.
Formed from the desiccation of ancient Pleistocene lakes, leaving an 8-metre-thick salt crust.
Rich in lithium brine beneath its surface; after rain it becomes the world's largest mirror.
r1730072041: A desert region in Oman named for the Bani Wahiba tribe, formerly known as Wahiba Sands.
A 1986 Royal Geographical Society expedition documented over 16,000 invertebrate species and 150 plant species there.
r1159103257: A desert in the Afar Triangle spanning Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti, among the hottest and lowest places on Earth.
Known for active volcanoes and extreme heat exceeding 50°C, with local Afar people mining salt there.
r1159103261: A desert and semi-desert region in southern Israel, with Beersheba as its largest city and Eilat on the Gulf of Aqaba at its southern tip.
Home to the Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and its desert research institutes.
Features sites like the Makhtesh Ramon crater and the ancient desert cities of the Incense Road.
r1159103263: A small desert in northern Kenya near the Ethiopian border, east of Lake Turkana.
Marsabit is its closest major urban centre.
r1159103265: The part of the Sahara lying east of the Nile River, bordered by the Gulf of Suez and the Red Sea.
Contains the Red Sea Hills mountain range running parallel to the coast.
Historically mined for building materials and precious metals, and crossed by trade routes to the Red Sea.
r1159103275: A desert in the Lake Eyre Basin spanning South Australia, Queensland and New South Wales.
One of three deserts, alongside the Tirari and Simpson, occupying parts of the Lake Eyre Basin.
r1159103279: Australia's fourth-largest desert, spanning the Northern Territory, South Australia and Queensland.
Contains the world's longest parallel sand dunes, including the 40 m Big Red dune.
Underlain by the Great Artesian Basin, one of the largest inland drainage systems in the world.
r1159103281: A desert in Australia's Northern Territory and Western Australia, among the last parts of the country explored by Europeans.
Its name derives from the Warlpiri word 'Jarnami', referring to rock holes said never to run dry.
r1159103283: An extremely arid desert plateau in southeastern Afghanistan, also known as the Sistan Desert.
Sparsely inhabited by Baluch and Pashtun nomads; a 1998 drought displaced around 100,000 of them.
Gradually encroaching westward onto surrounding agricultural land.
r1159103285: A desert in southern Afghanistan whose name means 'Desert of Death' in Dari.
The world's 20th largest desert, made up mostly of rocky-clayish plains.
r1159103287: A large desert in the middle of the Iranian Plateau, the world's 24th-largest desert.
Stretches from the Alborz mountains to the Lut Desert, forming a natural barrier to east-west migration.
Spread across the Iranian provinces of Khorasan, Semnan, Tehran, Isfahan and Yazd.
r1159103289: A desert in northern Saudi Arabia known for violent winds and large crescent-shaped reddish dunes.
Connected to the Rub' al Khali desert by the long gravel-and-dune corridor known as the Dahna.
Site of an 85,000-year-old fossilised human finger found in 2016, among the earliest evidence of modern humans outside Africa.
r1159103293: A region spanning Tanzania and Kenya famous for hosting one of the world's largest land animal migrations.
Renowned for its large lion population and high biodiversity of large mammals and birds.
r1159103307: A plain occupying most of modern Hungary, the largest part of the wider Pannonian Plain.
Shrank in extent after the 1920 Treaty of Trianon redrew Hungary's borders following World War I.
r1159103311: A large mesa, known as the Staked Plains, spanning eastern New Mexico and northwestern Texas.
One of the largest tablelands in North America, rising steadily from 3,000 to over 5,000 feet in elevation.
r1730072167: A historical region along the Bight of Benin and Bight of Biafra, spanning parts of Togo, Benin and Nigeria.
Named for its role as a major hub of the Atlantic slave trade from the 16th to 19th centuries.
European powers including Portugal, Britain, the Netherlands and France built forts there to facilitate the trade.
r1159103327: The Mediterranean coastal strip of southeast France, also called the Côte d'Azur, stretching from the Esterel massif to the Italian border at Menton.
Became a winter resort for the British upper class in the late 18th century, later drawing artists like Picasso and Matisse.
The microstate of Monaco sits as an enclave within the region.
r1730072209: The world's largest mangrove forest, spanning the Ganges Delta across Bangladesh and India's West Bengal.
Formed where the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers meet the Bay of Bengal.
Several of its protected areas are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, though it faces threats from cyclones and rising salinity.
r1159103345: A historical and cultural region in northwestern France, roughly matching the former Duchy of Normandy.
Includes both mainland France and the British Channel Islands of Guernsey and Jersey.
Takes its name from Viking ('Northmen') settlers who arrived from the 9th century, formalized by a 10th-century treaty with the Viking jarl Rollo.
Launching point of the 1066 Norman conquest of England, which tied Normandy and England together for nearly 150 years.
r1159103347: A peninsula and historical region in northwest France, homeland of the Breton people and one of the six Celtic nations.
