Was an independent kingdom and duchy before uniting with the Kingdom of France in 1532.
Home to some of the world's oldest standing architecture, including the Cairn of Barnenez, dating to the early 5th millennium BC.
r1159103353: A historic cultural region split between northwestern Russia and eastern Finland.
Long contested between Russia, Finland and Sweden, shaping the identity of both modern countries.
r1159103377: An island in Russia's Severnaya Zemlya archipelago in the Arctic, named after the Soviet Bolshevik political faction.
Part of the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago, first mapped by Soviet expeditions in the 1930s.
r1159103379: The largest island of Russia's Severnaya Zemlya group in the Arctic, named after the Russian Revolution.
Half covered by glaciers reaching into the sea, rising to 965 m at Mount Karpinsky.
r1159103387: The largest island of the Chiloé Archipelago off southern Chile's Pacific coast.
A geological continuation of the Chilean Coast Range, with the Sea of Chiloé submerging part of the Central Valley.
Its landscape includes rolling hills, forests and many coastal inlets and bays.
r1159103389: The largest island of Indonesia's Maluku province, north of the historically significant Ambon Island.
Located near the Banda Islands and other smaller islands.
r1159103391: The largest island in Indonesia's Maluku Islands, formerly known as Jilolo or Gilolo.
Home to Sofifi, the capital of North Maluku province.
Its population is roughly evenly split between Muslims and Christians.
r1159103393: An island in the Lesser Sunda chain, divided between Indonesia's West Timor and the independent nation of Timor-Leste.
Formerly split between Dutch and Portuguese colonial rule; Timor-Leste was occupied by Indonesia from 1975 to 1999.
r1159103395: The largest island of Palawan province in the Philippines, bordered by the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea.
Known for abundant wildlife, jungle mountains and white sandy beaches that draw tourists and developers.
r1159103399: The Philippines' fourth-largest and third most populous island, part of the Visayas group.
Its southern coastal waters lie within the Coral Triangle, a region of exceptionally high marine biodiversity.
r1159103401: A Philippine island in the Visayas, among the country's most populous islands with cities including Tacloban and Ormoc.
Site of significant geothermal power generation near Ormoc.
r1159103405: The third-largest island in the Philippines, in the Eastern Visayas, divided since 1965 into three provinces.
First sighted by a European when Ferdinand Magellan's expedition passed by in 1521.
Later the scene of a major uprising against American forces during the Philippine-American War, followed by a brutal pacification campaign.
r1159103407: The sixth-largest and fourth-most populous island in the Philippines, in the western Visayas.
Divided into four provinces, none of which bear the island's name, unlike other Visayan islands.
Bisected by the Central Panay Mountain Range, its longest mountain chain.
r1159103409: The seventh-largest island in the Philippines, located off southwestern Luzon.
Divided into Occidental and Oriental Mindoro provinces, with Mount Halcon as its highest point.
r1159103411: The third-largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia.
Dominated by the Troodos Mountains and the Kyrenia Range, separated by the Mesaoria plain.
Has experienced Greek, Byzantine, Ottoman and British influence over its long history.
r1159103413: One of the larger islands in Canada's Arctic Archipelago, separated from Victoria Island by Prince of Wales Strait.
Once home to the majority of the world's muskoxen, though disease has sharply reduced their numbers.
Had a population of just 104 people as of the 2021 census, all in the settlement of Sachs Harbour.
r1159103419: The largest and most populous island of Trinidad and Tobago, lying just off Venezuela's coast on the South American continental shelf.
The southernmost island in the Caribbean.
r1159103425: A rugged island forming part of Nova Scotia, linked to the mainland by the Canso Causeway.
Dominated at its centre by the saltwater inlet Bras d'Or ('Golden Arm').
r1159103427: Second-largest island in the Caribbean after Cuba, divided between the Dominican Republic and Haiti.
Site of the first European settlements in the Americas, including Santo Domingo.
Originally home to the Taíno and other Indigenous peoples before Spanish colonization began in 1492.
r1159103505: The delta where the Nile spreads out and empties into the Mediterranean Sea in Lower Egypt.
One of the world's largest river deltas, stretching 240 km along the coast from Alexandria to Port Said.
r1159103515: The world's largest river delta, covering the Bengal region of Bangladesh and India's West Bengal.
Formed by the combined waters of the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
Among the most fertile regions on Earth, earning the nickname the "Green Delta".
r1730072563: The southwestern coastal region of India, covering Kerala and parts of Karnataka.
Home to Kuttanad, India's lowest-elevation point, where farming takes place below sea level.
The first part of India to receive rain from the Southwest monsoon's Arabian Sea branch.
r1159103519: A coastal region on the southeastern Indian peninsula, bounded by the Bay of Bengal and backed by the Eastern Ghats.
Named after the Chola dynasty's realm, Cholamandalam; known in medieval Muslim sources as the Ma'bar Coast.
r1159103521: A mountain range in Morocco, part of the wider Atlas Mountains, running from the Atlantic coast to near Tafilalt.
Borders the Sahara to its south.
r1730072581: A 1,500 km system of mountain ranges and escarpments along Brazil's southeastern coast.
r1730072595: A 1.7-billion-year-old Precambrian geological formation in northeast South America, home to the tepui table-mountains.
Source of famous waterfalls including Angel Falls and Kaieteur Falls.
r1159103533: A major mountain range crossing Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras, known in Mexico as the Sierra Madre de Chiapas.
Part of the American Cordillera, the chain forming the western backbone of the Americas.
r1159103543: A mountain range in central Mongolia, about 400 km west of the capital Ulaanbaatar.
r1159103549: A mountain range of volcanoes running along the center of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula.
Its highest peak, Ichinsky, a stratovolcano, reaches 3,607 m; small glaciers still cling to the range.
r1159103553: A mountain system in northeastern Siberia's Magadan Oblast, along the Sea of Okhotsk.
Forms the watershed between the Kolyma River basin and the Pacific Ocean.
Its highest point is Mount Nevskaya at 1,828 m.
r1159103555: A mountain chain in northeastern Siberia between the Yana and Indigirka rivers, home to traditional Yakut cultural sites.
Its highest peak, Peak Pobeda, reaches 3,003 m.
r1159103567: A mountain range in southern Siberia's Tuva Republic, curving along the Mongolian border.
Mentioned in 13th-century sources such as The Secret History of the Mongols under an earlier name.
r1159103569: A Chinese mountain range running along the eastern edge of the Loess Plateau through Shanxi, Henan and Hebei provinces.
r1159103573: A major east-west mountain range in southern Shaanxi, China, dividing the Yangtze and Yellow River drainage basins.
Forms the natural boundary between North and South China and has historically blocked nomadic invasions from the north.
Its highest peak, Mount Taibai, reaches 3,767 m near the ancient capital Xi'an.
r1159103581: A mountain range in western Myanmar, separating Rakhine State's coast from the Irrawaddy River basin.
Includes the Naga, Chin and Patkai Hills, and resurfaces as the Andaman and Nicobar Islands after submerging in the Bay of Bengal.
r1159103587: A range in central India running parallel to the Vindhya Range, dividing the Indo-Gangetic Plain from the Deccan Plateau.
Source of the Narmada River, which drains its northern slope, and the Tapti River, which drains its southern slope.
r1159103597: The second of the two main Caucasus ranges, running parallel to the Greater Caucasus through the Armenian Highlands.
Separated from the Pontic range by the Kolkhida Lowland in the west and the Kura-Aras Lowland in the east.
Its western portion extends into eastern Turkey and northwestern Iran.
r1159103599: A range running along Turkey's southern Black Sea coast in northern Anatolia.
Known in Roman times as the Paryadres Mountains.
r1159103605: A mountain range in Bulgaria running from the Serbian border east to the Black Sea at Cape Emine.
Gives the Balkans their name; known in Bulgarian and Serbian as "Stara planina", or "old mountain".
Its highest peak, Botev, reaches 2,376 m, and its karst terrain holds caves with notable prehistoric cave art.
r1730072751: A mountain range separating the Balkan Peninsula from the Adriatic Sea, stretching from Italy to Albania.
Its highest section, the Accursed Mountains, holds the range's tallest peak, Maja Jezercë, at 2,694 m.
Formed largely of limestone and dolomite folded by the Adriatic microplate's collision with Europe.
r1159103609: A mountain system stretching over 300 km across northern Spain, from the Pyrenees to the Galician Massif along the Cantabrian Sea.
Popular for hiking and skiing, with resorts including Alto Campoo and San Isidro.
r1159103611: Contains Mulhacén, the highest point in continental Spain at 3,479 m.
A popular ski destination near the Mediterranean coast, despite the region's otherwise hot climate.
Home to the Sierra Nevada and Calar Alto astronomical observatories.
r1159103613: Stretches across southern Spain, forming the southern edge of the Meseta Central plateau.
Separates the Guadiana river valley to the north from the Guadalquivir valley to the south.
Steeped in Spanish legend, including tales of bandits and a child raised by wolves.
r1730072769: A historic region in southern Arabia, spanning Yemeni governorates and parts of Oman and Saudi Arabia.
Home to the Hadharem people, who historically spoke the ancient Hadramautic language.
Stretches from the Empty Quarter desert toward the Arabian Sea coast.
r1159103623: A vast sandy desert in the south-central Sahara, spanning northeastern Niger to western Chad.
Bounded by the Aïr, Hoggar and Tibesti mountains and the basin of Lake Chad.
Was the centre of the Neolithic Tenerian culture and contains the dune field known as the Erg of Bilma.
r1730072791: A mountain range in the Sahara desert in southeastern Algeria, whose name means 'plateau of rivers'.
Holds one of the world's most important groupings of prehistoric cave art.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982.
r1159103631: A large field of sand dunes in the Sahara, mostly in northeastern Algeria, the second-largest erg in the country.
Borders the Atlas and Aurès Mountains to the north and spills over into Tunisia.
r1159103633: A field of sand dunes in the northern-central Algerian Sahara, also called the Western Sand Sea.
The third-largest erg in Algeria, after Erg Chech and the Grand Erg Oriental.
r1159103641: The largest hot desert in North America, spanning northern Mexico and the southwestern United States.
Its largest expanse lies in the Mexican state of Chihuahua.
A geologically young desert, existing for only about 8,000 years.
r1159103643: A hot desert spanning parts of Arizona, California and northwestern Mexico, home to the iconic saguaro cactus.
Distinct from nearby deserts for its subtropical winter warmth and two annual rainy seasons.
Considered a contender for the hottest desert on Earth.
r1159103645: A dry lake bed in northern Utah, between the Great Salt Lake and the Nevada border.
Known for the white evaporite salt deposits of the Bonneville Salt Flats.
r1159103647: Australia's fifth-largest desert, located in Western Australia in an almost pristine state.
Home to a small group of Indigenous Australians.
r1159103649: A desert and steppe region in Inner Mongolia, China, comprising the Kubuqi Desert in the north and Mu Us Desert in the south.
Wedged between the arable Hetao region and the Loess Plateau, with soil poorly suited to farming.
r1159103651: A desert in the Tarim Basin of northwestern China, ringed by the Kunlun, Pamir and Tian Shan mountains and the Gobi Desert.
r1159103653: An Iranian desert of salt flats and dunes in Kerman and Sistan-Baluchestan provinces.
Holds the record for the highest land surface temperature ever measured on Earth, 70.7°C.
Added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2016.
r1730072855: A historical region on Croatia's Adriatic coast, a narrow coastal belt backed by the rugged Dinaric Alps.
Named after the ancient Illyrian Dalmatae tribe; its largest city is Split, followed by Dubrovnik.
Was ruled in turn by Rome, Byzantium, Venice and the Habsburgs before becoming part of Croatia.
r1159103661: Easternmost point of continental Asia, in Russia's Far East.
Known as Chukotka, home to the Indigenous Chukchi people.
r1730072879: A peninsula in Quebec, Canada, on the south side of the St. Lawrence River, separated from New Brunswick by Chaleur Bay.
Its name comes from the Mi'kmaq word gespe'g, meaning 'end of the land'.
Slightly larger in area than Belgium.
r1159103669: A peninsula in East Asia bordered by China and Russia and separated from Japan by the Korea Strait, divided since 1945 into North and South Korea.
Home to a continuous line of Korean kingdoms since antiquity, including Goguryeo, Silla and the Joseon dynasty founded in 1392.
The division at the 38th parallel led to the Korean War of 1950-1953.
r1159103675: The northernmost point of the Eurasian continent and of mainland Russia, at the tip of the Taymyr Peninsula.
Lies just over 1,370 km from the North Pole.
r1159103677: A peninsula in Liaoning province, Northeast China, between the Daliao and Yalu rivers.
Encompasses the city of Dalian; its name means "Liao region's east".
r1159103679: Also known as Saurashtra, a peninsula in Gujarat, India, bordering the Arabian Sea.
Bounded by the Gulf of Kutch to the northwest and the Gulf of Khambhat to the east.
Its ports have been trading centres since at least the 16th century.
r1159103681: A peninsula in southern Guangdong province, China, whose largest city is Zhanjiang.
r1159103689: A plateau in west-central Africa stretching from Nigeria through Cameroon to the Central African Republic.
Source of the Benue River and known for bauxite deposits; named after Fulani leader Modibo Adama.
r1159103699: A geo-cultural highland region covering northern Arkansas and southern Missouri.
The most extensive highland region between the Appalachians and the Rocky Mountains.
Includes the Boston Mountains and the ancient St. Francois Mountains.
r1159103713: A transboundary clay desert plateau shared by Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
Home to a semi-nomadic population herding camels, goats and sheep.
r1159103717: A vast plateau in north-central China formed from wind-blown dust (loess), bordering the Gobi Desert.
One of the largest and thickest loess deposits in the world, home to around 108 million people despite severe wind erosion.
r1159103721: A hyperarid basin in Qinghai Province, China, about a quarter of which is covered by saline lakes and playas.
r1159103729: A vast semi-arid plateau in eastern Ethiopia, overwhelmingly inhabited by Somali people.
Known for oil and gas reserves and over a century of Somali self-determination movements.
Represents the westernmost region inhabited by Somalis in the Horn of Africa.
r1730073011: An administrative region in southeastern Somalia covering the city of Mogadishu, the country's capital.
The only Somali region that does not belong to any of the country's seven federal states.
r1159103735: A historic narrow corridor in western Gansu, China, linking the country to Central Asia as part of the Northern Silk Road.
A string of oases flanked by the Qilian Mountains and the Mongolian and Tibetan plateaus.
r1159103737: A historical region of desert and mountains straddling Pakistan, Iran and Afghanistan, home to the ethnic Baloch people.
Significant for its mineral wealth, long Arabian Sea coastline and potential oil and gas reserves.
r1159103739: Spans the northernmost regions of Sweden, Finland, Norway and Russia, mostly within the Arctic Circle.
Traditional homeland of the Sámi people and home to Rovaniemi's Santa Claus Village.
r1159103741: A steep canyon carved by the Colorado River in Arizona, over a mile deep and up to 18 miles wide.
Exposes nearly two billion years of geological history as the river cut through the uplifting Colorado Plateau.
Has been inhabited by Native Americans for thousands of years, who considered it a holy site.
r1159103751: A broad, flat valley running through the interior of California, bounded by the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada.
One of the most agriculturally productive regions in the US, supplying much of the country's fruits, vegetables and nuts.
Its Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys meet at a delta that empties into San Francisco Bay.
r1159103767: An archipelago at the southern tip of South America, across the Strait of Magellan, split between Chile and Argentina.
Named "Land of Fire" after fires early European explorers saw lit by its indigenous inhabitants.
Cape Horn, at its southernmost extent, lies just north of 56 degrees south latitude.
r1159103769: A Maritime province on Canada's east coast, comprising a peninsula and Cape Breton Island linked to the mainland by the Isthmus of Chignecto.
Settled by the Mi'kmaq before becoming the French colony of Acadia in 1605; Britain later deported the French-speaking Acadians en masse.
Its capital, Halifax, holds over 45% of the province's population.
r1159103771: The largest and most populous Pacific island along the Americas' west coast, part of British Columbia, Canada.
Home to Victoria, the provincial capital, and one of Canada's mildest climates, warm enough in places to grow olives.
Named after British naval captain George Vancouver, who explored the Pacific Northwest in the early 1790s.
r1159103773: A large Arctic Archipelago island straddling Nunavut and the Northwest Territories, Canada's second-largest island.
The eighth-largest island in the world, slightly larger than Great Britain but smaller than Honshu.
Named after Queen Victoria; its small population is split between Cambridge Bay and Ulukhaktok.
r1159103775: The mainland region of Newfoundland and Labrador province, separated from the island of Newfoundland by the Strait of Belle Isle.
Makes up 71% of the province's area but only 6% of its population, home to Inuit and Innu indigenous peoples.
r1159103777: Canada's northernmost and third-largest island, part of the Arctic Archipelago's Queen Elizabeth Islands.
Home to Cape Columbia, the northernmost point of land in Canada, and the Arctic Cordillera, its most mountainous range.
Had a 2021 population of just 144 people across three remote settlements.
r1159103779: The largest island in Canada and the fifth-largest in the world, located in Nunavut.
Inhabited for at least 3,000 years; its capital-area settlement, Iqaluit, sits on Frobisher Bay at the island's southern tip.
r1159103783: A large island off eastern Canada, blocking the mouth of the Saint Lawrence River to form the Gulf of Saint Lawrence.
Home to over 90% of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador's population, mostly on the Avalon Peninsula.
Cape Spear near the capital St. John's is the easternmost point in North America excluding Greenland.
r1159103785: An Indonesian island east of Borneo and the world's 11th-largest island.
Shaped by four peninsulas separated by the Gulf of Tomini, Gulf of Tolo and Gulf of Boni.
Separated from Borneo to the west by the Makassar Strait.
r1159103787: One of the Greater Sunda Islands in Indonesia, bordered by the Indian Ocean and the Java Sea.
The world's most populous island, home to over half of Indonesia's population on just 7% of its land.
Formed by volcanic eruptions from subduction of the Australian Plate, giving it a spine of volcanic mountains.
Was the center of Hindu-Buddhist empires, Islamic sultanates and Dutch colonial rule.
r1159103789: Second-largest island in the Philippines, after Luzon, and seventh most populous island in the world.
Home to the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region, the country's most predominantly Islamic region.
Davao City is its largest city, followed by Zamboanga City and Cagayan de Oro.
r1159103791: The largest and most populous island in the Philippines, home to the capital Manila.
Economic and political center of the country, with over half of the Philippines' population.
r1159103793: Lies about 180 km across the Taiwan Strait from mainland China's Fujian province.
Its highest peak, Yu Shan at 3,952 m, makes it the world's fourth-highest island.
The eastern two-thirds consist of rugged mountain ranges, while most of the population lives on the flatter western plains.
r1159103795: The third-largest and most southerly of Japan's four main islands.
Historically known as Tsukushi-no-shima and governed through the Dazaifu administrative centre established under the 8th-century Taihō Code.
Some traditions hold it was once home to an independent dynasty with a culture distinct from Honshu's.
r1159103797: The smallest of Japan's four main islands, lying south of Honshu and northeast of Kyushu.
Its name, meaning 'four provinces', refers to the four historic provinces that made up the island.
r1159103801: The second-largest and northernmost of Japan's four main islands, separated from Honshu by the Tsugaru Strait and linked to it by the Seikan Tunnel.
Originally inhabited by the indigenous Ainu people before Japanese annexation and colonisation in 1869.
Its capital, Sapporo, is the island's largest city.
r1159103803: Russia's largest island, lying in the Sea of Okhotsk off the coast of Khabarovsk Krai near Hokkaido, Japan.
Contested for centuries between China, Russia and Japan; split between Russia and Japan after the 1905 Russo-Japanese War.
Has been entirely under Russian control since the final days of World War II in 1945.
r1159103805: Second-largest island in the Mediterranean after Sicily, lying between the Italian Peninsula and Tunisia, just south of Corsica.
Retains traces of the prehistoric Nuragic civilization across its landscape.
Its indigenous Sardinian language is one of Italy's officially protected minority languages.
r1159103807: Fourth-largest island in the Mediterranean, lying immediately north of Sardinia.
Ruled by the Republic of Genoa for centuries before being ceded to France in 1768 and annexed in 1769.
r1730073315: A sub-range of the Atlas Mountains, mainly in Algeria with its eastern end reaching Tunisia.
Its summits are more rugged than the parallel, coast-hugging Tell Atlas range.
r1159103879: The highest section of Morocco's Atlas Mountains, home to Jbel Toubkal, North Africa's highest peak.
Acts as a weather barrier separating the Sahara from Morocco's Mediterranean north.
Home to Berber communities who developed efficient Agdal garden-farming techniques in the dry highlands.
r1159103881: The eastern portion of southern Africa's Great Escarpment, forming much of the border between South Africa and Lesotho.
Stretches more than 1,000 km and includes features like the Blyde River Canyon and Three Rondavels in Mpumalanga.
r1159103885: A mountain range in the central Sahara, mostly in northern Chad, home to Emi Koussi, the highest point in both Chad and the Sahara.
Its central third is volcanic, with five peaks topped by large depressions formed by a continental hotspot active since the Oligocene.
Known as the domain of the Toubou people; its name means 'place where the mountain people live'.
r1159103891: A triangular mountain massif in northern Niger's Sahara, rising over 1,800 m and forming an island of Sahel climate amid desert.
Supports pastoral and farming communities and notable prehistoric archaeological sites.
r1159103895: A mountain range spanning China's Heilongjiang province and neighboring Russian regions.
r1159103897: A mountain range in Russia's Far East, extending about 900 km northeast from Vladivostok along the Pacific coast.
Its highest summit is Tordoki Yani.
r1159103899: A mountain range in Russia's Sakha Republic, near the famously frigid settlement of Verkhoyansk.
Part of the East Siberian Mountains, lying near the Eurasian-North American tectonic plate boundary.
Contains coal, silver, lead, tin and zinc deposits.
r1159103903: A mountain range forming the border between Qinghai and Gansu provinces in China, an outlier of the Kunlun Mountains.
r1730073379: A mountain range in Russia's Transbaikal region, forming the primary watershed between the Arctic and Pacific Oceans.
Rich in tin deposits, with the Trans-Siberian Railroad passing through.
Mongolia's capital, Ulaanbaatar, lies at the range's southwestern edge.
r1159103915: A mountain range along India's west coast, formed when India separated from Africa during the breakup of Gondwana.
Runs almost continuously from the Tapti River to Kanyakumari, meeting the Eastern Ghats at the Nilgiris.
r1159103917: A discontinuous mountain range running 1,750 km along India's eastern coast, meeting the Western Ghats at the Nilgiris.
Formed in the Archeozoic era as part of the ancient supercontinents Rodinia and Gondwana.
Crossed by major rivers including the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri as they flow to the Bay of Bengal.
r1159103919: A discontinuous chain of hill ranges and plateau escarpments in west-central India, running roughly parallel to the Narmada River.
Mentioned in ancient texts as the traditional southern boundary of Āryāvarta, the Vedic cultural region.
r1159103921: A mountain range in China's Fujian province known for producing famous oolong and black teas, including Da Hong Pao and lapsang souchong.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site valued for its rare endemic plants and dramatic river valleys.
r1159103927: A mountain range in northwestern China separating the Tarim Basin from the Tibetan Plateau.
Its eastern section forms the border between Qinghai and the Xinjiang/Gansu region.
r1730073425: Stretches along Iran's Caspian Sea coast, part of the Alpide mountain belt.
Home to Mount Damavand, Iran's highest peak.
r1159103935: A mountain range running the length of the Scandinavian Peninsula, forming Norway's dramatic fjords on its steep western slopes.
Forms much of the border between Norway and Sweden, reaching 2,000 m near the Arctic Circle.
Galdhøpiggen, its highest peak, is the tallest point in mainland Northern Europe.
r1159103937: An arc of mountains across Central and Southeast Europe, the third-longest range in Europe after the Urals and Scandinavian Mountains.
Its highest peaks rise in the Tatra Mountains, closely followed by Romania's Southern Carpathians.
Provide habitat for Europe's largest populations of brown bears, wolves, chamois and lynxes.
r1159103941: Stretches nearly 500 km along the France-Spain border from the Cantabrian Mountains to the Mediterranean, with the microstate of Andorra sandwiched between the two countries.
Its highest point, Aneto, reaches 3,404 m.
Historically straddled by the Crown of Aragon and the Kingdom of Navarre, which extended on both sides of the range.
r1159103945: A mountain range in southern Mexico running 1,000 km from Michoacán to the Isthmus of Tehuantepec in Oaxaca.
r1159103947: A series of mountain ranges stretching along North America's West Coast from Alaska to central Mexico.
Part of the North American Cordillera, including the Coast Mountains, Cascade Range and California Coast Ranges.
r1159103949: A mountain range in northeastern Mexico, part of the American Cordillera backbone running through the Americas.
r1159103951: A mountain range in the western United States, mostly in California, forming part of the American Cordillera's western backbone.
Home to Mount Whitney, the highest point in the contiguous US, and Lake Tahoe, the largest alpine lake in North America.
Yosemite Valley, carved by glaciers from hundred-million-year-old granite, lies within its boundaries.
Hosts the General Sherman Tree, the largest tree in the world by volume, within Sequoia National Park.
r1159103953: A major Mexican mountain range running along the Gulf of California, part of the American Cordillera backbone of the Americas.
r1159103971: A range of the Peruvian Andes containing Huascarán, Peru's highest mountain, and over 700 individual glaciers.
Protected within Huascarán National Park since 1975; its glaciers have shrunk by about a third since the 1970s.
A key year-round water source for northern Peru and part of the country's hydroelectric power supply.
r1159103977: The delta of the Niger River on Nigeria's Gulf of Guinea coast, historically known for palm oil trade.
A petroleum-rich region notorious for extensive oil pollution from multinational drilling operations.
r1159103981: The largest river delta in Europe, where the Volga River drains into the Caspian Sea in Russia's Astrakhan Oblast.
Has grown dramatically over the 20th century, from about 3,222 km2 in 1880 to over 27,000 km2 today, due to changes in Caspian Sea level.
Lies in an arid climate zone with strong winds that form linear dunes across the delta.
r1159103983: Second largest river delta in Europe, after the Volga Delta, and the continent's best preserved.
Lies mostly in Romania where the Danube empties into the Black Sea, with a small part in Ukraine.
Its combined territory with the Razim-Sinoe lagoons is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
r1159103987: The region of southwestern Vietnam where the Mekong River empties into the sea through a network of distributaries.
Settled as early as the 4th century BC and shaped by Khmer, Vietnamese, Chinese and French influence.
A biologically rich region where over 1,000 animal species were recorded between 1997 and 2007, but vulnerable to sea level rise.
r1159103991: A roughly 6,500 km chain of connected depressions running from Syria through the Red Sea to Mozambique.
Named by British geologist John Walter Gregory in 1896, building on earlier work identifying the linked rift system.
Includes the East African Rift, home to many of Africa's great lakes and volcanoes.
r1159103993: A peninsula in Far North Queensland, Australia, the largest wilderness area in northern Australia.
In 1606, Dutch sailor Willem Janszoon became the first European to land in Australia here.
Home to eucalyptus savannahs and tropical rainforest preserved for their global ecological significance.
r1159103999: A peninsula on the Black Sea's northern coast, linked to mainland Ukraine by the Isthmus of Perekop and to Russia by the Crimean Bridge since 2018.
Historically on the boundary between the Greek/Roman/Byzantine world and the Eurasian steppe, later home to the Crimean Khanate.
Annexed by Russia in 2014, a move internationally unrecognised, with Ukraine still considered its de jure sovereign.
r1159104001: A large peninsula in Russia's extreme northwest, mostly within the Arctic Circle, bordered by the Barents and White Seas.
Became heavily industrialised and militarized in the Soviet era due to its strategic ice-free Atlantic coast and apatite deposits.
Historically home to the Sámi people before Russian settlement expanded from the 12th century on.
r1159104005: A narrow Mexican peninsula separating the Gulf of California from the Pacific Ocean.
Stretches from Mexicali in the north to Cabo San Lucas in the south, with about 65 offshore islands.
Separated from mainland Mexico by the Gulf of California and the Colorado River, and home to four distinct desert regions.
r1159104007: Separates the Gulf of Mexico from the Caribbean Sea, connected to Cuba across the Yucatán Channel.
Almost entirely composed of porous limestone with low relief.
Sits on the Maya Block, the southernmost part of the North American tectonic plate.
r1159104009: A long peninsula extending from mainland Alaska toward the Aleutian Islands, separating the Pacific Ocean from Bristol Bay.
One of several major Alaskan peninsulas, alongside the Kenai and Seward peninsulas.
r1159104011: Occupies about two-thirds of the US state of Florida, between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean, giving it the longest coastline in the contiguous US.
Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León made landfall here in 1513, and St. Augustine, founded in 1565, is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the US.
Major cities on the peninsula include Miami, Tampa and Orlando.
r1159104013: An Argentine peninsula on the Atlantic coast of Chubut Province, bordered by the San Matías Gulf.
A key wildlife reserve, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999.
r1159104017: A peninsula in eastern China's Shandong province, between the Bohai Sea and the Yellow Sea.
Also known as the Jiaodong Peninsula.
r1159104025: A large mountainous plateau in Siberian Russia, near the restricted city of Norilsk.
Contains some of the world's largest known nickel deposits.
r1159104027: A highland region in southwest China spanning Yunnan and Guizhou provinces.
Flatter plateau terrain in the southwest gives way to mountainous karst topography in the northeast.
r1159104029: A plateau in northeastern Thailand's Isan region, named after the city of Nakhon Ratchasima.
r1159104035: A desert plateau region centered on the Four Corners area of the southwestern United States.
Drained mostly by the Colorado River, it contains the Grand Canyon and nine US national parks including Zion and Arches.
Known as "Red Rock Country" for its colorful, eroded sandstone formations.
r1159104037: A wide flood basalt plateau spanning Washington, Oregon and Idaho.
Lies between the Cascade Range and the Rocky Mountains, cut through by the Columbia River.
r1730073629: A large arid plateau covering much of northern and central Mexico, flanked by the Sierra Madre Occidental and Oriental.
Home to Mexico's major interior cities including Mexico City, Guadalajara and Puebla.
r1159104045: The most extensive high plateau on Earth outside Tibet, spanning Bolivia, Peru, Chile and Argentina at the widest part of the Andes.
Home to Lake Titicaca, South America's largest lake, on the Bolivia-Peru border.
Was the site of pre-Columbian cultures including the Tiwanaku and the Inca Empire before Spanish conquest in the 16th century.
r1159104049: An extensive plateau region covering roughly half of Brazil's land area across its eastern, southern and central portions.
Shaped largely by ancient basaltic lava flows, now geologically quiet with no active seismicity or volcanism.
Home to the vast majority of Brazil's population, including its narrow adjacent coastal strip.
r1159104055: A flat, arid plain on Australia's Great Australian Bight coast, the world's largest single exposure of limestone bedrock.
Stretches about 1,100 km across the border between South Australia and Western Australia.
r1159104059: A coastal desert stretching along the Atlantic coasts of Angola, Namibia and South Africa.
Possibly the oldest desert in the world, having been arid for 55-80 million years.
Its dunes are the second-largest in the world, and coastal fog from the cold Benguela Current sustains desert life.
The fog has also wrecked over a thousand ships along the aptly named Skeleton Coast.
r1159104061: Part of Egypt's Sahara, lying west of the Nile and covering about two-thirds of the country's land area.
Includes the Great Sand Sea and a chain of oases stretching from Siwa to Kharga.
Was the scene of major fighting during World War II.
r1159104063: Part of the eastern Sahara, lying between the Nile River and the Red Sea in Sudan.
The Nile passes through most of its cataracts as it crosses the desert.
Historically crossed by ancient Egyptian traders seeking gold and goods from Nubia.
r1159104065: Australia's second-largest desert, straddling Western Australia's Pilbara and Kimberley regions and the Northern Territory.
r1159104067: A region of the northeastern Sahara spanning eastern Libya, Egypt's Western Desert and northwestern Sudan.
Among the most arid, least populated parts of the Sahara, historically blocking trans-Saharan caravan trade due to scarce water.
r1159104071: Australia's largest desert, spanning Western Australia and South Australia.
A sparsely populated ecoregion and interim bioregion.
r1159104073: An arid region straddling northwestern India and Pakistan, one of the largest subtropical deserts in Asia.
About two-thirds of it lies in India, mostly in Rajasthan, bordered by the Aravalli Range to the east.
Formed partly because an ice sheet over the Tibetan Plateau during the last glacial maximum weakened the monsoon, leading to desertification.
r1159104075: Covers parts of Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, merging south into the Arabian Desert.
Accounts for about 85% of Jordan's land area and 55% of Syria's.
r1159104077: The 12th-largest desert in the world, covering about 70% of Turkmenistan.
Its name means 'black sand', referring to shale-rich sand beneath the surface, and it is extremely sparsely populated and dry.
r1159104079: A desert in Central Asia between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, split among Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
Its name means "Red Sand" in Turkic languages.
r1159104081: A desert plateau on Chile's Pacific coast, the driest non-polar desert and largest fog desert on Earth.
Shielded from rainfall by both the Andes and the Chilean Coast Range plus the cold Humboldt Current.
Its dry air and dark skies make it a premier astronomical site, hosting the ALMA and Very Large Telescope observatories.
19th-century nitrate deposits here sparked the War of the Pacific between Chile, Bolivia and Peru.
r1159104083: The shortest overland route between the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific Ocean, in southern Mexico.
Served as a major overland transport route between the two oceans before the Panama Canal opened.
Named for the town of Santo Domingo Tehuantepec, from a Nahuatl word meaning 'jaguar mountain'.
r1159104085: A narrow strip of land linking North and South America between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean, home to the Panama Canal.
Formed around 3 million years ago, separating the Atlantic and Pacific and helping create the Gulf Stream.
Fossil evidence from the isthmus helped inspire Alfred Wegener's theory of continental drift.
r1159104091: A fertile lowland basin in southwestern China, anchored by Chengdu and Chongqing and drained by the upper Yangtze.
Supports over 100 million people and is considered the breadbasket of China for its rice cultivation.
r1159104093: An endorheic basin in China's Xinjiang region, the largest basin in northwest China, bounded by the Tian Shan and Kunlun mountains.
Dominated by the Taklamakan Desert and known historically to the Uyghur as Altishahr, meaning 'six cities'.
Now a major site for solar and wind energy development, with transmission lines ringing the desert.
r1159104095: The narrowest part of the Malay Peninsula, in southern Thailand.
At its narrowest point, only 44 km separates the Andaman Sea from the Gulf of Thailand.
Marks the boundary between the Phuket Range and the mountain chain running from Tibet.
r1159104097: A plateau region in the eastern US, between the Atlantic Plain and the Blue Ridge Mountains.
Its eastern boundary is marked by the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line.
Named after the Italian region at the foot of the Alps.
r1159104101: The world's largest tropical wetland and largest flooded grassland, mostly within Brazil's Mato Grosso do Sul state.
Extends into Bolivia and Paraguay, with roughly 80% of its floodplains submerged during the rainy season.
Supports a biologically diverse range of aquatic plants and a dense array of animal species.
r1159104107: A vast, poorly drained plain in western Siberia between the Ural Mountains and the Yenisei River.
Home to some of the world's largest swamps and was the source of most Soviet oil and gas production in the 1970s-80s.
r1159104109: A low-lying flatland surrounding the northern Caspian Sea, part of the wider Aral-Caspian Depression.
Includes Karagiye near Aktau, at 132 m below sea level, the lowest point in the region.
r1159104111: A vast swamp in South Sudan formed by the White Nile, one of the largest wetlands in the world.
Its dense vegetation historically blocked river navigation, stopping both ancient Egyptian and Roman expeditions from penetrating further south.
Its thick floating vegetation mats gave the swamp its name, from the Arabic word for 'barrier'.
r1159104115: Historical region within the Tigris-Euphrates river system, corresponding roughly to modern Iraq.
Known as the cradle of civilization, site of the Neolithic Revolution and early developments including the wheel and writing.
Home to the Sumerians, Akkadians, Assyrians and Babylonians, including the Neo-Assyrian Empire.
r1159104121: The world's second-largest island, separated from Australia by the narrow Torres Strait.
Shares the continental shelf with Australia; the two were joined as the landmass of Sahul during past ice ages.
Has the third-largest remaining rainforest in the world and the highest plant biodiversity of any island.
Politically split between Papua New Guinea in the east and Indonesia's Papua provinces in the west.
r1159104125: The third-largest island in the world, split between Indonesia (as Kalimantan), Malaysia and Brunei, and crossed by the equator.
Home to some of the world's oldest tropical rainforests and high levels of biodiversity and endemic species.
Historically ruled by coastal sultanates such as Brunei and Sulu, while the interior remained governed by diverse indigenous communities.
r1159104127: The largest Indonesian island entirely within the country's territory and the sixth-largest island in the world.
Separated from the Malay Peninsula by the narrow Strait of Malacca and from Java by the Sunda Strait.
The volcanic Bukit Barisan mountains run the length of the island as its backbone.
r1159104129: Largest of Japan's four main islands, lying between the Pacific Ocean and the Sea of Japan.
Seventh-largest island in the world and historical center of Japanese political and cultural power, including the former capitals Kyoto, Nara and Kamakura.
Home to Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, and Lake Biwa, its largest lake.
r1159104131: Second-largest island of the British Isles, separated from Great Britain by the Irish Sea and North Channel.
Divided between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom.
Low-lying mountains surround a central plain, with woodland now covering only about 10% of the island.
r1159104133: The largest island in Europe and the ninth-largest in the world, comprising England, Scotland and Wales.
Was connected to mainland Europe by a land bridge, Doggerland, until it was submerged around 9,000 years ago.
Has been inhabited by modern humans for roughly 30,000 years.
r1159104151: Forms the northernmost part of mainland Eurasia, in Russia's Far North.
r1159104153: A peninsula in northwest Siberia, Russia, bordered by the Kara Sea and the Gulf of Ob.
Its name means "End of the Land" in Nenets, the language of its indigenous inhabitants.
r1159104155: A peninsula in the Russian Far East, bounded by the Sea of Okhotsk to the west and the Bering Sea to the east.
Home to the volcanoes of Kamchatka, part of the Pacific Ring of Fire and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Most of its roughly 320,000 inhabitants live in Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky and nearby Yelizovo.
r1159104157: A landmass in Mainland Southeast Asia reaching the southernmost point of the Asian mainland at Tanjung Piai.
Divided by the Strait of Malacca from Sumatra, and backed by the Titiwangsa Mountains.
r1159104161: The largest area of contiguous endorheic (no ocean outlet) watersheds in North America, spanning Nevada, Utah and parts of neighbouring states.
Contains both the lowest point in the contiguous US, Badwater Basin, and nearby Mount Whitney, the highest.
r1159104163: The largest and deepest artesian basin in the world, underlying 22% of Australia.
Provides the only source of fresh water through much of inland Australia.
Reaches up to 3,000 m deep and holds an estimated 64,900 cubic km of groundwater.
r1159104165: A rugged mountainous region across Ethiopia and Eritrea, often called the 'Roof of Africa' for its height and extent.
Bisected by the Great East African Rift System, part of the rift chain stretching from Syria to Mozambique.
r1159104167: A mountain range spanning Iran, northern Iraq and southeastern Turkey, running to the Persian Gulf.
Its highest point, Mount Dena, reaches 4,409 m, and the range ends near the Strait of Hormuz.
r1159104169: A mountain range in Central Asia where Russia, China, Mongolia and Kazakhstan meet, source of the Irtysh and Ob rivers.
Its highest peak, Belukha, reaches 4,506 m; the range merges southeast into the Gobi Desert plateau.
Home to a sparse, ethnically diverse population of Turkic peoples, Mongols and Volga Germans.
r1159104171: A volcanic mountain range about 1,200 km long in Inner Mongolia, China, and easternmost Mongolia.
Originally called the Xianbei Mountains, after the Xianbei people, a branch of the ancient Donghu.
r1159104173: A mountain range in Russia's Sakha Republic and Amur Oblast, also known as the Outer Khingan Range.
First scientifically described by Russian researcher Alexander von Middendorff.
r1730073913: A major mountain range running about 1,100 km through Laos, Vietnam and northeastern Cambodia.
r1159104181: A Central and South Asian mountain range at the junction of the Tian Shan, Karakoram, Kunlun, Hindu Kush and Himalayas.
Mostly located in Tajikistan's Gorno-Badakhshan region, with the Wakhan Corridor bordering it to the south.
Known since the Victorian era as the 'Roof of the World'.
r1159104183: An 800-km mountain range west of the Himalayas, stretching from Afghanistan into Pakistan and Tajikistan.
Divides the Amu Darya valley to the north from the Indus River valley to the south.
A historically significant centre of Buddhism, home to the Bamiyan Buddhas.
r1159104185: A mountain range spanning Pakistan, China and India, containing four of the world's fourteen 'eight-thousanders' including K2.
The most heavily glaciated area on Earth outside the polar regions, with the Siachen and Biafo glaciers among the longest outside them.
Bounded by the Yarkand and Karakash rivers to the north and the Pamir Mountains and Hindu Kush to the west.
r1159104187: One of the longest mountain chains in Asia, running over 3,000 km along the northern edge of the Tibetan Plateau in western China.
Known in China as the 'Forefather of Mountains'.
According to the historian Sima Qian, Emperor Wu of Han named the range after sending men to find the Yellow River's source.
r1159104189: A mountain range in North Africa separating the Sahara from the Mediterranean and Atlantic, stretching through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.
Its highest peak, Toubkal in Morocco, reaches 4,167 m.
Primarily inhabited by Berber populations, whose word for mountain is believed to be the origin of the name Atlas.
r1159104191: A mountain range in eastern North America running about 3,300 km from central Alabama to Newfoundland.
Geologically related to the Scottish Highlands, Atlas Mountains and Scandinavian Mountains, all once part of the ancient Central Pangean Mountains.
Formed over hundreds of millions of years, beginning with the creation of the supercontinent Rodinia around 1.1 billion years ago.
r1159104193: A mountain range stretching across northern Alaska into Canada's Yukon, about 126 million years old.
Crossed by the Dalton Highway and Trans-Alaska Pipeline en route to the Prudhoe Bay oil fields.
Home to the Red Dog mine, the largest zinc mine in the world.
r1159104197: A major mountain range in western North America, running from the Yukon through British Columbia's coast to the Fraser River.
Part of the larger Pacific Coast Ranges within the American Cordillera.
Includes extensive ice fields and the northern end of the volcanic Cascade system.
r1159104199: A mountain range running from southern British Columbia through Washington and Oregon to Northern California.
Part of the Pacific Ring of Fire; its volcanoes are responsible for every US eruption in the contiguous states in 200 years.
Mount St. Helens, part of this range, erupted dramatically in 1980.
r1159104201: A narrow mountain range in southcentral Alaska, home to Denali, the highest peak in North America.
One of the highest mountain ranges in the world, after the Himalayas and the Andes.
Stretches from Lake Clark to the White River in Canada's Yukon Territory.
r1159104205: A low-lying desert basin stretching from southern Turkmenistan through Uzbekistan into Kazakhstan.
r1730073981: A vast steppe stretching from the northern Black Sea coast to the Caspian Sea, part of the larger Eurasian Steppe.
Corresponds to the lands of ancient Cimmeria, Scythia and Sarmatia.
Served for millennia as a corridor for nomadic horsemen, many of whom went on to conquer settled regions of Europe and Asia.
r1159104217: A vast semiarid lowland spanning Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina, South America's second-largest forested ecoregion.
Home to over 3,400 plant species and animals including jaguars and giant armadillos.
Sparsely inhabited for centuries by Indigenous peoples including the Wichí, Qom and Guaraní.
r1159104219: A vast tropical grassland plain east of the Andes in Colombia and Venezuela.
A major tropical savanna ecoregion supporting extensive cattle ranching.
r1159104221: Fertile low grasslands covering more than 1,200,000 km2 across Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil.
Interrupted only by the low Ventana and Tandil hills near Bahía Blanca and Tandil in Argentina.
Transformed by humans through the introduction of cattle, pigs and sheep grazing on the plains.
r1159104223: A vast fertile plain across northern India, Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh, named for the Indus and Ganges rivers that built it.
Formed from alluvium deposited by the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers, making it one of the world's most densely populated and farmed regions.
r1159104227: A vast mountainous plateau region of Siberia, one of Russia's major geographic regions.
r1159104229: An inland plateau in East Asia spanning Mongolia and parts of China and Russia, including the Gobi Desert.
Bounded by the Greater Hinggan, Yin, Altai, Sayan and Khentii mountains, forming the heart of the Mongol homeland.
r1159104233: A plateau covering much of western, central and southern India, flanked by the Eastern and Western Ghats.
Formed largely by the Deccan Traps, massive basaltic lava flows from an eruption at the end of the Cretaceous period.
Home over centuries to major Indian kingdoms including the Chalukyas, Vijayanagara Empire and the Deccan sultanates.
r1159104237: A fertile valley in Central Asia split between Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, watered by the Naryn and Kara Darya rivers.
Founded as Alexandria Eschate by Alexander the Great over 2,300 years ago, later home to Mughal founder Babur.
Ethnically mixed and often tense due to border lines drawn during the Soviet era that cut across local communities.
r1159104239: Fourth-largest peninsula in the world, comprising Somalia, Djibouti, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somaliland.
Lies along the southern Red Sea, strategically important for shipping through the Gulf of Aden.
Home to the Cushitic and Ethio-Semitic speaking peoples historically known as Horn Africans.
r1159104241: Bordered by the Adriatic, Ionian and Aegean Seas, the Turkish Straits and the Black Sea.
Takes its name from the Balkan Mountains, which stretch across Bulgaria.
Was largely part of the Ottoman Empire for centuries, when the region was known as Rumelia.
r1159104243: A desert zone in central Kazakhstan, also known as the 'Hungry Steppe'.
r1159104247: The 'Empty Quarter', a vast desert covering most of the southern Arabian Peninsula across Saudi Arabia, Oman, the UAE and Yemen.
Part of the larger Arabian Desert, one of the driest and most remote regions on Earth.
r1159104251: A semi-arid shrubland and thorn-forest ecoregion in interior northeastern Brazil, named "white forest" in Old Tupi.
The only biome found exclusively in Brazil, home to 26 million people and over 2,000 species found nowhere else.
r1159104253: A large semiarid sandy savanna in Southern Africa, covering much of Botswana and parts of Namibia and South Africa.
r1159104259: A peninsula in West Asia, also known as Asia Minor, that makes up most of Turkey's land area.
Bounded by the Mediterranean, Aegean and Black seas, with the Sea of Marmara separating it from Thrace in Europe.
An early centre of farming in the Neolithic period, from which agriculture spread into Europe roughly 9,000 years ago.
r1159104261: Spans the southern end of South America, governed by Argentina and Chile, from the Andes to the Atlantic.
Features glaciers, fjords and temperate rainforests in the west and deserts and steppes to the east.
Bounded to the south by the Strait of Magellan, Beagle Channel and Drake Passage.
r1159104263: The world's largest island, lying between the Arctic and Atlantic Oceans east of Canada's Arctic Archipelago.
An autonomous territory of Denmark whose capital is Nuuk; was settled by Norse colonists from the 10th century.
Politically tied to Norway for centuries before coming under Danish rule in 1814.
r1159104271: A vast geologic shield of exposed Precambrian igneous and metamorphic rock forming the ancient core of the North American continent.
Glaciation has left it with only a thin soil layer, exposing bedrock shaped by its long volcanic history.
Extends across central and eastern Canada and into the northern contiguous United States.
r1159104295: A system of mountain ranges, plateaus and hills running parallel to Australia's east coast, the longest mountain chain entirely within a single country.
Stretches over 3,500 km from the Torres Strait through Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria.
Serves as the main watershed for eastern Australia's river systems and includes several World Heritage Areas such as the Greater Blue Mountains.
r1159104297: Stretch roughly 1,200 km across France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria and other Alpine countries, from Nice to Vienna.
Formed over tens of millions of years as the African and Eurasian plates collided, pushing marine sedimentary rock into peaks like Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn.
Hannibal famously crossed the range with elephants, and it later became the birthplace of modern mountaineering and winter tourism.
r1159104299: A large mountain system in Central Asia whose highest peak, Jengish Chokusu, reaches 7,439 m in Kyrgyzstan.
Sacred in Tengrism, with its second-highest peak, Khan Tengri, meaning 'Lord of the Spirits'.
Its eastern and western portions are separate UNESCO World Heritage Sites, listed in 2013 and 2016.
r1159104301: Runs north-south through Russia from the Arctic Ocean to near the Caspian Sea, forming the conventional boundary between Europe and Asia.
Highest point is Mount Narodnaya at 1,895 m, with most peaks between 1,000 and 1,300 m.
Rich in metal ores, coal and gemstones, and a major center of Russian metallurgy since the 18th century.
r1159104305: Stretches between the Black Sea and Caspian Sea at the intersection of Europe and Asia.
Home to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe at 5,642 metres.
Divided into the Greater Caucasus in the north and Lesser Caucasus in the south, once part of the Silk Road.
r1159104307: Separates the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau and contains Mount Everest, the world's highest peak.
Formed by the ongoing collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
Sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism; peaks including Kailash and Gangkhar Puensum are off-limits to climbers.
Source of the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers, whose combined basin is home to some 600 million people.
r1159104309: The longest continental mountain range in the world, running along the entire western edge of South America through seven countries.
Its highest peak, Aconcagua in Argentina, is the tallest mountain outside Asia.
Hosts high plateaus, including the Altiplano, the world's second-highest after Tibet, on which major cities like La Paz and Bogotá sit.
r1159104311: The largest mountain system in North America, stretching from western Canada to New Mexico.
Formed 55 to 80 million years ago during the Laramide orogeny, when oceanic plates slid beneath the continent.
Distinct from the younger Cascade Range and Sierra Nevada further west.
r1159104313: China's largest alluvial plain, formed by Yellow River sediment and bordered by the Yanshan and Taihang mountains.
The cradle of Chinese civilization, home to Beijing, Tianjin, and the capitals of several imperial dynasties.
One of the most densely populated and agriculturally important regions in the world.
r1159104315: A vast grassland region of Central Asia spanning northern Kazakhstan and parts of Russia, also called the Great Steppe.
Forms the central and western part of the wider Eurasian Steppe, between the Pontic-Caspian steppe and the Emin Valley steppe.
Known as the Kirghiz Steppe before the mid-19th century.
r1159104317: A vast lowland covering parts of Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Denmark and Poland, between the Central European Highlands and the North Sea/Baltic coasts.
Connects to the East European Plain, together forming most of the Great European Plain.
r1159104319: A broad expanse of prairie and grassland east of the Rocky Mountains, spanning the central US and western Canada.
Covers most of Kansas, Nebraska and the Dakotas along with parts of several other US states and Canadian provinces.
r1159104323: The sedimentary basin of the Congo River in Central Africa, containing Africa's largest rainforest.
Second in size only to the Amazon rainforest and an important global carbon sink.
r1159104325: The region of South America drained by the Amazon River and its tributaries, spanning eight countries.
Covers the Amazon rainforest, the largest rainforest on Earth at about 6 million km2 and the most biodiverse region in the world.
Sparsely populated overall, aside from cities like Manaus and Belém, with many indigenous communities relying on fishing and agriculture.
r1159104327: A physiographic region of Asia covering most of the Himalayas and the land south of them, projecting into the Indian Ocean between the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea.
Politically split among Bangladesh, India and Pakistan, whose territories were part of British India before its 1947 partition.
Distinguished from the broader term 'South Asia', which also includes Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives and Sri Lanka.
r1159104329: A peninsula and cultural region of northern Europe usually comprising Norway, Sweden and Denmark, with strong shared history and language.
Geography ranges from Norwegian fjords and mountains to Denmark's flat lowlands.
Base of the Viking Age, when Scandinavian seafarers raided, traded and explored as far as North America.
r1159104331: The continental portion of Southeast Asia, historically known as Indochina, comprising Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia and Peninsular Malaysia.
The name Indochina reflected the historical cultural influence of India and China on the region.
r1159104333: The world's largest peninsula, occupying most of the Arabian plate between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.
Mostly covered by the Arabian Desert, an extension of the Sahara.
United politically and religiously under Prophet Muhammad in the 7th century AD.
Formed between 56 and 23 million years ago by the Red Sea Rift splitting the African and Arabian plates.
r1159104335: Sixth-largest desert in the world, spanning southern Mongolia and northern China.
A cold desert and grassland region, distinct from sandy deserts.
Its name comes from the Mongolian word for 'dryland'.
r1159104337: Largest hot desert in the world, stretching from the Red Sea and Mediterranean coast to the Atlantic Ocean.
Bordered to the south by the Sahel, a semi-arid savanna belt along the Niger River valley.
Has alternated between desert and savanna in roughly 20,000-year cycles driven by shifts in Earth's axis.
r1159104343: A peninsula in southwestern Europe occupied mainly by Spain and Portugal, separated from the rest of the continent by the Pyrenees.
Also includes Andorra, Gibraltar and a small part of southern France.
The second-largest peninsula in Europe by area, after the Scandinavian Peninsula.
r1159104345: The world's largest and highest plateau, often called 'the Roof of the World'.
Surrounded by mountain ranges including the Himalayas, home to Everest and K2.
Averages over 4,500 m in elevation and feeds the headwaters of several of Asia's major rivers.
r1159104347: A narrow land bridge between Mexico and Colombia, bordered by the Caribbean to the east and the Pacific to the southwest.
High volcanic and seismic activity here stems from the Central America Volcanic Arc and several active fault lines.
Spanish colonisation began in 1502; most of the region later formed the short-lived Federal Republic of Central America before splitting into separate states.
r1159104349: Non-contiguous US state bordering Canada's Yukon and British Columbia, with a maritime border with Russia across the Bering Strait.
Larger in area than Texas, California and Montana combined, making it the largest US state by far.
The Chukchi and Beaufort Seas lie to its north and the Pacific Ocean to its south.
r1159104351: Spans North Asia from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific, covering about three-quarters of Russia's territory though home to only a quarter of its population.
Conquered by Russia between 1582 and 1778, starting with the fall of the Khanate of Sibir.
Known for extremely harsh winters, with January averages around -25°C.
r1159104361: Bordered by the Pacific Ocean to the west, the Atlantic to the north and east, and the Drake Passage to the south, with the Caribbean to the northwest.
Dominated by the Andes along its western edge, while the east holds vast lowlands drained by rivers such as the Amazon, Orinoco and Paraná.
Brazil holds almost half the continent's population and generates about half its GDP.
r1159104363: Smallest of the traditional continents, including mainland Australia, Tasmania and New Guinea.
Was joined to New Guinea and Tasmania in the single landmass Sahul until rising sea levels separated them 18,000 to 10,000 years ago.
Separated from New Guinea by the Arafura Sea and Torres Strait, and from Tasmania by the Bass Strait.
r1159104365: Straddles the equator and the prime meridian, bordered by the Mediterranean Sea, the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
Has the youngest population of any continent and is home to the greatest diversity of megafauna species.
Contains 54 sovereign states; Algeria is the largest by area and Nigeria the largest by population.
Highly vulnerable to climate change, facing desertification, deforestation and water scarcity.
r1159104367: Covered almost entirely by the Antarctic ice sheet, which holds about 70% of Earth's fresh water.
Contains the geographic South Pole and is the coldest, driest and windiest continent on Earth.
First confirmed landing was by a Norwegian team in 1895, after earlier Russian, French, American and British expeditions explored its coasts.
r1159104369: Makes up two-thirds of the Antarctic continent, separated from West Antarctica by the Transantarctic Mountains.
Contains the geographic South Pole and the Gamburtsev Mountain Range, buried under its ice sheet.
Supports breeding colonies of penguins, seabirds and several seal species along its coasts.
r1159104371: One of Antarctica's two major regions, including the Antarctic Peninsula and separated from East Antarctica by the Transantarctic Mountains.
Covered by the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, with the Antarctic Peninsula's west coast among the fastest-warming places on Earth.
r1159104505: Divides East and West Antarctica, stretching from Cape Adare to Coats Land.
First sighted by the British Ross expedition in 1841 and first crossed in 1901-1904.
r1730074339: An entirely volcanic Antarctic island on the east side of McMurdo Sound.
Home to Mount Erebus, an active volcano, and the extinct Mount Terror.
Site of the US McMurdo Station, the largest human settlement in Antarctica.
r1159104437: The highest mountain ranges in Antarctica, containing Mount Vinson, the continent's highest point at 4,892 m.
Split by the Minnesota Glacier into the Sentinel Range and Heritage Range.
Lie within the Chilean Antarctic territorial claim.
r1159104439: The northernmost part of mainland Antarctica, protruding roughly 1,300 km toward South America across the Drake Passage.
Subject to overlapping, internationally unrecognised sovereignty claims by Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom.
One of the most rapidly warming regions on Earth, with declining sea ice and shifting penguin populations.
r1730074507: The largest island of Antarctica, lying in the Bellingshausen Sea west of Palmer Land.
The George VI Ice Shelf fills the sound separating it from the mainland, physically connecting it to Palmer Land.
The second-largest uninhabited island in the world, after Devon Island.
r1159104525: A vast high plateau in East Antarctica, home to the geographic South Pole and the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.
Averages about 3,000 m in elevation across roughly 1,000 km.
r1159104543: A mountainous South Atlantic island, part of the British Overseas Territory of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.
First landed on and claimed for Britain by Captain James Cook in 1775, who named it after King George III.
Served historically as a whaling base, most notably at Grytviken; its research station today has a population of about 20.
r1159104597: Shares the Eurasian landmass with Europe; the boundary between them is a historical and cultural construct rather than a clear physical divide.
Bounded by the Pacific Ocean to the east, the Indian Ocean to the south and the Arctic Ocean to the north.
Birthplace of most of the world's major religions, including Islam, Christianity, Hinduism, Buddhism and Judaism.
China and India traded places as the world's largest economy from 1 to 1800 CE, with the Silk Road as the main east-west trade route.
r1159104603: Bordered by the Arctic Ocean, Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea, and separated from Asia roughly by the Ural Mountains and Caucasus.
Shares the Eurasian landmass with Asia and is divided into about fifty sovereign states, with Russia the largest.
Its culture traces shared roots to ancient Greece and Rome, and it drove the Renaissance, the Age of Discovery and global colonisation from the 16th century onward.
r1159104607: Bordered by the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic to the east, and the Pacific to the south and west.
The third-largest continent by area, after Asia and Africa.
Split into the subregions of Northern America (Canada, the US, Greenland) and Middle America (Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean).
r1159104617: The third-largest and southernmost inhabited island of New Zealand, separated from the South Island by Foveaux Strait.
Over 80% of the island forms Rakiura National Park.
Most residents live in the small settlement of Oban.
r1159104619: A rocky peninsula on New Zealand's South Island, formed by two now-extinct volcanoes.
Includes Lyttelton and Akaroa Harbours; Christchurch lies immediately to its north.
Named by James Cook in 1770 after botanist Joseph Banks, who he mistook it as naming an island for.
r1159104623: A mountain range running along much of New Zealand's South Island, reaching its highest points on the western side.
Its Main Divide separates the wetter west coast from the more populated eastern regions.
r1159104625: The larger of New Zealand's two main islands by area, though less populous than the North Island.
Shaped by the Southern Alps, which include Aoraki/Mount Cook, New Zealand's highest peak.
Its east side holds the Canterbury Plains, while the west coast and Fiordland are known for rugged coastlines and native bush.
r1159104629: One of New Zealand's two main islands, separated from the South Island by Cook Strait.
Home to 76% of New Zealand's population and the capital Wellington, at its southwestern tip.
r1159104633: A peninsula on New Zealand's North Island, sheltering the Hauraki Gulf from the Pacific Ocean.
Visible from Auckland across the Hauraki Gulf on clear days.
r1159104641: A peninsula forming continental Denmark and part of northern Germany, stretching from the Grenen spit to the Elbe.
Crossed by the Kiel Canal, the world's busiest artificial waterway, so ships can avoid sailing around the peninsula to reach the Baltic.
West Jutland is flat and heath-covered, while the east is more fertile with lakes and forests.
r1730070381: An unincorporated US territory and atoll in the Pacific, closed to public entry and under US Air Force jurisdiction.
Used since 1934 as a naval refuelling depot, airbase, and testing site for nuclear, biological and chemical weapons, including Agent Orange storage.
Its surrounding waters are now protected as a National Wildlife Refuge within the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument.
r1159102451: A small, uninhabited atoll in the central Pacific, roughly midway between Hawaii and Australia.
Claimed as a US territory since 1857; attacked by Japan during World War II.
Made a nature preserve in the 1970s.
r1159102483: A small volcanic island south of Tokyo, part of Japan's Ogasawara Archipelago, formerly known as Sulfur Island.
Site of the fierce 1945 Battle of Iwo Jima, where both the US and Japan suffered over 20,000 casualties each.
Joe Rosenthal's photograph of the flag-raising on Mount Suribachi became an iconic image of World War II.
Returned to Japan in 1968 after US occupation; it has no permanent civilian residents today.
r1730070601: The world's second-largest coral atoll after Kiritimati, part of the Seychelles' remote Outer Islands.
Lies about 1,120 km southwest of the Seychelles capital, Victoria.
r1159102673: Part of French Polynesia's Society Islands, centred on the remnants of an extinct volcano.
Surrounded by a lagoon and barrier reef; a major luxury tourist destination.
r1159102571: A remote Chilean archipelago in the South Pacific, made up of Robinson Crusoe, Alejandro Selkirk and Santa Clara islands.
Named after its 1570s discoverer; sailor Alexander Selkirk was marooned here for over four years, inspiring Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe.
r1159102573: A remote New Zealand-administered archipelago about 800 km east of the South Island, including the country's easternmost point.
First settled by the Moriori people, who were nearly exterminated after an 1835 Māori invasion.
Keeps its own time zone, 45 minutes ahead of mainland New Zealand.
r1159102581: A dependent territory of New Zealand made up of three coral atolls in the southern Pacific.
The first nation in the world to be powered entirely by solar energy.
Has one of the smallest populations and economies of any country or territory.
r1159102585: An island group in the Caroline Islands of the western Pacific, part of the Federated States of Micronesia.
The name also refers to the broader Yap State, including its outer islands.
r1159102601: An archipelago in the South China Sea controlled by China but disputed by Taiwan and Vietnam.
Comprises about 130 small coral islands and reefs, mostly in the Amphitrite and Crescent Groups.
Its name comes from the Portuguese word for a submerged reef.
r1159102889: A group of eight atolls in Kiribati, between the Gilbert Islands and the Line Islands in the central Pacific.
The Phoenix Islands Protected Area, established in 2008, is one of the world's largest marine protected areas.
Essentially uninhabited except for a few families on Canton Island.
r1159102893: A volcanic archipelago in Melanesia, east of northern Australia and northeast of New Caledonia.
First inhabited by Melanesian peoples; a Spanish expedition led by Fernandes de Queirós reached it in 1606.
Jointly administered by Britain and France as the New Hebrides from 1906 until independence as Vanuatu in 1980.
r1730071301: A French territory in the southwest Pacific, southwest of Vanuatu and east of Australia.
Its main island, Grande Terre, is nicknamed 'le Caillou' by locals; pro-independence Kanak parties call the territory Kanaky.
The indigenous Melanesian Kanak people make up 41% of the population.
r1730071307: A Polynesian archipelago of three reef islands and six atolls in the Pacific, roughly midway between Hawaii and Australia.
One of the world's smallest and least populated countries, with a land area of only about 25 km2.
First settled by Polynesians migrating from Samoa and Tonga around three thousand years ago.
r1159102901: A crescent-shaped chain of mostly dormant volcanic peaks in the northwest Pacific, divided between the US territory of Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.
Home to the indigenous Chamorro people, who likely arrived via one of the longest ocean voyages in early human history.
First reached by Europeans during Ferdinand Magellan's expedition in the early 16th century.
r1159102903: A French Polynesian archipelago at the southeast end of the Tuamotu chain, culturally closer to the Marquesas Islands.
Made up of the volcanic Mangareva Islands and the uninhabited Temoe atoll.
r1730071319: A Polynesian archipelago in French Polynesia, home to Tahiti, its largest and most populous island.
Other major islands in the group include Bora Bora, Moʻorea and Raʻiātea.
r1159102907: A group of volcanic islands in French Polynesia in the southern Pacific, settled around the 10th century AD by West Polynesian voyagers.
Named after the 16th-century Spanish Marquis of Cañete by navigator Álvaro de Mendaña in 1595.
Known for a culture, biology and language that has stayed remarkably uniform across centuries.
r1159102909: A volcanic archipelago in the Pacific straddling the equator, about 900 km west of mainland South America.
Famous for its endemic species, studied by Charles Darwin in the 1830s, which helped inspire his theory of evolution by natural selection.
Discovered by Europeans only in 1535, by Bishop Tomás de Berlanga, after limited pre-Columbian contact.
r1159102913: The largest of the Kuril Islands, separating the Sea of Okhotsk from the North Pacific, claimed by both Russia and Japan.
Formally claimed as Japanese territory in 1855 before the Soviet Union occupied it in 1945 and expelled its Japanese residents.
Inhabited since at least the 14th century by the Indigenous Ainu people.
r1159102915: An archipelago in the central South Pacific comprising independent Samoa and most of American Samoa, forming part of Polynesia.
Home to roughly 250,000 people who share the Samoan language and the fa'a Samoa culture.
The oldest known evidence of human activity dates to around 1050 BC, from a Lapita site on Upolu island.
r1159102943: Part of the Aleutian Islands chain in the Russian Far East, east of the Kamchatka Peninsula.
Treeless and sparsely populated, consisting mainly of Bering Island and Medny Island.
r1159102951: A subantarctic archipelago of New Zealand lying 465 km south of the South Island.
Currently uninhabited, though archaeological finds on Enderby Island mark the most southerly known Polynesian outpost.
Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998 along with other New Zealand Subantarctic Islands.
r1159102955: A group of islands in the Ionian Sea west of mainland Greece, traditionally called the Heptanese, or "Seven Islands".
Kept outside Ottoman control for centuries under Venetian rule, giving them a distinct Italian-influenced culture.
Joined the modern Greek state in 1864.
r1159102957: An island chain off western Scotland, the longest archipelago in the British Isles and a Gaelic-language heartland.
Was part of the Norse kingdom of the Suðreyjar for over 400 years before passing to Scotland in 1266.
The 19th-century Highland Clearances devastated many of its communities.
r1159102959: An archipelago off the north coast of Scotland, part of the Northern Isles along with Shetland.
Inhabited for at least 10,000 years, with Neolithic and Bronze Age farming settlements.
Annexed by the Kingdom of Norway in 875 before passing to the Scottish crown in 1472.
r1159102961: A North Atlantic archipelago between Iceland, Norway and Scotland, and an autonomous territory of Denmark.
Rugged terrain of fjords and cliffs, first settled by Norse people in the early 9th century.
Capital Tórshavn receives fewer recorded hours of sunshine than any other city in the world.
r1159102963: Scotland's northernmost archipelago, lying between Orkney, the Faroe Islands and Norway.
Its largest island, 'the Mainland', is the fifth-largest in the British Isles.
Lerwick has been its capital since 1708.
r1159102965: An Aegean archipelago southeast of mainland Greece, named for the islands ringing the sacred island of Delos.
Naxos is the largest island, while Syros is the most populated.
r1159103431: A volcanic archipelago stretching from Hokkaido in Japan to Kamchatka in Russia, separating the Sea of Okhotsk from the Pacific.
Under Russian administration since the Soviet invasion in 1945.
Japan claims the four southernmost islands, fuelling the ongoing Kuril Islands dispute.
r1730072397: A Melanesian archipelago of more than 330 islands, formed mostly by volcanic activity starting around 150 million years ago.
Most people live on the two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, with the capital Suva on Viti Levu.
Became a British colony in 1874 and gained independence in 1970, later experiencing several coups.
r1159103449: A large island in Papua New Guinea's Bismarck Archipelago, named after the island of Ireland.
Separated from New Britain by Saint George's Channel.
Was renamed Neumecklenburg during the German New Guinea colonial period.
r1159103461: The largest and highest island in Samoa, though significantly less populated than the smaller Upolu.
The sixth-largest island in Polynesia, after New Zealand's main islands and Hawaii's Hawaii and Maui.
Known in formal Samoan oratory by its classical name, Salafai.
r1159103469: A Pacific atoll of Kiribati, also called Christmas Island, and one of the world's largest atolls by land area.
Lies in the world's furthest-forward time zone, UTC+14, making it among the first places to see the New Year.
Was the site of British and American nuclear weapons tests in the late 1950s and 1962.
r1159103471: The third-largest and most populated of the Hawaiian Islands, home to the state capital Honolulu.
Site of Pearl Harbor and well-known landmarks such as Waikīkī and Diamond Head.
r1159103473: One of the main Hawaiian Islands, nicknamed the "Garden Isle" for its lush landscape.
Home to Waimea Canyon and the dramatic Nā Pali Coast.
r1159103477: The second-largest island of Fiji, lying north of the larger Viti Levu, formerly known as Sandalwood Island.
r1159103479: Westernmost point and territory of the United States, the largest island in Micronesia.
Settled by the Chamorro people roughly 3,500 years ago; first reached by Europeans when Magellan landed in 1521.
Served as an important stopover for Spanish Manila galleons between the 17th and 19th centuries.
r1730072495: The largest of Japan's Ryukyu Islands, about 640 km south of Kyushu.
Has been a strategic US military location since the Battle of Okinawa at the end of World War II.
Naha, on its southwest coast, is the seat of Okinawa Prefecture.
r1159103487: A chain of islands in the southwestern Philippines, forming the border between the Sulu and Celebes seas.
Home to the indigenous Tausug and Sama peoples, including the seafaring Bajau, and formerly the seat of the Sultanate of Sulu.
