r1159103489: An archipelago of ten volcanic islands off the coast of West Africa, part of the Macaronesia ecoregion along with the Azores, Canaries and Madeira.
Uninhabited until Portuguese explorers settled it in the 15th century, later becoming a key stopover in the transatlantic slave trade.
The capital Praia is on Santiago, the most populous of the islands.
r1159103491: A Spanish archipelago off northwest Africa, an autonomous community with capitals in Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas.
Popular year-round destination thanks to a mild, sunny climate despite its Atlantic location.
r1159103495: An archipelago off British Columbia, Canada, formerly called the Queen Charlotte Islands, renamed in 2010 to honor the Haida people.
Home to the Haida Nation for 13,000 years; in 2024 British Columbia transferred title of over 200 islands back to the Haida.
Separated from the mainland by the Hecate Strait, with Graham and Moresby as its two main islands.
r1159103497: A 300-mile archipelago of about 1,100 islands off southeastern Alaska, sheltering the northern Inside Passage.
Home to the Tlingit and Kaigani Haida peoples, with Ketchikan and Sitka as its largest towns.
Mostly within the Tongass National Forest, with fishing, logging and tourism as main industries.
r1159103811: The largest island in Vanuatu, usually called Santo, though less populous than Efate, home to the capital Port Vila.
Its only true town is Luganville.
r1730073191: An archipelagic nation of coral atolls in Micronesia, with 98.47% of its territory being lagoon waters, the highest ratio of water to land of any sovereign state.
Settled by Austronesian peoples as early as the 2nd millennium BC.
Named after British captain John Marshall, who explored the region in 1788; it was a German, then Japanese, then American-administered territory before independence.
r1159103821: Largest chain of atolls in the world, part of French Polynesia.
Major islands include Rangiroa, Anaa and Fakarava, inhabited by Polynesians who settled the archipelago.
r1159103823: A group of islands off northeastern New Guinea, part of Papua New Guinea's Islands Region.
r1159103825: The main island of the Autonomous Region of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea, and the largest in the Solomon Islands archipelago.
Was formerly linked to the German Empire as part of the North Solomons.
Voted for independence from Papua New Guinea in a 2019 referendum, with full independence planned for 2030.
r1159103827: Largest island in the Solomon Islands by area and population.
Site of the major Guadalcanal campaign between Japanese and Allied forces in 1942-43.
Honiara, its north coast town, became the capital of the British Solomon Islands after World War II.
r1159103831: The largest island of the Society Islands in French Polynesia, formed from two eroded, now-extinct shield volcanoes joined by an isthmus.
Hosts Papeʻete, the capital of French Polynesia, and the region's only international airport.
Settled by Polynesians between about 900 and 1100 CE.
r1159103833: Second-largest island in the Hawaiian archipelago, dominated by the Haleakalā volcano and the West Maui Mountains.
The two volcanic areas are joined by a narrow isthmus, giving Maui its nickname 'the Valley Isle'.
Lahaina, a historic town on the island, was largely destroyed by fire in 2023.
r1159103837: Fiji's largest island, home to the national capital and largest city, Suva.
Houses the large majority of Fiji's population.
r1159103839: A group of islands in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar, including Mauritius and France's Réunion.
Named after Portuguese navigator Pedro Mascarenhas, who first visited in 1512.
Share a geological origin on the Mauritia microcontinent, once wedged between India and Madagascar before they separated about 70 million years ago.
r1159103843: An archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, with the capital Victoria about 1,500 km east of mainland Africa.
Was uninhabited until French colonization in the 18th century, when enslaved Africans were brought to work sugar plantations.
Came under full British control in the early 19th century before later independence.
r1159103847: A Russian Arctic archipelago off Siberia's Taymyr Peninsula, separating the Kara and Laptev Seas.
The last sizeable archipelago on Earth to be discovered, first charted in 1930-1932.
Home to the Academy of Sciences Glacier, the largest glacier in Russia.
r1159103851: A Norwegian archipelago in the Arctic Ocean, about midway between mainland Norway and the North Pole.
The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 gave Norway sovereignty while keeping it a demilitarized free economic zone.
Home to the Svalbard Global Seed Vault and about 60% covered by glaciers.
r1159103855: An uninhabited Russian Arctic archipelago of 192 islands, about 85% covered by glaciers.
First reliably documented by the 1873 Austro-Hungarian North Pole expedition, which named it after Emperor Franz Joseph I.
Became part of the Russian Arctic National Park in 2012 after being a protected nature sanctuary since 1994.
r1159103857: A Russian Arctic archipelago between the Barents and Kara Seas, with its northern cape marking the easternmost point of Europe.
Used by the Soviet Union as one of its two main nuclear test sites, including the 1961 detonation of the Tsar Bomba, the most powerful nuclear weapon ever tested.
r1730073279: A Mediterranean archipelago off Spain's eastern coast, an autonomous community with Palma as its capital.
Divided into the western Pityusic Islands (Ibiza, Formentera) and eastern Gymnesian Islands (Mallorca, Menorca).
Ibiza is known worldwide for its electronic music and nightclub scene.
r1159103861: An Indonesian and Timorese archipelago, now officially called the Nusa Tenggara Islands, meaning 'Southeast Islands'.
Mostly lies within the Wallacea biogeographic region, except Bali, which sits on the Sunda Shelf.
Part of the volcanic Sunda Arc formed by subduction along the Sunda Trench.
r1159103863: A disputed archipelago in the South China Sea off the Philippines, Malaysia and Vietnam, named after a 19th-century British whaling captain.
Contains less than 200 hectares of natural land spread across hundreds of square kilometres of sea.
Its strategic shipping lanes and potential oil and gas reserves make its roughly 45 islands a flashpoint for competing territorial claims.
r1159103865: A remote Russian Arctic archipelago between the East Siberian and Laptev Seas.
r1159103867: A grouping of the Caribbean's larger islands: Cuba, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and Jamaica, plus the Cayman Islands.
Cuba is the largest island, located at the group's western end.
Together with the Lesser Antilles and Lucayan Archipelago, they form the West Indies.
r1159103873: An arc of Caribbean islands running from near Puerto Rico southeast through the Leeward and Windward Islands before turning west along Venezuela's coast.
Distinguished from the larger Greater Antilles to the west; together they form the Antilles within the West Indies.
Partly volcanic in origin, and historically dominated by the Indigenous Kalinago people, unlike the more diverse Greater Antilles.
r1159104137: An archipelago of about 200 islands in the Indian Ocean southwest of Myanmar, part of India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Home to the Andamanese indigenous peoples, including the Sentinelese on North Sentinel Island, whom visitors are banned from approaching.
r1159104139: An Indian archipelago in the eastern Indian Ocean, separated from Thailand by the Andaman Sea.
Forms a maritime boundary between the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea alongside the Andaman Islands.
Great Nicobar Island was added to UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves in 2013.
r1159104143: An archipelago in eastern Indonesia, historically known as the Spice Islands for the nutmeg, mace and cloves found only there.
That spice trade drew European colonial interest from the 16th century onward.
Split in 1999 into Maluku Province, with a larger Christian population centred on Ambon, and North Maluku, predominantly Muslim with its capital at Sofifi.
r1159104145: A chain of volcanic islands stretching about 1,200 miles from the Alaska Peninsula toward Kamchatka.
Separates the Bering Sea from the Pacific Ocean.
Contains both the westernmost and easternmost points of the United States by longitude, since it crosses the 180th meridian.
r1159104147: An island subregion comprising the Greater Antilles, Lesser Antilles and Lucayan Archipelago.
Includes 13 independent countries and 18 dependencies; the term is often used interchangeably with 'Caribbean'.
r1159104149: The northernmost cluster of islands in Canada's Arctic Archipelago, split between Nunavut and the Northwest Territories.
Hold roughly 14% of the world's glacier and ice cap area outside Greenland and Antarctica.
Their southern islands are known as the Parry Islands.
r1159104273: An archipelagic nation of 32 atolls and islands straddling the equator and the 180th meridian in the central Pacific.
Its easternmost islands sit in UTC+14, the most advanced time zone on Earth, because the International Date Line swings far east around the country.
Annexed as a British protectorate in 1892 and independent since 1979; most of the population lives on Tarawa.
r1159104275: A chain of volcanic islands formed by the Hawaiian hotspot on the Pacific Plate, part of the Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain.
About 1,860 miles from the nearest continent, among the most isolated major island groups on Earth.
The US state of Hawaii is the only state entirely on an archipelago and not geographically connected to North America.
r1159104277: A chain of 11 volcanic atolls in the central Pacific, split between Kiribati and US territories, stretching over 2,350 km.
Kiritimati, part of the chain, has the largest land area of any atoll in the world.
The International Date Line runs through the islands, placing Kiribati's portion in UTC+14, the world's most advanced time zone.
r1159104279: A scattered Pacific archipelago north of New Guinea, divided between the Federated States of Micronesia and Palau.
Once governed from Manila as part of the Spanish East Indies, earning the historical name 'New Philippines'.
r1159104281: The largest island in Papua New Guinea's Bismarck Archipelago, formed largely by volcanic activity.
A major 1994 eruption of the volcano Tavurvur buried the provincial capital Rabaul in ash, forcing the capital to move to nearby Kokopo.
Known during German colonial rule as Neupommern ('New Pomerania').
r1159104283: The largest of the Hawaiian Islands, nicknamed the "Big Island", in the North Pacific Ocean.
Holds 63% of the Hawaiian archipelago's land but only 13% of its population; largest city is Hilo.
r1159104287: The four largest Indonesian islands - Borneo, Java, Sulawesi and Sumatra - grouped together in the Sunda Islands.
Known for exceptional ecological diversity and rich, varied local cultures.
r1159104289: An archipelago of about 7,641 islands in the western Pacific, divided into Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao.
Named after King Philip II of Spain after Ferdinand Magellan's arrival began Spanish colonization.
Passed from Spanish to American control after 1898, was occupied by Japan in WWII, and gained independence in 1946.
r1159104291: An archipelago of over 14,000 islands running along the Pacific coast of East Asia, stretching from the Sea of Okhotsk to the East China and Philippine seas.
Made up of three island arcs: the Northeastern Japan Arc, the Southwestern Japan Arc, and the Ryukyu Island Arc.
The largest island country in East Asia and the fourth-largest island country in the world.
r1159104293: A group of 36,563 islands north of mainland Canada, excluding Greenland and Iceland, mostly within Nunavut and the Northwest Territories.
Showing effects of climate change, with melting projected to add 3.5 cm to global sea level rise by 2100.
r1159104353: A subregion of Oceania stretching from New Guinea to Fiji, including the Arafura Sea.
The name was coined in 1832 by French navigator Jules Dumont d'Urville alongside Micronesia and Polynesia.
Includes the independent countries of Fiji, Vanuatu, Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea.
r1159104355: A subregion of Oceania made up of roughly 2,000 small islands in the northwestern Pacific.
Includes the Caroline, Gilbert, Mariana and Marshall Islands archipelagos.
Politically divided among six sovereign nations and territories, including Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and Kiribati.
r1159104359: A subregion of Oceania made up of over 1,000 islands scattered across the central and southern Pacific, including Hawaii at its northern vertex.
Its name, coined in 1756, groups islands sharing related Polynesian languages, culture and traditions.
r1159104471: An Antarctic island group in the Drake Passage, about 120 km north of the Antarctic Peninsula.
Claimed without international recognition by the UK, Chile and Argentina, with sovereignty held in abeyance under the Antarctic Treaty.
Home to numerous research stations, mostly on King George Island.
r1159104529: A remote subantarctic archipelago in the southern Indian Ocean, part of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands.
Among the most isolated places on Earth, with no indigenous inhabitants and no airport, reachable only by ship.
r1159104531: A group of coral atolls and reefs in the central Indian Ocean, including the Great Chagos Bank, the world's largest atoll by area.
Over half its small total land area lies on Diego Garcia.
Holds a quarter to half of the Indian Ocean's reef area still in excellent condition, largely free of local pollution and development.
r1159104535: A sub-Antarctic archipelago of small islands in the southern Indian Ocean, part of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands.
r1159104539: Two uninhabited subantarctic volcanic islands in the southern Indian Ocean, administered by South Africa.
Named Marion Island and Prince Edward Island; protected as Special Nature Reserves and a marine protected area.
Home only to staff of a South African research station on Marion Island.
r1159104541: An Antarctic island group in the Southern Ocean, claimed without international recognition by Britain and Argentina.
Hosts Argentina's Orcadas base, established in 1904, and Britain's Signy Research Station, founded in 1947.
r1159104599: The world's largest archipelago by area, lying between mainland Southeast Asia and Australia with over 25,000 islands.
Spans Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei, East Timor and Papua New Guinea.
Also known historically as the East Indies or Nusantara.
r1159104601: An archipelago off northwestern Europe comprising Great Britain, Ireland, the Isle of Man and thousands of smaller islands.
Includes two sovereign states, the Republic of Ireland and the United Kingdom.
Contains some of the oldest rocks on Earth, dated to 2.7 billion years, found in Ireland, Wales and northwest Scotland.
r1159104631: Comprises two main landmasses, the North Island and the South Island, plus over 700 smaller islands, east of Australia across the Tasman Sea.
Its rugged terrain, including the Southern Alps, was shaped by tectonic uplift and volcanic activity.
Among the last large habitable landmasses settled by humans; Polynesians arrived between about 1280 and 1350 and developed Māori culture.
The Dutch explorer Abel Tasman sighted it in 1642, and Captain James Cook mapped it for Britain in 1769.
r1159104651: A Portuguese archipelago of nine volcanic islands in the Atlantic, about 1,400 km west of mainland Portugal.
Sits at the Azores triple junction, where the North American, Eurasian and Nubian tectonic plates meet.
Mount Pico, on Pico island, is Portugal's highest point at 2,351 m.
p1159104689: The most westerly point of mainland England and the most south-westerly point in Great Britain.
A popular tourist destination on Cornwall's Penwith peninsula, between the English Channel and the Celtic Sea.
p1159104701: A headland in Greenland and the country's southernmost point, an important navigational landmark.
p1159104707: An uninhabited volcanic island off southern Iceland that emerged from the sea in a 1963-1967 eruption.
Named after Surtr, a fire giant from Norse mythology, and intensively studied as plant and animal life colonised it from scratch.
Shrinking steadily from wave erosion; it is expected to remain above sea level until at least 2100.
p1159104715: The largest island of the Chagos Archipelago in the central Indian Ocean, used as a joint UK-US military base since the 1970s.
Its original Chagossian population was forcibly removed between 1968 and 1973 to make way for the base.
Under a 2025 treaty, sovereignty is set to transfer from the UK to Mauritius while the base stays under British control for decades.
p1159104725: An external territory of Australia in the Pacific, between New Zealand and New Caledonia.
Served as a British penal settlement from 1788 to 1855, then was resettled in 1856 by descendants of the Bounty mutineers from Pitcairn Island.
Its native Norfolk Island pine is a symbol of the island.
p1159104733: An island state within the Federated States of Micronesia, part of the Caroline Islands archipelago.
The smallest state of the FSM by both area and population.
Its capital is Tofol, and Mount Finkol is its highest point.
p1159104793: An uninhabited coral island near the equator in the central Pacific, part of the US Minor Outlying Islands.
Best known as the island Amelia Earhart was trying to reach when her plane disappeared in 1937.
Managed today as a strict nature reserve with no economic activity.
p1159104811: An uninhabited raised coral atoll in the Pitcairn Islands group, part of a British Overseas Territory.
One of only two raised atolls in the world with ecosystems largely untouched by humans, alongside Aldabra; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.
p1159104827: The largest and most populous island of the Cook Islands, home to about 72% of the country's population.
Its capital, Avarua, hosts the national parliament and international airport.
Settled by Polynesians late in the first millennium, well before European contact in 1814.
p1159104835: A remote Chilean territory in the southeastern Pacific, at a corner of the Polynesian Triangle.
Famous for nearly 1,000 monumental moai statues carved by the Rapa Nui people.
The date Polynesians first settled it is debated, with estimates ranging from around 800 to 1200 CE; Chile annexed the island in 1888.
p1159104837: The largest island of the US Virgin Islands, nicknamed 'Twin City' for its towns of Frederiksted and Christiansted.
Its highest point is Mount Eagle.
p1159104847: A flat, sparsely populated island in Antigua and Barbuda, dominated by the Codrington Lagoon.
Nearly destroyed by Hurricane Irma in 2017, which forced the evacuation of the entire population to Antigua.
p1159104849: A Leeward Island in the Caribbean, the most populous island of Antigua and Barbuda.
Home to English Harbour's Nelson's Dockyard, a UNESCO World Heritage Site named after Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson.
St. John's, its capital, has a deep harbour able to accommodate large cruise ships.
p1159104855: An island in the Lesser Antilles of the eastern Caribbean, an overseas department and region of France.
Mount Pelée and the Pitons du Carbet were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
Part of the European Union as an outermost region, though outside the Schengen Area.
p1159104859: The largest island of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, a volcanic island in the southern Caribbean.
Home to La Soufrière, the country's highest peak and an active volcano that erupted as recently as 2021.
Was the site of 18th-century wars between the Garifuna people and Britain before being ceded to the British.
p1159104865: An island of Trinidad and Tobago lying northeast of the larger island of Trinidad.
p1159104867: The largest island in Venezuela's Nueva Esparta state, off the country's northwest coast in the Caribbean Sea.
p1159104869: A southern Caribbean island roughly 65 km north of Venezuela, forming part of the ABC islands with Aruba and Bonaire.
Colonised by the Dutch in 1634, who turned it into a hub of the Atlantic slave trade and later a major oil refining centre after 1914.
Known for its liqueur Curaçao, flavoured with the peel of the local laraha citrus fruit.
p1159104871: A small island in the southern Caribbean, lying on the South American continental shelf north of Venezuela.
Became a constituent country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1986, with Oranjestad as its capital.
Has an arid, sunny climate unlike the humid tropics typical of much of the Caribbean.
p1159104881: A headland on the coast of Moroccan-occupied Western Sahara, whose original Arabic name means "father of danger".
Marked a historic barrier that European sailors feared rounding for centuries.
p1159104883: A rocky headland in South Africa, the southernmost point of South Africa and the geographic southern tip of the African continent.
Marks the traditional dividing line between the Atlantic and Indian oceans.
Historically notorious among sailors as a hazard on the clipper route, once known in English as Cape L'Agulhas.
p1159104885: A headland in Somalia's Puntland state, forming the geographical apex of the Horn of Africa.
The second easternmost point on mainland Africa, after Ras Hafun.
Named after the offshore Guardafui Channel.
p1159104887: A waterfall on the Zambezi River on the Zambia-Zimbabwe border, 1,708 m wide and one of the world's largest.
Known locally as 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' ('the smoke that thunders'); named Victoria Falls by Scottish missionary David Livingstone in 1855.
p1159104971: A cape on Norway's Magerøya island, the northernmost point in Europe reachable by car via European route E69.
Features a 307 m cliff and plateau popular for viewing the midnight sun over the Barents Sea.
p1159104973: The southwesternmost point of Portugal and of mainland Europe, in the Algarve.
Site of the 1797 Battle of Cape St Vincent between British and Spanish fleets.
p1159105003: A headland on Alaska's Arctic coast, northeast of Utqiagvik, the northernmost point of all US territory.
The northernmost point on the North American mainland, Murchison Promontory in Canada, lies 64 km farther north.
p1159105007: Site of the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and near the Kennedy Space Center, on Florida's Space Coast.
Separated from Merritt Island by the Banana River.
Home to Port Canaveral, one of the busiest cruise ports in the world.
p1159105011: A resort city at the southern tip of Mexico's Baja California peninsula.
Known for its sea arch, El Arco, scuba diving and marine wildlife including marlin and sharks.
Forms the Los Cabos metro area together with neighbouring San José del Cabo.
p1159105015: A peninsula extending into the Atlantic from southeastern Massachusetts, named in 1602 by Bartholomew Gosnold.
Separated from the mainland since 1914 by the Cape Cod Canal, crossed by the Sagamore and Bourne bridges.
p1159105019: A group of three waterfalls on the Niagara River between Ontario, Canada and New York, USA.
Horseshoe Falls, the largest and most powerful by flow rate in North America, straddles the border.
Formed when glaciers receded at the end of the last ice age, carving through the Niagara Escarpment.
A major source of hydroelectric power and a popular honeymoon destination.
p1159105027: The second-largest of Chile's Juan Fernández Islands, renamed in 1966 to honor its literary connection.
Home to marooned sailor Alexander Selkirk from 1704 to 1709, who partly inspired Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe.
p1159105049: Southernmost headland of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago, marking where the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans meet.
First rounded in 1616 by Dutch navigators Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire.
Known for hazardous waters with strong winds, currents and icebergs; a major clipper-ship route until the Panama Canal opened in 1914.
p1159105051: The world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, dropping over the edge of the Auyán-tepui mountain in Venezuela.
Located within Canaima National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Gran Sabana region.
Feeds into the Churún and Carrao rivers, tributaries of the Orinoco.
p1159105053: A waterfall system on the Iguazu River on the Argentina-Brazil border, forming the largest waterfall system in the world.
Most of the falls lie on the Argentine side, though the river flows mostly through Brazil before reaching them.
Protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on both the Argentine and Brazilian sides since the mid-1980s.
p1159105055: An uninhabited coral atoll in the eastern Pacific, the only French territory in the North Pacific.
Claimed by both France and Mexico; Mexico established a small military colony there in 1905.
During the Mexican Revolution the colony was largely abandoned after most colonists died and a lighthouse keeper briefly ruled the island as self-declared king.
p1159105057: A remote volcanic island of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands in the southern Indian Ocean.
The northernmost volcanic island on the Antarctic Plate, home only to a small seasonal research station.
p1159105063: A small, uninhabited tropical atoll in the Mozambique Channel, claimed by both France and Madagascar.
Garrisoned by a French detachment and visited mainly by scientists studying its green sea turtle breeding grounds.
p1159105067: An isolated volcanic island in the South Atlantic, roughly midway between Africa and South America.
Part of the British Overseas Territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha.
Discovered by Portuguese navigator João da Nova in 1501 and named for Ascension Day in 1503.
Served as an important refuelling stop for ships and flying boats, and as an Allied air and naval base in World War II.
p1159105071: A rugged volcanic island in the South Atlantic, a dependency of Tristan da Cunha.
One of the most remote places with a constant human presence, home only to weather station personnel since 1956.
Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Gough and Inaccessible Islands', one of the world's most important seabird colonies.
p1159105073: An uninhabited, glacier-covered volcanic island in the South Atlantic and the world's most remote island, a Norwegian dependency since 1930.
First sighted in 1739 by French navigator Jean-Baptiste Bouvet de Lozier but not landed on reliably for nearly two centuries.
p1159105083: A remote Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, south of Java and Sumatra.
Named for its discovery on Christmas Day 1643; mined for phosphate deposits from the late 19th century.
Its geographic isolation has produced a high level of endemism among its flora and fauna.
p1159105087: A subantarctic island roughly halfway between Tasmania and Antarctica, governed as part of Tasmania since 1880.
Home to the entire royal penguin population during its nesting season, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
p1159105093: An uninhabited volcanic island in the Bellingshausen Sea, claimed as a dependency of Norway.
Nearly entirely covered by glacier and surrounded by pack ice most of the year.
First sighted in 1821 by Fabian von Bellingshausen; no one set foot on it until 1929.
p1159105101: An uninhabited rocky islet near Lord Howe Island, the eroded plug of a shield volcano formed 6.4 million years ago.
The tallest volcanic sea stack in the world, and home to the Lord Howe Island stick insect, rediscovered in 2001 after being presumed extinct.
p1159105103: A crescent-shaped volcanic remnant in the Tasman Sea between Australia and New Zealand, part of New South Wales.
Settled permanently in 1834 as a whaling provisioning port, later built an economy on exporting endemic kentia palms.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, with the uninhabited volcanic spire Ball's Pyramid nearby.
p1159105105: A remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic Ocean, west of Africa and east of Brazil.
Served as a key stopover for ships rounding Africa before the Suez Canal opened in 1869.
Site of Napoleon Bonaparte's second exile, from 1815 until his death in 1821.
p1159105151: A tiny, uninhabitable granite islet in the North Atlantic, far from any coast, west of Scotland's Outer Hebrides.
Formed during the Paleogene as part of the North Atlantic Igneous Province.
Nearby waters recorded a 29-metre wave in 2006, among the largest ever measured in the open ocean.
p1159105153: An island off Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula in the Caribbean Sea, near Playa del Carmen.
Designated a Pueblo Mágico by the Mexican government in 2023 for its cultural and historical importance.
p1159105165: A rocky headland on South Africa's Cape Peninsula, often mistaken for Africa's southernmost point, which is actually Cape Agulhas further east.
First rounded by Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias in 1487, opening a sea route to the Far East.
Marks where ships begin travelling more eastward than southward along Africa's coast, making it a key waypoint on old trade routes.
p1159105171: A peninsula in Senegal and the westernmost point of the African mainland.
Home to Dakar, Senegal's capital, which occupies its southern tip.
p1159105173: A peninsula in far northeastern Tunisia, known in antiquity as the Cape of Mercury.
e1159105269: The highest peak in Morocco, the Atlas Mountains, North Africa and the Arab world.
Visible from Marrakesh, about 63 km to the north.
The highest peak for over 2,000 km in any direction.
e1159105283: The highest mountain in Ethiopia, located within Simien Mountains National Park.
e1159105297: The second-highest mountain in Africa and the namesake of Kenya, just south of the equator.
A volcano whose ice cap has eroded heavily since formation, leaving radiating valleys and rapidly shrinking glaciers that may vanish by 2050.
Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997 for its ecological significance.
e1159105301: A dormant stratovolcano in Tanzania and the highest mountain in Africa, as well as the tallest free-standing mountain in the world.
First climbed to its highest point, Uhuru Peak, in 1889 by German geographer Hans Meyer.
Formed by volcanic activity linked to the East African Rift, it carries Africa's largest glaciers, which have lost over 80% of their ice in the past century.
e1159105349: An active stratovolcano in Cameroon, the highest point in sub-Saharan western and central Africa.
Part of the Cameroon Volcanic Line, which also includes Lake Nyos, site of a deadly 1986 gas disaster.
Erupted most recently in 2012, with an earlier 1909 eruption forcing German colonial authorities to relocate temporarily to Douala.
e1159105397: The southernmost active volcano on Earth, on Ross Island in Antarctica's Ross Dependency.
Named by Captain James Clark Ross in 1841 after his ship, HMS Erebus.
Has had a persistent lava lake in its summit crater since at least the early 1970s.
e1159105413: Largest mountain massif in Antarctica, within the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains.
Contains Mount Vinson, Antarctica's highest peak at 4,892 m, first climbed in 1966.
Named after US congressman Carl Vinson for his support of Antarctic exploration.
e1159105501: The highest mountain on the Indochinese peninsula, nicknamed "the Roof of Indochina", in Vietnam's Hoang Lien Son range.
e1159105613: Taiwan's highest mountain, giving the island the fourth-highest high point of any island in the world.
Protected within Yushan National Park, Taiwan's largest and least accessible national park.
Known during Japanese colonial rule as Mount Niitaka.
e1159105621: Japan's most active volcano, a former island now connected to Kyushu as a peninsula.
Its fertile volcanic soil produces the famous Sakurajima daikon radish and komikan orange.
e1159105623: An active stratovolcano on Honshu and the highest mountain in Japan, visible from Tokyo on clear days.
Last erupted in 1707-1708 and is revered as one of Japan's Three Holy Mountains.
A UNESCO World Heritage cultural site since 2013, long inspiring Japanese art, poetry and pilgrimage.
e1159105637: An active stratovolcano near Russia's Bering Sea coast, the highest mountain in Siberia and the highest active volcano in Eurasia.
Part of the Volcanoes of Kamchatka UNESCO World Heritage Site, almost continuously active since its first recorded eruption in 1697.
e1159105649: Highest peak in Iran and Western Asia, a dormant stratovolcano in the Alborz range.
Holds special significance in Persian mythology and folklore.
Part of the Volcanic Seven Summits mountaineering challenge.
e1159105691: The highest mountain in Tajikistan and in the former Soviet Union, located in the Pamir Range.
Named after Ismail Samani, a ruler of the medieval Samanid Empire.
e1159105701: A sacred Buddhist site in Shanxi Province, China, surrounded by flat-topped peaks.
Home to over 53 monasteries and temples, making it one of China's most important Buddhist sites.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009.
e1159105705: The seventh-highest mountain in the world and the highest point located entirely within one country, Nepal.
First climbed in 1960 by a Swiss-Austrian-Nepali expedition.
Separated from neighboring Annapurna by the Kali Gandaki Gorge, the world's deepest gorge.
e1159105709: The highest peak of the Altai Mountains, on the border of Russia and Kazakhstan.
Part of the Golden Mountains of Altai UNESCO World Heritage Site.
e1159105715: The highest mountain on Earth above sea level, lying in the Himalayas on the China-Nepal border at its summit.
Known as Sagarmatha in Nepali and Chomolangma in Tibetan.
Climbed via two main routes, from the southeast in Nepal or from the north in China; hundreds of climbers have died on its slopes.
Many bodies remain on the mountain because retrieving them is too dangerous.
e1159105721: A fault-bounded trough in China's Xinjiang region, home to Lake Ayding, among the lowest depressions on Earth.
One of the hottest and driest places in China during summer.
e1159105729: The second-highest mountain on Earth after Everest, straddling the Pakistan-China border in the Karakoram range.
Nicknamed the 'Savage Mountain' for its brutal difficulty; historically about one climber died for every four who reached the summit.
First summited in 1954 by Italian climbers Lino Lacedelli and Achille Compagnoni.
e1159105733: A mountain in Tibet near the source of four major rivers: the Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra and Ghaghara.
Considered sacred in Bon, Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism, drawing pilgrims who circle the mountain on foot.
Has never been successfully climbed, and ascent is prohibited by China due to its religious significance.
e1159105751: The highest peak of the Hindu Kush range and the highest mountain outside the Himalaya-Karakoram system, in Pakistan's Chitral District.
e1159105775: The highest mountain in the Tian Shan range, on the border of Kyrgyzstan and China.
Part of the Kakshaal Too, the highest section of the Tian Shan, southeast of Lake Issyk-Kul.
e1159105787: An active stratovolcano on the China-North Korea border, the tallest mountain in both North Korea and Northeast China.
Its caldera holds Heaven Lake, source of the Songhua, Tumen and Yalu rivers.
Considered the mythical ancestral homeland of Korean and Manchu peoples; depicted on North Korea's national emblem.
A 946 AD eruption here was among the most powerful on Earth in the last 5,000 years.
e1159105789: The highest mountain in Afghanistan, on the border with Pakistan in the Hindu Kush range.
The westernmost 7,000 m peak in the world, accessible mainly from the Wakhan District of Afghanistan.
e1159105791: The ninth-highest mountain on Earth, the westernmost major peak of the Himalayas in Pakistan.
One of the 14 eight-thousanders, nicknamed "Killer Mountain" for its high number of climbing fatalities.
The fastest-growing mountain in the world, rising about 7 mm per year.
e1159105799: A dormant compound volcano in easternmost Turkey, consisting of Greater and Little Ararat.
Identified since the Middle Ages with the biblical resting place of Noah's Ark.
The principal national symbol of Armenia, depicted on its coat of arms, though located outside Armenia's borders.
e1159105823: The third-highest mountain in the world, straddling the border of Nepal and India's Sikkim state.
Was long thought to be the world's highest peak until surveys in 1849 showed Everest was taller.
First climbed in 1955 by a team that stopped short of the true summit out of respect for its sacred status.
e1159105847: A shield volcano that makes up much of South Korea's Jeju Island, the country's highest point.
Protected within Hallasan National Park and considered one of South Korea's three main mountains, along with Jirisan and Seoraksan.
e1159105855: The highest point in Georgia, on the Georgia-Russia border in the Greater Caucasus range.
The third-highest peak in the Caucasus, behind Dykh-Tau and standing southeast of Mount Elbrus, Europe's highest mountain.
e1159105865: The highest mountain in Bhutan and the highest unclimbed mountain in the world.
Its name means 'White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers' in Dzongkha.
Mountaineering has been entirely banned in Bhutan since 2003.
e1159105881: A peak in the Greater Caucasus on the border between Azerbaijan and Russia's Dagestan region.
The highest point in both Azerbaijan and Dagestan.
Its name means 'turn to the market, bazaar', recalling medieval multinational fairs once held nearby in the Shahnabad Valley.
e1159105889: An isolated four-peaked volcano massif in Armenia, whose northern summit is the highest point in the country and the Lesser Caucasus.
Covers about a fifth of Armenia's total land area.
e1159105901: The highest peak in the High Tatras, Slovakia and the entire Carpathian Mountains.
Has had four different names amid 20th-century geopolitical changes affecting Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Slovakia.
Rises about 2,000 m above the valley floor.
e1159105915: The highest mountain in the Pyrenees and Spain's third-highest peak.
Its northern side holds the largest glacier in the Pyrenees, which has lost more than half its surface in the last 100 years and may disappear by 2050.
e1159105919: The highest mountain on the Iberian Peninsula, part of the Sierra Nevada range in Spain's Penibaetic System.
Named after Abu'l-Hasan Ali, the penultimate Muslim ruler of Granada, said to be buried at its summit.
The highest peak in Southern Europe outside the Alps, climbable in a single day without major technical difficulty.
e1159105927: The highest peak in the Southern Ural Mountains, within Russia's South Ural Nature Reserve.
Rumoured by US officials to house a large secret underground bunker complex.
e1159105929: A near-symmetric pyramidal peak of the Pennine Alps straddling the border between Switzerland and Italy.
Often called the 'Mountain of Mountains' and considered among the most photographed mountains in the world.
Overlooks the Swiss resort town of Zermatt to the northeast and Italy's Breuil-Cervinia to the south.
e1159105931: Sweden's highest mountain, in the Scandinavian range in Swedish Lapland north of the Arctic Circle.
Has two main peaks; the glaciated southern peak, once the taller, has shrunk enough that the icefree northern peak is now highest.
Lies near the Kungsleden hiking trail between Abisko and Hemavan.
e1159105935: The highest mountain in Norway, Scandinavia and Northern Europe, located in Jotunheimen National Park.
e1159105939: Highest peak in Bulgaria, the Rila Mountains and the entire Balkan Peninsula.
Within Rila National Park, one of the easiest places in Europe to see the wallcreeper bird.
A cosmic ray research station was built on its summit in 1960.
e1159105943: Romania's highest mountain peak, in the Făgăraș Mountains of the Southern Carpathians.
Had a distant star named after it, XO-1, in 2019.
e1159105945: The highest mountain in Austria and in the Alps east of the Brenner Pass.
Its pyramid-shaped summit consists of two pinnacles, the Großglockner and Kleinglockner.
The Pasterze, Austria's longest glacier, lies on its eastern slope.
e1159105949: The highest mountain in the Alps and in Europe outside the Caucasus, straddling the France-Italy border.
Ownership of its summit has long been disputed between France and Italy.
The 11.6 km Mont Blanc Tunnel beneath it, built between 1957 and 1965, is a major transalpine transport route.
e1159105953: The highest mountain in Russia and in Europe, a dormant twin-summited stratovolcano in the Caucasus.
Its eastern summit was first climbed in 1829 and the higher western summit in 1874 by a British-led expedition.
e1159105955: The highest mountain in Germany, in the Wetterstein Mountains, with the Austria-Germany border running across its western summit.
Home to Germany's largest glaciers, the Northern Schneeferner and Höllentalferner.
First climbed in 1820 by Josef Naus and companions; today reached via three main routes including the Jubilee Ridge.
e1159105957: The highest point in the European part of the Netherlands, in the province of Limburg near the town of Vaals.
Lost its status as the Netherlands' overall highest point in 2010, when the volcanic Caribbean island of Saba was incorporated as a special municipality.
e1159105963: Slovenia's highest mountain and the highest peak of the Julian Alps.
The pre-eminent national symbol, appearing on Slovenia's coat of arms and flag.
Was also the highest peak in Yugoslavia before Slovenia's 1991 independence.
e1159105965: The highest peak in Estonia and the Baltic states, located in the gently hilly Haanja Upland near the Latvian and Russian borders.
e1159105967: A mountain on the Czech Republic-Poland border, the highest point in the Czech Republic and in the entire Sudetes range.
The most prominent point of the Silesian Ridge within the Giant Mountains.
e1159105983: The highest point in San Marino, part of the Apennines, with the capital city straddling its ridge.
Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008 together with San Marino's historic centre.
Legend holds a small monastery stood on the mountain as early as the 8th century.
e1159105985: A mountain massif on the Italy-Switzerland border in the Pennine Alps.
Its main summit, the Dufourspitze, is the second-highest peak in the Alps and western Europe, after Mont Blanc.
Its northwestern face holds one of the largest Alpine glaciers, near Zermatt.
e1159106007: Hungary's highest mountain, in the Mátra range.
The country's third most popular tourist attraction after Lake Balaton and the Danube, with skiing pistes and a TV tower at its summit.
e1159106011: A fell straddling the Norway-Finland border, whose Finnish side is the highest point in Finland.
The actual summit lies in Norway, just north of the border, due to a 1734 Swedish-Danish border treaty defined by natural features.
Ridnitšohkka, nearby, is the highest peak located entirely within Finland.
e1159106019: The highest mountain in Ukraine, part of the Ukrainian Carpathians in the Chornohora region.
Its slopes hold beech and spruce forest below alpine meadows, and it is the source of the Prut River.
Became a popular tourist and extreme-sports destination from the late 19th century onward.
e1159106027: A mountain massif in northwestern Montenegro, part of the Dinaric Alps, bounded by the Tara and Piva river canyons.
Its national park, founded in 1952, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.
e1159106029: A 100-km mountain range in the Dinaric Alps on the Bosnia-Croatia border, composed of limestone and dolomite.
Its peak Sinjal/Dinara gives the whole Dinaric Alps their name; Troglav is the range's actual highest point.
e1159106091: One of Mexico and North America's most active volcanoes, part of the Colima Volcanic Complex.
Has erupted more than 40 times since 1576, with one of its largest eruptions in 1913.
Most of its surface actually lies in Jalisco state rather than Colima, despite its name.
e1159106093: The highest volcano in North America and Mexico's tallest peak, on the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt.
Currently dormant, with its last eruption in the 19th century; the second most topographically prominent volcano on Earth after Kilimanjaro.
e1159106177: The highest mountain in Canada and the second-highest in North America after Denali, in Yukon's Kluane National Park.
Believed to have the largest base circumference of any non-volcanic mountain on Earth.
Still slowly rising due to ongoing tectonic uplift.
e1159106291: A desert valley in eastern California's northern Mojave Desert, recorded as the hottest surface location on Earth.
Furnace Creek within the valley holds the highest reliably recorded air temperature on the planet, 54.4°C in 2020 and 2021.
Forms the principal feature of the Mojave and Colorado Deserts Biosphere Reserve.
e1159106297: The highest mountain peak in North America, in Alaska's Alaska Range, with one of the greatest vertical rises above surrounding terrain on Earth.
Long known as Denali by the Koyukon people before being renamed Mount McKinley in 1896; the US federal name has since switched between Denali and McKinley.
First verifiably summited in 1913 by Hudson Stuck, Harry Karstens, Walter Harper and Robert Tatum.
e1159106313: The highest point in the contiguous United States, in California's Sierra Nevada range.
Its summit is the southern terminus of the 211-mile John Muir Trail from Yosemite Valley.
e1159106339: An active stratovolcano in Washington's Cascade Range, the highest mountain in that state.
Considered one of the world's most dangerous volcanoes due to its eruption potential and proximity to Seattle.
Its glacial ice could trigger massive lahars threatening river valleys home to about 80,000 people.
e1159106509: A stratovolcano in Colombia, the highest point in both the Caldas and Tolima departments.
Its 1985 eruption triggered a lahar that destroyed the town of Armero, killing an estimated 25,000 people, the deadliest lahar on record.
Melting of its summit glaciers during eruptions continues to pose a lahar risk to nearby towns.
e1159106519: The highest of the Pacaraima chain of flat-topped tepuis, at the junction of Brazil, Guyana and Venezuela.
Surrounded by cliffs 400-1,000 m high, home to much endemic flora and fauna due to its isolation.
First climbed by a British expedition in 1884.
e1159106545: The highest volcano on Earth, a dormant complex volcano on the Argentina-Chile border and the highest peak in Chile.
Hosts the highest lake of any kind in the world, a crater lake near its summit despite the mountain's extreme aridity.
Was debated for decades as a rival to Aconcagua for South America's highest peak, a question settled in Aconcagua's favor.
e1159106633: A stratovolcano on Norway's remote island of Jan Mayen, the world's northernmost active subaerial volcano.
The only active volcano in Norway, topped by a largely ice-filled crater about 1 km wide.
e1159106673: A large sandstone monolith near the centre of Australia's Northern Territory, also known as Ayers Rock.
Sacred to the Pitjantjatjara Aboriginal people, with surrounding springs, waterholes and ancient rock paintings.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Australia's most recognisable natural landmarks.
e1159106753: The highest mountain on mainland Australia, located on the Main Range of the Snowy Mountains in New South Wales.
Named after the Polish national hero Tadeusz Kościuszko.
Lies within Kościuszko National Park, part of the Australian Alps National Parks and Reserves.
e1159106815: The highest mountain in Scotland, the United Kingdom and the British Isles, at the western end of the Grampian Mountains near Fort William.
Its 700-metre cliffs on the north face offer some of Scotland's premier rock and ice climbing.
Has hosted a foot race to its summit since 1898 and was home to a staffed weather observatory from 1883 to 1904.
e1159106827: The highest mountain in Wales and in the British Isles south of the Scottish Highlands.
Shaped by Ordovician-period volcanic rock and extensively sculpted by glaciation.
Among the busiest mountains in the UK, climbed by over 540,000 walkers in 2022; also reachable by the Snowdon Mountain Railway.
e1159106835: The highest mountain in Ireland, on the Iveragh Peninsula at the center of the MacGillycuddy's Reeks range.
Composed mainly of sandstone, with glacially carved features like the Eagle's Nest corrie popular with climbers.
Most commonly climbed via the Devil's Ladder route; access is by landowner permission, as it lies outside any national park.
e1159107023: Iceland's highest point, a pyramidal peak on the rim of the Öræfajökull volcano's summit crater.
e1159107181: The highest mountain in Malaysia and in Maritime Southeast Asia, on the island of Borneo in Sabah.
Protected within Kinabalu Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for exceptional biodiversity, including Rafflesia plants and orangutans.
A 1997 satellite resurvey of its summit, Low's Peak, found it slightly lower than previously published.
e1159107205: An active stratovolcano on Sumbawa in Indonesia's Lesser Sunda Islands.
Its 1815 eruption was the largest in recorded history, ejecting up to 150 cubic kilometres of material at VEI-7.
The resulting global cooling caused 1816 to become known as the 'Year Without a Summer'.
e1159107215: The highest mountain on Java and an active volcano in a subduction zone where the Indo-Australian Plate meets the Eurasian Plate.
Named after Mount Meru (Sumeru), the central mountain of the gods in Hindu cosmology.
e1159107245: A volcanic caldera in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra, formed after the catastrophic 1883 eruption destroyed most of the original island.
A new island, Anak Krakatoa ('Child of Krakatoa'), emerged from the caldera in 1927 and later caused the deadly 2018 Sunda Strait tsunami after a partial collapse.
e1159107269: The highest mountain in Sumatra and an active stratovolcano, within Kerinci Seblat National Park.
Home to the endangered Sumatran tiger amid its surrounding rainforest.
e1159107313: An active stratovolcano in the Philippines whose 1991 eruption was the second-largest terrestrial eruption of the 20th century.
Cooled global temperatures by about 0.5°C for several years by injecting huge amounts of ash and sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere.
Timely evacuation ahead of the eruption, which coincided with a typhoon, saved tens of thousands of lives.
e1159107349: An active stratovolcano on Lombok, Indonesia's second-highest volcano, holding the crater lake Sagara Anak.
Sacred to the indigenous Sasak people, who hold ceremonies at the mountain and its lake.
Its 1257 eruption is considered one of the most powerful volcanic events of the last 2,000 years.
e1159107539: Highest mountain peak of any island on Earth, located in Indonesia's Sudirman Range on New Guinea.
One of the Seven Summits, with an elevation exceeding the highest peaks of Papua New Guinea, New Zealand and Australia.
Ranked 5th in the world by topographic isolation.
e1159107729: Highest mountain in New Zealand, in the Southern Alps of the South Island.
Consists of three summits: the Low Peak, Middle Peak and High Peak.
Ranked 10th in the world by topographic isolation.
e1159107739: An active stratovolcano and the largest active volcano in New Zealand, within Tongariro National Park.
Home to the North Island's major ski resorts and only glaciers, with a crater lake between its three peaks.
e1159107857: An active stratovolcano on Tenerife in the Canary Islands and the highest point in Spain.
Measured from the ocean floor, it is the third-tallest volcanic structure on Earth.
Began forming about 170,000 years ago after a catastrophic landslide; last erupted in 1909.
Its national park is the most visited in Spain and Europe, and hosts the Teide astronomical Observatory.
e1159107911: A dormant shield volcano on the island of Hawaii, the highest point in Hawaii, about 38 m taller than its massive neighbour Mauna Loa.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, it rises more than Everest's height above sea level, leading some to call it the tallest mountain in the world.
About one million years old, it has passed its most active shield-building stage and now erupts thicker, more viscous lava.
e1159108379: An active stratovolcano at the northern end of Martinique in the Lesser Antilles.
Its 1902 eruption destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre, killing around 29,000-30,000 people in the worst volcanic disaster of the 20th century.
Became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
e1159108555: A dormant stratovolcano on the Argentina-Chile border in the Puna de Atacama, the second-highest active volcano in the world.
Site of the highest-known archaeological location on Earth; the mummified 'Children of Llullaillaco' were found at its summit in 1999, believed to be human sacrifices.
e1159108575: An extinct volcano in Bolivia's Oruro Department, the country's highest peak.
A composite volcano built from a stratovolcano atop several lava domes, within Sajama National Park.
Covered by an ice cap, with Polylepis tarapacana trees growing on its slopes up to 5,000 m.
e1159108665: A mountain in Peru's Cordillera Blanca, whose southern summit is the highest point in Peru and in the entire tropics.
The fourth-highest peak in South America, after Aconcagua, Ojos del Salado and Monte Pissis.
e1159108681: An active stratovolcano in Colombia near the city of Pasto, currently the country's most active volcano.
A 1993 eruption killed nine people, including six scientists studying the crater to help predict future eruptions.
e1159108689: A stratovolcano in Ecuador's Cordillera Occidental, part of the Andes, last known to have erupted around AD 550.
Ecuador's highest mountain, though well below Everest's elevation above sea level.
Due to Earth's equatorial bulge, its summit is the point on the planet's surface farthest from the Earth's center.
e1159108707: The highest mountain in Venezuela, named after independence hero Simón Bolívar, reachable only on foot.
The Mérida cable car, once the world's highest and longest, reaches a neighboring peak from which climbers continue to the summit.
e1159108719: The highest mountain outside Asia, located in Argentina's Andes, and one of the Seven Summits.
Formed by subduction of the Nazca Plate and was once an active stratovolcano before activity stopped in the Miocene.
First climbed in 1897, it is technically straightforward but its extreme altitude earns it the nickname "Mountain of Death."
l1159106721: Largest lake entirely within Canada and the eighth-largest in the world, on the Arctic Circle in the Northwest Territories.
Named for the Sahtu Dene people, whose name means 'grizzly bear-water people'.
Drains via the Great Bear River into the Mackenzie River.
l1159106729: A lake in Canada's Northwest Territories, the deepest lake in North America at 614 m.
Shares its name with the Dene people, called "Slavey" by their Cree rivals.
The territorial capital Yellowknife sits on its shore.
l1159106747: 12th largest lake on Earth and Canada's sixth-largest freshwater lake, north of the city of Winnipeg.
Its eastern shore's boreal forests were inscribed as the Pimachiowin Aki UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018.
Used by Manitoba Hydro as one of the world's largest hydroelectric reservoirs.
l1159106757: The shallowest and southernmost of the Great Lakes, with its deepest point still above sea level.
Shared by Ontario and the US states of Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and New York.
Cleveland is its largest city; the Detroit River is its primary inlet and the Niagara River its outflow.
l1159106765: The last and easternmost of the Great Lakes, draining into the Atlantic via the St. Lawrence River.
Shared between the Canadian province of Ontario and the US state of New York.
Its primary inlet is the Niagara River, flowing from Lake Erie.
l1159106775: A freshwater lake between Ontario and Michigan, linking Lake Huron to Lake Erie via the St. Clair and Detroit rivers.
Not one of the five Great Lakes, but part of the connected Great Lakes system; a maintained shipping channel keeps it navigable despite its shallow depth.
l1159106781: The largest freshwater lake entirely within the contiguous United States (excluding the connected Great Lakes), in Florida.
Exceptionally shallow for its size, averaging just 9 feet deep, fed primarily by the Kissimmee River.
Its center is the only point in the US where more than four counties meet.
l1159106791: The largest freshwater lake in Central America, of tectonic origin, located in Nicaragua.
Was long considered as a route for an interoceanic canal before the Panama Canal was built instead.
Historically raided by Caribbean pirates who attacked the lakeside city of Granada.
l1159106825: A lake spanning Ontario and Manitoba, Canada, and Minnesota, USA, containing over 14,552 islands.
The sixth-largest freshwater lake partly within the United States, separating Minnesota's Northwest Angle from the rest of the country.
Provides nesting habitat for piping plovers and American white pelicans.
l1159106833: The largest lake entirely within Ontario, Canada, part of the Great Lakes drainage basin.
Drains into Lake Superior via the Nipigon River.
l1159106843: A lake in the Canadian province of Manitoba, northwest of the capital Winnipeg, among the world's 35 largest lakes.
l1159106851: Canada's eleventh-largest lake, in Manitoba about 300 km northwest of Winnipeg.
Its name is a diminutive of Lake Winnipeg, meaning 'little muddy waters.'
l1159106863: Straddles the Saskatchewan-Alberta border in northern Canada, mostly within Saskatchewan.
Fed by the Athabasca River, with its outflow continuing north via the Slave and Mackenzie rivers to the Arctic Ocean.
l1159106907: The largest alpine lake in North America, straddling the California-Nevada border in the Sierra Nevada.
Known for its exceptionally clear water; its depth of about 501 m makes it the second-deepest lake in the US after Crater Lake.
l1159106925: A cold freshwater lake toward the south of Baffin Island, Nunavut, the world's largest lake situated on an island.
The largest lake in Nunavut, fed by Amadjuak Lake and draining west into Foxe Basin via the shallow Koukdjuak River.
Home to ringed seals and three recorded fish species, with surrounding tundra important for caribou calving.
l1159106953: A large freshwater lake lying mostly between New York and Vermont, extending north into Quebec.
Nicknamed 'The Sixth Great Lake' for its connections to the St. Lawrence Seaway and the Hudson River via canal.
Historic Fort Ticonderoga lies near its southern end.
l1159107241: Guatemala's largest lake, draining to the Caribbean via the Rio Dulce.
Guarded historically by the colonial fortress Castillo de San Felipe de Lara against pirate attacks.
Home to manatees, jaguars and howler monkeys, making it a popular birdwatching destination.
l1159107251: Mexico's largest freshwater lake since Lake Texcoco dried up in the early 17th century.
Straddles the states of Jalisco and Michoacán.
l1159107259: A freshwater lake in Nicaragua, also called Lake Xolotlán, on whose southwestern shore the capital Managua sits.
l1159112991: Largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area, and the northernmost and highest of the Great Lakes.
Straddles the Canada-US border, bounded by Ontario, Minnesota, Michigan and Wisconsin.
Drains into Lake Huron via the St. Marys River, eventually reaching the Atlantic via the St. Lawrence River.
l1159113005: One of the five Great Lakes, the only one located entirely within the United States.
Hydrologically joined to Lake Huron via the Straits of Mackinac, together forming the world's largest freshwater lake by area.
Major port cities on its shores include Chicago and Milwaukee.
l1159113021: One of the five Great Lakes of North America, shared by Ontario, Canada, and Michigan, USA.
Hydrologically one body of water with Lake Michigan, together forming the largest freshwater lake by area in the world.
Water flows through it faster than any other Great Lake, with a retention time of just 22 years.
l1159113095: A freshwater lake in northwestern Russia near Saint Petersburg, the largest lake located entirely in Europe.
A methane lake on Saturn's moon Titan, Ladoga Lacus, is named after it.
l1159113111: A lake in southeastern Kazakhstan fed mainly by the Ili River within a closed desert basin.
One of the largest lakes in Asia, but shrinking due to water diversion, much like the Aral Sea.
Split by a narrow strait into a freshwater western half and a saline eastern half.
l1159113127: A rift lake in southern Siberia, Russia, and the deepest lake in the world at 1,642 m.
Holds about 22-23% of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water, more than all the Great Lakes combined.
The world's oldest lake at 25-30 million years, home to many species found nowhere else.
Declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
l1159113145: A lake shared by Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Africa's sixth-largest lake.
The second-largest of Uganda's Great Lakes, once renamed Lake Mobutu Sese Seko under Congo's former dictator.
l1159113163: An African Great Lake and the southernmost in the East African Rift system, shared by Malawi, Mozambique and Tanzania.
Home to more fish species than any other lake in the world, including over 700 cichlid species.
A meromictic lake, meaning its water layers remain permanently stratified rather than mixing.
l1159113185: The world's longest freshwater lake and second-deepest after Lake Baikal, shared by Tanzania, the DRC, Burundi and Zambia.
Drains via the Lukuga and Congo rivers into the Atlantic Ocean.
l1159113191: Africa's largest lake by area and the world's largest tropical lake, shared by Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya.
Home to many fish species found nowhere else, especially cichlids, though invasive Nile perch have driven some to extinction.
l1159113219: An endorheic freshwater lake at the junction of Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon.
Shrank dramatically from 25,000 km2 in 1960 to just 2,000 km2 by 1980 due to climate change and water diversion.
A vital wetland ecosystem and freshwater fishery for West-Central Africa.
l1159113235: Sweden's largest lake and the largest in the European Union, draining to the Kattegat via the Göta älv.
Linked to Lake Vättern and the east coast by the 19th-century Göta Canal.
l1159113251: Europe's second-largest lake after Lake Ladoga, located in northwestern Russia.
Home to Kizhi Island's wooden church complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and ancient rock petroglyphs on its eastern shores.
l1159113265: Ethiopia's largest lake and the source of the Blue Nile, in the northwestern Ethiopian Highlands.
Fed by the Gilgel Abay, Reb and Gumara rivers, and regulated by a weir controlling flow to the Blue Nile Falls and a hydropower station.
l1159113279: A high-altitude lake in the Andes on the border of Peru and Bolivia, often called the world's highest navigable lake.
South America's largest lake by both volume and surface area, with slightly brackish water.
l1159113295: Finland's largest lake and the fourth-largest natural freshwater lake in Europe, located in the Finnish Lakeland.
l1159113323: A deep glacial lake in Patagonia shared by Chile and Argentina, known as Lake Buenos Aires on the Argentine side.

Enjoys an unusually sunny microclimate compared to the generally cold, humid surrounding region.
l1159113343: Chile's second-largest lake, in the Los Lagos Region, shaped by glaciers during the Quaternary ice ages.
Offers views of Volcán Osorno, making nearby Puerto Varas a popular tourist town.
l1159113373: The largest freshwater lake in Mongolia by volume, nicknamed 'Mother Sea'.
Second-largest lake in the country by area, after Uvs Lake.
l1159113395: The second largest lake in Finland, draining into the Gulf of Finland via the Kymi River.
An underground aqueduct, the Päijänne Water Tunnel, supplies drinking water to the Greater Helsinki area.
Jyväskylä is the largest city on its shores.
l1159113405: A freshwater lake on the Congo River's longest arm, on the border between Zambia and the DRC.
Lies between the river's Luapula and Luvua segments; its name simply means "lake" in several Bantu languages.
l1159113423: A freshwater lake on the border between Russia's Primorsky Krai and China's Heilongjiang province.
l1159113439: The largest freshwater lake in Southeast Asia, part of the Mekong river system in central Cambodia.
Designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve for its exceptional biodiversity.
Its water level swings dramatically with the seasons, rising up to 10 m higher after the monsoon.
l1159113513: Also called Dalai Lake, a large lake in China's Inner Mongolia region.
One of the largest lakes in China, lying amid the grasslands of Inner Mongolia near the Mongolian border.
l1159113531: A freshwater lake in northern Zambia whose name means "where the water meets the sky", surrounded by vast wetlands.
Sits in the upper Congo River basin; its largest tributary, the Chambeshi, is the ultimate source of the Congo River.
l1159113545: The largest lake in Sápmi and the third-largest in Finland, north of the Arctic Circle in Lapland.

Drains northward through the Paatsjoki into the Barents Sea.
l1159113563: The largest trans-boundary lake in Europe, lying on the Estonia-Russia border.
Fifth-largest lake in Europe, after Ladoga, Onega, Vänern and Saimaa.
Comprises three connected basins: Lake Peipus, Lake Pskov and the Warm Lake channel between them.
l1159113577: One of the African Great Lakes, lying in the Albertine Rift between the DR Congo and Rwanda.
One of only three lakes known to undergo limnic eruptions, releasing dissolved carbon dioxide from its depths.
Volcanic activity about 10,000 years ago reversed its drainage, cutting it off from the Nile watershed.
l1159113595: One of the smaller African Great Lakes, located in the Albertine Rift on the border between the DR Congo and Uganda, just south of the equator.
Connects to Lake George to its north and drains south into Lake Albert via the Semliki River.
l1159113611: The third-largest freshwater lake entirely within China, in the Yangtze Delta.
Contains about 90 islands and is linked to the Grand Canal.
Surrounded by the major cities of Suzhou, Wuxi, Changzhou and Huzhou.
l1159113621: Argentina's largest freshwater lake, in Patagonia within Los Glaciares National Park.
Fed by meltwater from glaciers including the Upsala and Perito Moreno glaciers, which carve 'trenches' into the lakebed where they meet the water.
Drains to the Atlantic Ocean via the Santa Cruz River.
l1159113637: A mountain lake on the Tibetan Plateau north of the Nyenchen Tanglha range, also called 'Heavenly Lake'.
l1159113927: The largest lake in China's Xinjiang region, fed mainly by the Kaidu River.
Supports an active fishery, with introduced carp species and European perch dominating catches since the 1970s.
l1159114015: The largest freshwater lake in China, in Jiangxi Province, draining into the Yangtze River.
Its area fluctuates dramatically by season and has shrunk overall in recent years due to drought and dam operations.
Winters host up to 90% of the world's critically endangered Siberian cranes.
l1159114143: A deep lake on the north side of the Alps shared between Switzerland and France, the largest on the Rhône's course.
About 60% of the lake belongs to Switzerland and 40% to France.
l1159114155: The largest lake on the island of Ireland and in the British Isles.
Supplies about 40.7% of Northern Ireland's drinking water.
Has suffered pollution from blue-green algae blooms since 2023.
l1159114173: Sweden's second-largest lake after Vänern, and the sixth-largest in Europe.
Relatively deep for its size, connected since 1832 via the Göta Canal to Vänern and onward to the Atlantic.
l1159114189: A lake on Russia's Taymyr Peninsula, lying south of the Byrranga Mountains.
One of the largest lakes north of the Arctic Circle, frozen for most of the year and drained by the Taymyra River.
l1159114237: The fifth largest lake in Sweden and the largest in the central region, in Jämtland County.
Home to Storsjöodjuret, a legendary lake monster similar to the Loch Ness Monster.
The city of Östersund sits on its eastern shore.
l1159114259: Lies on the Rhine at the meeting point of Germany, Switzerland and Austria.
Comprises Upper and Lower Lake Constance connected by the Seerhein stretch of the Rhine.
The exact location of the three countries' borders within the lake remains disputed.
l1159114279: A large, shallow lake in Uganda through which the Victoria Nile flows between Lake Victoria and Lake Albert.
Part of the African Great Lakes system, though not itself classed as one of the great lakes.
Much of its shallow water is covered by water lilies, papyrus and invasive water hyacinth, forming floating islands.
l1159114299: An endorheic lake in southwestern Tanzania's Rukwa Valley.
The third largest inland body of water in the country.
l1159114361: A lake in North Sumatra, Indonesia, filling the caldera of the Toba supervolcano and the largest volcanic lake in the world.

The eruption's possible global climate effects are the basis of the contested Toba catastrophe theory of human population decline.
l1159114391: Sweden's fourth-largest lake, draining through Lake Mälaren to the Baltic Sea near Stockholm.
Rebel leader Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson was assassinated on an islet in the lake in 1436.
l1159114537: A saltwater lake in Tibet, lying just west of Lake Manasarovar and south of Mount Kailash.
Sits at a lower elevation than nearby Lake Manasarovar, with the Sutlej River's source nearby.
l1159114553: A high-altitude freshwater lake near Mount Kailash in Tibet, at about 4,600 m elevation.
Sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and the Bon religion, drawing pilgrims who trek to it and circle nearby Mount Kailash.
Overflows into the adjacent salt lake Rakshastal; the sources of the Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra and Karnali rivers lie nearby.
l1159114573: A lake in northwestern Vologda Oblast, Russia, the second-largest natural lake in the region and among Europe's ten biggest.
The town of Belozersk sits on its shore.
l1159114609: The largest lake in Central Europe, located in Hungary's Transdanubian region.
Its northern shore is a historic wine region, while the flatter southern shore developed into a popular resort area.
l1159114641: A Patagonian trough lake in Argentina's Santa Cruz province, formed by melting glacial ice.
The second largest perennial lake entirely within Argentina, fed by the Viedma Glacier.
Near the town of El Chaltén and the Andes peaks Cerro Torre and Fitz-Roy.
l1159114879: A freshwater lake in northeast Israel, fed mainly by the Jordan River flowing north to south through it.
The lowest freshwater lake on Earth, lying well over 200 m below sea level.
l1159115043: The largest lake located entirely within Estonia, and the country's second-largest overall after Lake Peipus.
Drains via the Emajõgi River into Lake Peipus.
l1159115109: Armenia's largest lake and one of the largest freshwater alpine lakes in Eurasia, at nearly 1,900 m elevation.
Fed by 28 rivers and streams, with most of its water lost to evaporation rather than drainage.
Heavily exploited for irrigation and hydropower during the Soviet era, which sharply lowered its water level and turned Sevan Island into a peninsula.
l1159115429: The largest lake in Southern Europe, straddling the border of Albania and Montenegro.
A karst lake named after the Albanian city of Shkodër on its southeastern shore.
Its Montenegrin section is a national park, while the Albanian part is a protected Ramsar wetland site.
l1159115641: The largest freshwater lake in Japan, located in Shiga Prefecture near Kyoto.
An ancient lake, over 4 million years old and estimated to be the 13th oldest lake in the world.
Frequently referenced in Japanese literature and poetry due to its proximity to Kyoto.
l1159115773: A high-altitude endorheic lake split between Indian-administered Ladakh and Chinese-administered Tibet.

l1159115833: A large freshwater loch in the Scottish Highlands, famed for claimed sightings of the "Loch Ness Monster".
Lies along the Great Glen Fault and holds more water than any other lake in Great Britain.
l1159122891: Sweden's third-largest freshwater lake, after Vänern and Vättern, draining into the Baltic Sea near Stockholm.

Crossed by several bridges, including at Kvicksund and between Strängnäs and Enköping.
l1159123091: A freshwater lake in East Kazakhstan, the largest in its region, frozen from November to April.
Its shrinkage has been stabilized since it became part of the Bukhtarma Hydroelectric Power Plant's reservoir.
l1159123217: A lake on Russia's Kola Peninsula just beyond the Arctic Circle, with three interconnected basins.
Known for its clear water and abundant fish; drains via the Niva River into the White Sea.
l1159123281: A large lake in Russia's Novgorod Oblast that formed part of the medieval trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks.

Fed by 52 rivers, with the Volkhov draining it onward into Lake Ladoga and eventually the Gulf of Finland.
l1159123301: Finland's fifth-largest lake, in the Kainuu region, nicknamed the 'Kainuu Sea'.
Drained by the Oulu River, which flows northwest into the Gulf of Bothnia.
l1159124989: A former reservoir on Ukraine's Dnieper River, created in 1956 by the Kakhovka Dam.
Completely drained after the dam was breached in June 2023 during the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
l1159125013: A reservoir on the middle Volga and lower Kama rivers in Russia, the largest reservoir in Europe and third-largest in the world by area.
Created by the Zhiguli Hydroelectric Station dam, filled between 1955 and 1957.
Its filling submerged several towns, including the old fortress town of Stavropol-on-Volga, replaced by the city of Tolyatti.
l1159125055: The world's largest artificial lake and reservoir by volume, on the Zambezi River between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Filled between 1958 and 1963 after the Kariba Dam flooded the Kariba Gorge.
Displaced communities led to the growth of towns including Kariba, Siavonga and Binga.
l1159125095: A huge reservoir straddling Egypt and Sudan, created by the Aswan High Dam and named after President Gamal Abdel Nasser.

Egypt refers to its larger share as Lake Nasser, while Sudan calls its portion Lake Nubia.
l1159125149: The largest artificial reservoir in the world by surface area, formed behind the Akosombo Dam.
Generates a substantial share of Ghana's electricity and lies entirely within the country.
l1159126421: The largest saltwater lake in the Western Hemisphere, in northern Utah, a remnant of the prehistoric Lake Bonneville.
Its area fluctuates greatly with a shallow average depth of under 5 m; it fell to a record low in 2021 after years of drought and water diversion.
Fed by the Jordan, Weber and Bear rivers, which deposit about 1.1 million tons of minerals into the lake each year.
l1159126453: A shallow, highly saline endorheic lake in Southern California, lying on the San Andreas Fault.
Formed repeatedly over centuries as the Colorado River alternately flowed into or diverted around the Salton Trough, drying completely around 1580.
Became a resort destination in the 20th century before suffering fish and bird die-offs from farm runoff contamination.
l1159126631: A closed-off freshwater lake in the central Netherlands, named after the IJssel river that flows into it.
l1159126655: A saline, endorheic lake in the Tian Shan mountains of eastern Kyrgyzstan.
The eighth-deepest lake in the world, which rarely freezes despite its elevation and cold winters due to its salinity.
A Ramsar wetland site of globally significant biodiversity.
l1159126669: A saline lake in Kenya's Rift Valley, the world's largest permanent desert lake and largest alkaline lake.
Ranks fourth in the world by volume among salt lakes, after the Caspian Sea, Issyk-Kul and Lake Van.
Threatened by Ethiopia's Gilgel Gibe III Dam, which has reduced the flow of the Omo River that supplies most of its water.
l1159126693: A brackish lagoon on the Baltic Sea, split between Poland and Russia's Kaliningrad exclave.
Separated from Gdańsk Bay by the narrow Vistula Spit.
l1159126709: Mongolia's largest lake by surface area, a highly saline body of water within its own closed basin.
A remnant of a much larger saline sea that covered the region thousands of years ago.
l1159126725: Largest lake in China, an alkaline endorheic salt lake in Qinghai Province.
Shrank for much of the 20th century but has grown again since 2004.
l1159126747: A landlocked salt lake on the Jordan-Israel-West Bank border, fed mainly by the Jordan River, with shores at the lowest land elevation on Earth.

Rapidly shrinking: its surface area has fallen from 1,050 km2 in 1930 to about 605 km2 today.
l1159126761: An endorheic salt lake in Iranian Azerbaijan, once the largest lake in West Asia and the sixth-largest saltwater lake on Earth.

Nearly dried up entirely by 2025 despite temporary recoveries from rainfall and water diversion efforts.
l1159126775: The largest lake in Turkmenistan, lying roughly midway between the Caspian and Aral Seas.
Historically fed by the Uzboy River, a former Amu Darya distributary; now sustained mainly by an irrigation canal.
l1159126789: A lake in east-central Kazakhstan, part of the Dzhungarian Gate pass linking Kazakhstan to northwest China.
Its waters have been reputed to have medicinal properties since Silk Road times.
l1159126815: The second-largest lake in Turkey and one of the largest hypersaline lakes in the world, in the Central Anatolia Region.
Dried up completely in October 2021 due to climate change and unsustainable irrigation.
l1159126829: The largest lake in Turkey, a saline soda lake in the Armenian highlands.

Holds 38% of Turkey's surface water despite high salinity usually preventing it from freezing.
l1159126845: A lake in the Main Ethiopian Rift, reddish-brown from suspended sediment, with the town of Arba Minch on its shore.
Briefly renamed Lake Margherita in 1896 after the Italian queen by explorer Vittorio Bottego.
l1159126901: A crater lake in Djibouti, the lowest point on land in Africa at 155 m below sea level.
One of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth, about ten times saltier than the ocean, with salt extracted commercially from its shores.
l1159126917: A saline lake in Kazakhstan, notable as the site where the Soviet Soyuz 23 spacecraft unexpectedly splashed down through ice in 1976.
l1159127099: New Zealand's largest lake by surface area, sitting in the caldera of the Taupō supervolcano on the North Island.

l1159123579: A reservoir forming a major part of the Panama Canal, carrying ships 33 km across the Isthmus of Panama.
Created in 1913 when the Gatun Dam's spillway gates were closed.
xQ38120: One of the world's most powerful single-drop waterfalls, on the Potaro River in Guyana.
About four and a half times the height of Niagara Falls and twice the height of Victoria Falls.
xQ38519: A waterfall in the canyon of Iceland's Hvítá river, one of the country's most popular tourist attractions.
A key stop on 'Golden Circle' tours near Reykjavík.
xQ210280: Reputed to be the second most powerful waterfall in Europe after the Rhine Falls, in Iceland's Vatnajökull National Park.
